p: Polygenic traits are controlled by three or more genes, and the phenotype reflects the contribution of each allele (additive effect). They show continuous variation, like human height and skin colour. Environment also influences them.
Skin colour example with three genes A, B and C: dominant alleles A, B, C add to dark pigment. AABBCC is darkest, aabbcc lightest, and AaBbCc (three dominant alleles) is intermediate.
Pleiotropy: a single gene exhibits multiple phenotypic expressions. Usually the gene affects a metabolic pathway that contributes to different phenotypes.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an example: an inborn error of metabolism, autosomal recessive. The affected person lacks the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine. Phenylalanine accumulates and is converted into phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives.

Accumulation in the brain causes mental retardation, and these are also excreted in urine because of poor absorption by the kidney. Affected persons also show reduced hair and skin pigmentation, so one gene gives several effects (pleiotropy).

ex.q: In the three-gene model of skin colour, how many dominant alleles do AaBBCc and aaBbcc each carry? Which is darker?
st: AaBBCc: A (1) + B, B (2) + C (1) = 4 dominant alleles.
aaBbcc: B (1) = 1 dominant allele.
More dominant alleles add more pigment.
ex.a: 4 and 1; AaBBCc is darker.

topics.rl: Newborn screening programmes in several Indian states test for PKU so a special low-phenylalanine diet can prevent brain damage.

topics.t: Sex determination: XO, XY and ZW systems
topics.h: In birds, it is the mother who decides whether a chick is male or female. Biology does not follow one rule for all.
p: In 1891 Henking traced a specific nuclear structure during spermatogenesis of some insects. Half the sperms received it and half did not. He called it the X body; it was later named the X-chromosome.
Chromosomes involved in sex determination are sex chromosomes; the rest are autosomes.
XO type (e.g. grasshopper): all eggs carry an X; males have only one X besides autosomes (XO), and females have two X (XX).

XY type (e.g. Drosophila, humans): males have an X and a smaller Y (XY), females XX. Both XO and XY are examples of male heterogamety, since males produce two kinds of gametes (with or without X, or with X or Y).
ZW type (e.g. birds): females have one Z and one W (ZW) and males have two Z (ZZ). This is female heterogamety; females produce two kinds of gametes.

ex.q: In a bird species, what is the probability that a chick is female, and which parent's gamete decides it?
st: Females are ZW and produce Z eggs and W eggs in equal numbers.
Males are ZZ and produce only Z sperms.
A W egg + Z sperm gives a ZW female: probability 1/2.
ex.a: 1/2; decided by the mother's egg (female heterogamety).

topics.rl: Poultry farms in Namakkal sort chicks by sex for egg-laying units; the genetics behind the female deciding chick sex is the ZW system.

topics.t: Sex determination in humans and honey bees
topics.h: A male honey bee has a grandfather but no father, and it can have grandsons but never sons.
p: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes, the same in both sexes, and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males).

All eggs carry X. Males produce 50 per cent X-bearing and 50 per cent Y-bearing sperms. An X sperm gives a female (XX), a Y sperm a male (XY). So there is a 50 per cent probability of a male or female child in each pregnancy, and the father's sperm decides the sex. It is wrong to blame women for the sex of a child.
Honey bees show a haplodiploid system. An offspring from the union of a sperm and an egg develops as a female (queen or worker); an unfertilised egg develops as a male (drone) by parthenogenesis.

Males have half the number of chromosomes of females: females are diploid with 32 chromosomes and males haploid with 16. Males produce sperms by mitosis. Males have no father and so cannot have sons, but they have a grandfather and can have grandsons.

ex.q: Using a simple honey bee pedigree, explain why a drone has a grandfather but no father.
st: A drone develops from an unfertilised egg laid by the queen, so it has a mother but no father.
The queen herself developed from a fertilised egg, so she had a father (a drone).
That drone is the grandfather of our drone.
ex.a: A drone has a mother (queen) but no father; the queen's father is the drone's grandfather.

topics.rl: Beekeepers in Himachal Pradesh and Punjab know that drones come from unfertilised eggs; managing queen fertility is the key to a strong hive.

topics.h: A single wrong letter among millions in a gene can bend red blood cells into sickles.
p: Mutation is a phenomenon that results in alteration of DNA sequences and consequently changes the genotype and phenotype of an organism. Besides recombination, mutation is a source of variation.
Loss (deletion) or gain (insertion or duplication) of a segment of DNA results in alteration in chromosomes. Such chromosomal aberrations are commonly observed in cancer cells.
A point mutation is a change in a single base pair of DNA, e.g. sickle-cell anaemia. Deletions and insertions of base pairs cause frame-shift mutations.
Mutagens are chemical and physical factors that induce mutations; UV radiation is an example.

Sickle-cell anaemia: autosomal recessive; Glu is replaced by Val at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain due to a single base substitution at the sixth codon (GAG → GUG). The mutant haemoglobin changes RBCs from biconcave discs to elongated sickle shapes under low oxygen tension. HbᴬHbˢ heterozygotes are carriers with sickle-cell trait; disease needs both parents to be carriers or affected.

ex.q: Two carriers (HbᴬHbˢ) of sickle-cell trait plan a family. What is the probability that a child will (a) have the disease, (b) be a carrier?
st: HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ → HbᴬHbᴬ : HbᴬHbˢ : HbˢHbˢ = 1 : 2 : 1.
(a) Diseased (HbˢHbˢ) = 1/4.
(b) Carrier (HbᴬHbˢ) = 2/4 = 1/2.

topics.rl: India's National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission screens people in tribal regions, offering counselling to carrier couples, because the disease is common in parts of central India.

topics.t: Pedigree analysis, Mendelian disorders and thalassemia
topics.h: Family trees are not just for weddings. Doctors read them like maps to track a disease across generations.
p: Pedigree analysis is the study of a trait across several generations of a family. Standard symbols: square = male, circle = female, shaded symbol = affected, diamond = sex unspecified, horizontal line between male and female = mating, double line = consanguineous mating, vertical line down = offspring.

Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in a single gene. They follow Mendelian inheritance, can be traced by pedigree analysis, and may be dominant or recessive, autosomal or sex-linked. Examples: haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria, thalassemia.

Pedigree clues: autosomal dominant traits (e.g. myotonic dystrophy) appear in every generation and an affected child has at least one affected parent. Autosomal recessive traits (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia) can skip generations; two unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child; males and females are affected equally.

Thalassemia is an autosomal recessive blood disease transmitted when both parents are unaffected carriers. A mutation or deletion reduces the rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains (α or β), forming abnormal haemoglobin and causing anaemia.

α thalassemia: production of α globin is affected; controlled by two closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 of each parent (four genes in all); the more genes affected, the less α globin. β thalassemia: β globin affected; controlled by a single gene HBB on chromosome 11 of each parent. Thalassemia is a quantitative problem (too few globin molecules), while sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative problem (incorrectly functioning globin).

ex.q: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Is the trait dominant or recessive? Can it be X-linked recessive?
st: Unaffected parents with an affected child means the trait is recessive; both parents are carriers.
For an X-linked recessive daughter to be affected, her father must be affected.
The father is unaffected, so the trait must be autosomal recessive.
ex.a: Autosomal recessive; it cannot be X-linked recessive since the father is unaffected.

topics.rl: Many Indian states run thalassemia carrier screening for students and couples, since counselling two carriers can prevent a child's lifelong transfusion needs.

topics.t: Sex-linked disorders: haemophilia and colour blindness
topics.h: Queen Victoria was a carrier of haemophilia, and the gene spread through royal families of Europe.
p: Haemophilia: a sex-linked recessive disease in which a single protein in the cascade of clotting proteins is affected. A simple cut may lead to non-stop bleeding.

A heterozygous female (carrier) may transmit it to sons. A haemophilic female is extremely rare because her mother must be at least a carrier and her father must be haemophilic. Queen Victoria's family pedigree shows many haemophilic descendants, as she was a carrier.

Colour blindness: a sex-linked recessive disorder due to a defect in either the red or the green cone of the eye, causing failure to discriminate between red and green. The mutation is in certain genes on the X chromosome. It occurs in about 8 per cent of males and only about 0.4 per cent of females.

Cross problems: a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) × normal father (XᴴY) gives daughters 1/2 normal, 1/2 carrier; sons 1/2 normal, 1/2 affected. A daughter is colour blind only if her mother is at least a carrier and her father is colour blind.

ex.q: A carrier woman for haemophilia (XᴴXʰ) marries a normal man (XᴴY). What fraction of all their children will be haemophilic, and which sex will they be?
st: Mother's eggs: Xᴴ or Xʰ; father's sperms: Xᴴ or Y.
Children: XᴴXᴴ, XᴴY, XʰXᴴ, XʰY, each 1/4.
Only XʰY is haemophilic: 1/4 of all children, all sons.
ex.a: 1/4 of all children; affected children are sons (1/2 of the sons).

topics.rl: Haemophilia societies in Indian cities run clotting-factor treatment centres; family screening of carrier women uses exactly these Punnett squares.

topics.t: Chromosomal disorders: Down's, Klinefelter's and Turner's
topics.h: One extra copy of the smallest human autosome changes development dramatically. That is Down's syndrome.
p: Chromosomal disorders are caused by absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes. Failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division causes gain or loss of a chromosome: aneuploidy. Failure of cytokinesis after telophase increases a whole set of chromosomes: polyploidy, often seen in plants. Trisomy = an additional copy; monosomy = lack of one chromosome of a pair.

Down's syndrome: trisomy of chromosome 21. Features: short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with characteristic palm crease; physical, psychomotor and mental development is retarded. First described by Langdon Down in 1866.

Klinefelter's syndrome: an additional X chromosome, karyotype 47, XXY. Overall masculine development, but feminine development such as breast development (gynaecomastia) is also expressed. Such individuals are sterile.
Turner's syndrome: absence of one X chromosome, karyotype 45, X0. Such females are sterile as ovaries are rudimentary, and they lack other secondary sexual characters.

ex.q: Give the chromosome number and sex chromosomes for (a) Down's syndrome male, (b) Klinefelter's syndrome, (c) Turner's syndrome.
st: (a) Trisomy 21 adds one autosome to 46: 47, with XY in a male.
(b) One extra X: 47, XXY.
(c) One X missing: 45, X0.

topics.rl: Prenatal screening offered in Indian hospitals can detect trisomy 21 early, helping families prepare with medical and educational support.

topics.t: Nucleic acids, the polynucleotide chain and DNA length
topics.h: If you stretched out the DNA from just one of your cells, it would be about 2.2 metres long, yet it fits in a nucleus a few micrometres wide.
p: Nucleic acids are of two types: DNA and RNA. DNA acts as the genetic material in most organisms; RNA is the genetic material in some viruses. RNA mostly works as a messenger, adapter, structural and sometimes catalytic molecule.

DNA is a long polymer of deoxyribonucleotides. Its length is usually given as number of nucleotides (or base pairs). Bacteriophage φX174 has 5386 nucleotides, bacteriophage lambda 48502 bp, E. coli 4.6 × 10⁶ bp, and the haploid human genome 3.3 × 10⁹ bp.

A nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (ribose in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA) and a phosphate. Purines: adenine and guanine; pyrimidines: cytosine, uracil and thymine. Thymine is in DNA and uracil in RNA in its place; cytosine is in both.

Base + sugar (N-glycosidic linkage at the 1′C) = nucleoside. Nucleoside + phosphate (phosphoester linkage at the 5′C) = nucleotide. Nucleotides join by 3′–5′ phosphodiester linkages. A polynucleotide has a free phosphate at its 5′ end and a free 3′-OH at its 3′ end. In RNA every ribose also has a 2′-OH.

History: Friedrich Meischer first identified DNA as an acidic substance in the nucleus in 1869 and named it 'nuclein'. X-ray diffraction data from Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin helped Watson and Crick build the double helix. Length rule: distance between two consecutive base pairs = 0.34 nm, so length = number of bp × 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m.

ex.q: Calculate the length of DNA in a diploid human cell (6.6 × 10⁹ bp).
st: Length = number of bp × distance per bp.
ex.a: About 2.2 metres

topics.rl: Forensic labs in India, such as the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics in Hyderabad, work every day with this long, thin molecule.

topics.t: The double helix and the central dogma
topics.h: Watson and Crick's 1953 model was built partly from a blurry X-ray photo and a rule about base ratios.
p: Erwin Chargaff found that in double-stranded DNA the ratios A : T and G : C are constant and equal to one (A = T and G = C).
Watson–Crick double helix (1953): two polynucleotide chains with a sugar-phosphate backbone and bases projecting inside. The chains are antiparallel: one runs 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′.
Bases pair through hydrogen bonds: A with T (two H-bonds) and G with C (three H-bonds). A purine always faces a pyrimidine, giving a uniform distance between strands.

The two chains are coiled in a right-handed fashion. Pitch of the helix = 3.4 nm, with roughly 10 bp per turn, so the distance between bp is about 0.34 nm. Stacking of base-pair planes adds stability besides H-bonds.

Central dogma (Francis Crick): genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein. In some viruses the flow is reversed, from RNA to DNA (reverse transcription). Schematic practice: draw a polynucleotide chain, the double helix with antiparallel strands, and the central dogma arrow scheme.

ex.q: A double-stranded DNA sample has 20 per cent adenine. Find the percentages of T, G and C.
st: A = T, so T = 20%.
G = C, so each is 30%.

topics.rl: DNA sequencing companies in Bengaluru rely on complementary pairing: knowing one strand automatically gives the other.

topics.h: Packing 2.2 m of DNA into a nucleus a few micrometres wide is like packing kilometres of thread into a tennis ball, and histones are the spools.
p: Prokaryotes like E. coli have no defined nucleus, but their DNA is not scattered. Negatively charged DNA is held with some positively charged proteins in a region called the nucleoid, organised in large loops.
Eukaryotes use histones: positively charged basic proteins rich in lysine and arginine residues. Eight histone molecules form a histone octamer.

Negatively charged DNA wraps around the positively charged histone octamer to form a nucleosome. A typical nucleosome contains 200 bp of DNA helix. Nucleosomes are the repeating units of chromatin and look like 'beads-on-string' under the electron microscope.
Chromatin is packaged into chromatin fibres, which coil and condense further at metaphase to form chromosomes. Higher-level packaging needs non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins.
Euchromatin is loosely packed, stains light and is transcriptionally active. Heterochromatin is densely packed, stains dark and is inactive.

ex.q: A mammalian cell has 6.6 × 10⁹ bp of DNA. If each nucleosome holds about 200 bp, how many nucleosomes are present?
st: Number of nucleosomes = total bp ÷ bp per nucleosome.
ex.a: About 3.3 × 10⁷ nucleosomes

topics.rl: Many cancer drugs being researched in Indian labs target the proteins that modify histones, because packaging controls which genes are switched on.

topics.t: The search for the genetic material
topics.h: In 1952, a kitchen blender helped prove that DNA, not protein, is the genetic material.
p: Frederick Griffith (1928) used Streptococcus pneumoniae. S strain (smooth, with a polysaccharide coat) killed mice; R strain (rough) did not. Heat-killed S did not kill mice, but heat-killed S + live R did, and live S bacteria were recovered. Some 'transforming principle' from the dead S strain had transformed the R strain.
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty purified biochemicals from heat-killed S cells. Proteases and RNases did not stop transformation, but DNase did. They concluded that DNA is the hereditary material.

Hershey and Chase (1952) grew bacteriophages on radioactive phosphorus (³²P labels DNA) or radioactive sulphur (³⁵S labels protein). After infecting E. coli, they removed viral coats in a blender and separated bacteria by centrifugation.

Bacteria infected with ³²P phages were radioactive (DNA entered); with ³⁵S phages the bacteria were not radioactive and radioactivity stayed in the supernatant (protein stayed out). So DNA is the genetic material.
Criteria for genetic material: it should replicate; be chemically and structurally stable; allow slow changes (mutation) for evolution; and express itself as 'Mendelian characters'.

ex.q: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, where would radioactivity be found if protein were the genetic material?
st: ³⁵S labels protein; if protein entered the bacteria, the bacterial pellet would become radioactive with ³⁵S.
³²P (DNA) would then remain outside in the supernatant.
The actual result was the reverse, proving DNA is the genetic material.
ex.a: Bacteria would carry ³⁵S and ³²P would stay in the supernatant; the real result was the opposite.

topics.rl: The pneumococcal vaccine given in India's immunisation programme targets the same Streptococcus pneumoniae capsule that made Griffith's S strain deadly.

topics.t: DNA versus RNA, and the RNA world
topics.h: Some of the earliest enzymes on Earth were probably not proteins at all but RNA molecules.
p: The 2′-OH group present on every nucleotide of RNA is reactive, making RNA labile and easily degraded. RNA is also catalytic, hence reactive. DNA is chemically less reactive and structurally more stable. Thymine in place of uracil adds further stability to DNA.
Because RNA is unstable, it mutates faster. Viruses with RNA genomes and short life spans mutate and evolve faster.

RNA can directly code for proteins, so it expresses characters easily; DNA depends on RNA for protein synthesis. So DNA is preferred for storage of genetic information, and RNA is better for transmission.
RNA world: RNA was the first genetic material. Essential life processes (metabolism, translation, splicing) evolved around RNA. RNA acted both as genetic material and as a catalyst.

Being catalytic, RNA was reactive and unstable. So DNA evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable. DNA being double-stranded with a complementary strand also resists changes, through the evolution of repair.

ex.q: Influenza vaccines must be updated every year, but a tiger's genes barely change over centuries. Explain using the properties of RNA and DNA.
st: Influenza virus has an RNA genome.
RNA's reactive 2′-OH makes it less stable, so it mutates faster; short virus life cycles add up these changes.
Tigers store genes in stable, double-stranded DNA with repair mechanisms.
ex.a: RNA genomes mutate fast (unstable 2′-OH); DNA is stable and repairable.

topics.rl: Health agencies track flu and other RNA-virus strains every season because their RNA genomes change quickly.

topics.h: Every time a cell divides, it copies billions of letters of DNA with astonishing accuracy, using each old strand as a template.
p: Watson and Crick proposed semi-conservative replication: the two strands separate and each acts as a template; each new DNA has one parental and one new strand.

Meselson and Stahl (1958) grew E. coli for many generations on ¹⁵NH₄Cl (heavy, non-radioactive ¹⁵N), then moved them to ¹⁴NH₄Cl. DNA was separated by CsCl density gradient centrifugation. After one generation (20 minutes) all DNA was hybrid (intermediate density); after two generations (40 minutes) there were equal amounts of hybrid and light DNA. Taylor and colleagues (1958) showed the same in chromosomes of Vicia faba using radioactive thymidine.

The main enzyme is DNA-dependent DNA polymerase, which uses a DNA template to polymerise deoxynucleotides very fast and with high accuracy. Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates act as substrates and also provide energy (from their two terminal high-energy phosphates).

Replication occurs at a small opening of the helix, the replication fork. Polymerase works only in the 5′→3′ direction, so on the template with 3′→5′ polarity replication is continuous (leading strand), and on the other it is discontinuous (lagging strand); the fragments (Okazaki fragments) are joined by DNA ligase.

Replication starts at a definite region called the origin of replication (ori); polymerases cannot initiate on their own. In eukaryotes replication takes place in the S phase of the cell cycle; failure of cell division after replication causes polyploidy.

ex.q: E. coli with only ¹⁵N DNA is moved to ¹⁴N medium. What fraction of DNA molecules will be light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N) after three generations?
st: Gen 1: 2 molecules, both hybrid.
Gen 2: 4 molecules: 2 hybrid, 2 light.
Gen 3: 8 molecules: 2 hybrid, 6 light.
Light fraction = 6/8 = 3/4.
ex.a: 3/4 light, 1/4 hybrid

topics.rl: PCR kits used in Indian diagnostic labs copy DNA using the same rules: a template, a primer and polymerase working 5′→3′.

topics.h: Your cell does not photocopy the whole DNA book each time; it copies just one page, from just one side.
p: Transcription is copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA. Only a segment of DNA and only one of its strands is copied, using the complementarity principle (but with U instead of T).

Why only one strand? If both were templates, they would code for RNAs with different sequences and hence different proteins, complicating information transfer. Also, the two RNAs would be complementary and form double-stranded RNA, which cannot be translated.

A transcription unit has a promoter, a structural gene and a terminator. The promoter lies upstream, towards the 5′ end of the structural gene (with respect to the coding strand), and gives the binding site for RNA polymerase. The terminator lies downstream, towards the 3′ end of the coding strand.

The template strand has 3′→5′ polarity. The coding strand has 5′→3′ polarity and the same sequence as the RNA, except T in place of U; it does not code for anything and is displaced during transcription.
Writing exercise: to get mRNA from a template strand, write complementary bases (A→U, T→A, G→C, C→G) with antiparallel polarity; or copy the coding strand replacing T with U.

ex.q: The coding strand of a gene is 5′-ATGCATGC-3′. Write the template strand and the mRNA.
st: Template is complementary and antiparallel: 3′-TACGTACG-5′.
mRNA has the coding-strand sequence with U for T.
mRNA: 5′-AUGCAUGC-3′.
ex.a: Template 3′-TACGTACG-5′; mRNA 5′-AUGCAUGC-3′

topics.rl: COVID-19 mRNA vaccine design started from a DNA template sequence, using these exact transcription rules.

topics.t: Genes, RNA types and transcription in prokaryotes and eukaryotes
topics.h: Most of a eukaryotic gene is never seen by the ribosome: introns get cut out before the message leaves the nucleus.
p: A cistron is a segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide. Structural genes are mostly monocistronic in eukaryotes and polycistronic in bacteria. Eukaryotic genes are split genes: coding exons (which appear in mature RNA) are interrupted by introns (intervening sequences, which do not).
Three major RNAs: mRNA provides the template, tRNA brings amino acids and reads the code, rRNA has structural and catalytic roles.

In bacteria, a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase makes all RNAs. It binds the promoter with the initiation factor σ (sigma) to start (initiation), polymerises using nucleoside triphosphates (elongation) and stops with the termination factor ρ (rho) at the terminator. Bacterial mRNA needs no processing, and since there is no nucleus, transcription and translation can be coupled.

Eukaryotes have at least three nuclear RNA polymerases: RNA polymerase I makes rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S); RNA polymerase III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs; RNA polymerase II makes hnRNA, the precursor of mRNA.

hnRNA processing: splicing removes introns and joins exons; capping adds methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5′ end; tailing adds 200–300 adenylate residues at the 3′ end in a template-independent way. The processed mRNA moves to the cytoplasm.

ex.q: A eukaryotic gene has 4 exons and 3 introns. Which will be present in the mature mRNA, and what extra features will it carry at each end?
st: Splicing removes the 3 introns and joins the 4 exons.
Capping adds methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5′ end.
Tailing adds a poly-A tail (200–300 A) at the 3′ end.
ex.a: 4 exons only, with a 5′ cap and a 3′ poly-A tail.

topics.rl: Spinal muscular atrophy therapies now in use act by changing how a gene's RNA is spliced, so splicing is not just textbook trivia.

topics.h: Four letters, three at a time, give 64 words, enough to spell every protein in every living thing.
p: The genetic code is the relationship between the sequence of nucleotides on mRNA and the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. Physicist George Gamow argued that to code 20 amino acids with 4 bases, the code must be a triplet: 4³ = 64 codons.

Har Gobind Khorana's chemical method of synthesising RNA with defined combinations of bases, Marshall Nirenberg's cell-free system for protein synthesis and Severo Ochoa's enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase), which polymerises RNA without a template, helped decipher the code.

Properties: codons are triplets; 61 code for amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons. One codon codes only one amino acid (unambiguous and specific). Some amino acids have more than one codon (degenerate). Codons are read contiguously with no punctuation. The code is nearly universal (UUU codes Phe from bacteria to humans). AUG codes methionine and is also the initiator codon.
Codon-table use: read mRNA 5′→3′ in triplets from AUG until a stop codon, e.g. 5′-AUG UUU UAA-3′ → Met-Phe-stop.

Mutations: a point mutation, e.g. in the beta-globin gene, changes one amino acid (sickle-cell). Inserting or deleting one or two bases shifts the reading frame (frame-shift mutations), like 'RAM HAS RED CAP' becoming 'RAM HAS BRE DCA P' after inserting B. Inserting or deleting three bases adds or removes a codon and keeps the frame.

ex.q: How many amino acids are coded by the mRNA 5′-AUG GCU UUU AAA UAG GCA-3′?
st: Start at AUG: AUG (Met), GCU, UUU (Phe), AAA.
UAG is a stop codon: translation stops.
GCA after the stop is not translated.
ex.a: 4 amino acids

topics.rl: Har Gobind Khorana, born in Raipur village in undivided Punjab, shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on the genetic code.

topics.h: The ribosome's main enzyme is not a protein but an RNA, a living fossil of the RNA world.
p: tRNA is the adapter molecule. It has an anticodon loop with bases complementary to the codon and an amino acid acceptor end. tRNAs are specific for each amino acid; a special initiator tRNA starts translation. There are no tRNAs for stop codons. Its secondary structure looks like a clover-leaf; its 3-D structure is a compact inverted L.
Translation is the polymerisation of amino acids to form a polypeptide. Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds, which need energy.
Charging (aminoacylation) of tRNA: amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA. Two charged tRNAs close together favour peptide bond formation.

The ribosome has a large and a small subunit. Translation begins when the small subunit meets mRNA. In bacteria, 23S rRNA of the large subunit acts as the enzyme (ribozyme) for peptide bond formation. mRNA also has untranslated regions (UTRs) before the start codon (5′ UTR) and after the stop codon (3′ UTR), needed for efficient translation.

Steps: initiation (ribosome binds mRNA at start codon AUG, recognised only by the initiator tRNA); elongation (aminoacyl-tRNAs bind codons by anticodon pairing, peptide bonds form, ribosome moves codon by codon); termination (a release factor binds the stop codon and the polypeptide is released).

ex.q: The mRNA is 5′-AUG UUU GGC UAA-3′. Write the anticodons of the tRNAs used (5′→3′) and the number of peptide bonds formed.
st: Codons: AUG, UUU, GGC; UAA is a stop codon with no tRNA.
Anticodons (5′→3′): CAU, AAA, GCC.
3 amino acids are joined by 2 peptide bonds.
ex.a: Anticodons CAU, AAA, GCC; 2 peptide bonds

topics.rl: Some antibiotics used in Indian hospitals, like tetracyclines and streptomycin, work by jamming bacterial ribosomes during translation.

topics.t: Regulation of gene expression and the lac operon
topics.h: E. coli makes lactose-digesting enzymes only when lactose is around. It is the cell's version of switching off the geyser when no one needs hot water.
p: In eukaryotes, gene expression can be regulated at the transcriptional level (formation of the primary transcript), processing level (regulation of splicing), transport of mRNA from nucleus to cytoplasm, and translational level.

In prokaryotes, control of the rate of transcription initiation is the main site. Accessory proteins act positively (activators) or negatively (repressors). Access to promoters is often controlled by proteins binding to operators, which lie next to promoters; each operon has its own operator and repressor.

François Jacob and Jacques Monod first explained a transcriptionally regulated system: the lac operon. In an operon, polycistronic structural genes are regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes.

The lac operon has a regulatory gene i (from 'inhibitor') coding the repressor, and three structural genes: z codes β-galactosidase (hydrolyses lactose into galactose and glucose); y codes permease (increases permeability of the cell to β-galactosides); a codes transacetylase.

The repressor is made all the time (constitutively). Without inducer, it binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase: the operon is off. Lactose (or allolactose) is the inducer: it binds and inactivates the repressor, so RNA polymerase transcribes the operon. Regulation by the repressor is negative regulation; the lac operon is also under positive regulation.

ex.q: An E. coli cell has a mutation that makes the repressor unable to bind the operator. What happens to lac enzyme production when lactose is absent?
st: Normally, without lactose, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription.
If the repressor cannot bind, nothing blocks RNA polymerase.
So z, y and a are transcribed even without lactose.
ex.a: Lac enzymes are made all the time (constitutive expression).

topics.rl: The lac operon system is a workhorse in Indian biotech labs: genes placed under lac control can be switched on simply by adding an inducer.

topics.t: Human Genome Project: goals and methods
topics.h: Printing the human genome as text would need about 3300 books of 1000 pages each.
p: The Human Genome Project (HGP) was launched in 1990 and completed in 2003. At an initial estimated cost of US $3 per bp, sequencing about 3 × 10⁹ bp would cost about 9 billion US dollars. Stored as books with 1000 letters per page and 1000 pages per book, the DNA of a single human cell would need 3300 books.

Goals: identify all the approximately 20,000–25,000 genes; determine the sequence of the 3 billion base pairs; store this in databases; improve tools for data analysis; transfer related technologies to other sectors such as industry; address the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI).

The 13-year project was coordinated by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institute of Health. The Wellcome Trust (U.K.) became a major partner; Japan, France, Germany, China and others also contributed.

Applications: understanding human biology and new ways to diagnose, treat and prevent disorders. Non-human model organisms were also sequenced: bacteria, yeast, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, rice and Arabidopsis.
Two methods: Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs) identify all genes expressed as RNA; sequence annotation sequences the whole genome, coding and non-coding, and later assigns functions.

ex.q: Using NCERT's book analogy, how many pages would the haploid human DNA sequence (3.3 × 10⁹ letters) fill at 1000 letters per page, and how many 1000-page books?
ex.a: 3.3 × 10⁶ pages; 3300 books

topics.rl: India's Genome India project, led by the Department of Biotechnology, has sequenced thousands of Indian genomes to capture the country's genetic diversity, following the HGP's path.

topics.t: Sequencing the genome and its salient features
topics.h: Less than 2 per cent of your genome actually codes for proteins. The rest was once called 'junk', but it holds many surprises.
p: Sequencing method: total DNA is broken into random small fragments, cloned in hosts (bacteria and yeast) using vectors BAC (bacterial artificial chromosomes) and YAC (yeast artificial chromosomes), and sequenced by automated sequencers based on the method developed by Frederick Sanger. Overlapping fragments were aligned using specialised computer programs.
Genetic and physical maps were made using polymorphism of restriction endonuclease recognition sites and repetitive DNA sequences called microsatellites.

Salient features: the human genome has 3164.7 million bp. The average gene has 3000 bases; the largest known gene is dystrophin at 2.4 million bases. The total number of genes is estimated at about 30,000. Almost all (99.9 per cent) nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all people.

Functions are unknown for over 50 per cent of discovered genes. Less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins. Repeated sequences make up a large portion. Chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and Y the fewest (231). About 1.4 million locations of single-base differences (SNPs) were identified.
Future: instead of studying single genes, scientists can study all genes and all transcripts in a tissue, organ or tumour, and how thousands of genes and proteins work together in networks.

ex.q: If 99.9 per cent of the 3 × 10⁹ bp genome is identical between two people, how many base pairs differ?
st: Difference = 0.1% of 3 × 10⁹.
ex.a: About 3 × 10⁶ bp

topics.rl: Pharmacogenomics clinics in India use SNP data to choose drug doses, a direct payoff of HGP's SNP map.

topics.h: Except for identical twins, no two people share the same DNA band pattern, which makes a single hair a powerful witness.
p: DNA fingerprinting identifies differences in specific regions called repetitive DNA, where a small stretch of DNA is repeated many times. It was initially developed by Alec Jeffreys.

In density gradient centrifugation, bulk DNA forms a major peak; small peaks are satellite DNA. Based on base composition (A:T or G:C rich), length of segment and number of repeats, satellite DNA is classified as micro-satellites, mini-satellites etc. They normally do not code for proteins but show a high degree of polymorphism (variation at the genetic level), which arises due to mutations and is inherited from parents to children.

Jeffreys used a satellite DNA that shows very high polymorphism, the Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR), as a probe. VNTRs belong to mini-satellites; their copy number varies, so VNTR size varies from 0.1 to 20 kb.

Steps: (i) isolation of DNA; (ii) digestion by restriction endonucleases; (iii) separation of fragments by electrophoresis; (iv) blotting (transferring) separated DNA onto synthetic membranes like nitrocellulose or nylon (Southern blotting); (v) hybridisation using a labelled VNTR probe; (vi) detection by autoradiography.

Applications: forensic science (DNA from blood, hair-follicle, skin, bone, saliva, sperm shows the same polymorphism), paternity testing (polymorphisms are inherited) and studies of population and genetic diversity. PCR increases sensitivity, so DNA from a single cell can suffice.

ex.q: In a paternity case, a child has VNTR bands at positions 1, 3, 4 and 6. The mother has bands 1, 2, 4 and 5. Which bands must have come from the biological father?
st: Every band in the child comes from either the mother or the father.
Bands shared with the mother: 1 and 4.
Bands not explained by the mother: 3 and 6, so these must come from the father.
ex.a: Bands 3 and 6

topics.rl: India's forensic labs, including the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics in Hyderabad, use these methods to solve crimes and identify disaster victims.

topics.t: Origin of the universe, Earth and early ideas on life
topics.h: Every atom of iron in your blood was forged in stars long before Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago.
p: The Big Bang theory explains the origin of the universe as a singular huge explosion. The universe expanded and cooled; hydrogen and helium formed later and condensed under gravitation into galaxies. In the solar system of the Milky Way galaxy, Earth is believed to have formed about 4.5 billion years ago.

In early Earth there was no atmosphere. Water vapour, methane, carbon dioxide and ammonia released from the molten mass covered the surface. UV rays from the sun broke water into hydrogen and oxygen, and the lighter hydrogen escaped. Oxygen combined with ammonia and methane to form water, CO₂ and others. The ozone layer formed, and as it cooled, water vapour fell as rain, filling depressions to form oceans.
Life appeared about 500 million years after the formation of Earth, i.e. almost four billion years ago.

Panspermia: some scientists and early Greek thinkers proposed that units of life called spores were transferred to different planets, including Earth. It is still a favourite idea of some astronomers.

Spontaneous generation held that life came out of decaying and rotting matter like straw and mud. Louis Pasteur showed by careful experiments that life comes only from pre-existing life: in pre-sterilised flasks, no life arose from killed yeast, while in a flask open to air new organisms arose. This dismissed spontaneous generation.

ex.q: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago and life appeared about 500 million years later. How many years ago did life appear?
st: 4.5 billion = 4500 million years.
4500 − 500 = 4000 million years.
ex.a: About 4 billion (4000 million) years ago

topics.rl: ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission and other planetary missions ask the same question NCERT does: could life arise, or arrive, elsewhere?

topics.h: In 1953 a student filled a flask with gases, zapped it with sparks for a week, and found amino acids. Life's building blocks can form without life.
p: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g. RNA, protein) and that the formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution: formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents.
Conditions on early Earth: high temperature, volcanic storms and a reducing atmosphere containing CH₄, NH₃ etc.

In 1953, S. L. Miller, an American scientist, created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at 800 °C, and observed formation of amino acids. In similar experiments others observed formation of sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats. Analysis of meteorite content also revealed similar processes elsewhere in space.

The first non-cellular forms of life could have originated about 3 billion years ago. They would have been giant molecules (RNA, protein, polysaccharides etc.), which might have reproduced their own molecules.
The first cellular forms of life did not originate till about 2000 million years ago (mya); these were probably single cells living in water.

ex.q: Describe the set-up of Miller's experiment and what it simulated.
st: Flask with CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at 800 °C: the reducing early atmosphere.
Electric discharge: lightning on early Earth.
Result: amino acids formed, supporting chemical evolution.
ex.a: Gases CH₄, H₂, NH₃, H₂O at 800 °C + electric discharge → amino acids, simulating early Earth.

topics.rl: Astrobiologists study amino acids in meteorites, the same molecules Miller made, to ask whether life's ingredients are common in space.

topics.h: A five-year sea voyage turned a young naturalist into the author of the most famous idea in biology.
p: The theory of special creation had three connotations: all living organisms (species) today were created as such; the diversity was always the same since creation and will be the same in future; and Earth is about 4000 years old. These ideas were strongly challenged in the nineteenth century.

Charles Darwin, on a sea voyage around the world in the sailing ship H.M.S. Beagle, concluded that existing living forms share similarities to varying degrees among themselves and with life forms that existed millions of years ago. Many such forms no longer exist; there have been extinctions, and new forms have arisen at different periods.
Alfred Wallace, a naturalist who worked in the Malay Archipelago, came to similar conclusions around the same time.

Darwin concluded that there has been gradual evolution of life forms. Any population has built-in variation in characteristics. Those characteristics that enable some to survive better in natural conditions would outbreed others. Fitness ultimately means reproductive fitness: those better fit in an environment leave more progeny.
All life forms are related by common ancestry, and natural selection is the mechanism Darwin proposed for evolution.

ex.q: According to special creation, Earth is about 4000 years old; according to NCERT, Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. By what factor does the scientific estimate exceed the special-creation estimate?
st: 4.5 billion = 4,500,000,000 years.
ex.a: About 1.125 million times greater

topics.rl: The Galápagos Islands that inspired Darwin now attract research teams worldwide, while Indian islands like the Andamans offer similar natural labs for studying evolution.

topics.h: Fossils of ancient whales that still had legs have been dug up in the Kutch region of Gujarat, a stone record of evolution.
p: Palaeontological evidence: rocks form sediments, and a cross-section of Earth's crust shows layers one over another. Different-aged rock layers contain fossils of different life forms, which probably died during the formation of that layer. Some resemble modern organisms; some, like dinosaurs, are extinct.
The age of fossils can be estimated by the radioactive-dating method, which shows that life forms varied over time and certain forms are restricted to certain geological time spans.
Molecular homology: similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function among diverse organisms give clues to common ancestry.

Embryological evidence was proposed by Ernst Haeckel based on features common to vertebrate embryos but absent in adults, e.g. all vertebrate embryos, including humans, develop a row of vestigial gill slits just behind the head, though they are functional only in fish.
This proposal was disproved on careful study by Karl Ernst von Baer, who noted that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.

ex.q: A fossil is found in a deeper rock layer than another fossil in the same undisturbed cross-section. Which is likely older, and how could scientists estimate the actual age?
st: In undisturbed sediments, deeper layers formed earlier.
So the fossil in the deeper layer is likely older.
Radioactive dating gives an estimate of the actual age.
ex.a: The deeper fossil is older; its age can be estimated by radioactive dating.

topics.rl: Fossil-rich sites such as the dinosaur beds near Jabalpur and at Balasinor in Gujarat preserve layer-by-layer records of past life in India.

topics.h: A bat's wing, a whale's flipper and your arm have the same bones inside. A butterfly's wing does the same job with none of them.
p: Comparative anatomy shows similarities and differences among organisms. Homologous organs have the same basic structure but perform different functions, indicating common ancestry. Forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetah and human share humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges.

Homology arises by divergent evolution: the same structure developed along different directions due to adaptations to different needs. Other examples: vertebrate hearts and brains; in plants, thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita.
Analogous organs are not anatomically similar but perform similar functions. They arise by convergent evolution: different structures evolving for the same function, due to similar habitats.
Examples of analogy: wings of butterfly and of birds; eye of octopus and of mammals; flippers of penguins and dolphins; sweet potato (root modification) and potato (stem modification).
Board exercise: differentiate homologous and analogous organs with examples, and recall that Miller's set-up used CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour with electric discharge (chemical evolution).

ex.q: Classify: (a) thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita; (b) eye of octopus and eye of a cow. Name the type of evolution in each.
st: (a) Same origin, different functions → homologous → divergent evolution.
(b) Different structure, same function (vision) → analogous → convergent evolution.
ex.a: (a) Homologous, divergent; (b) Analogous, convergent

topics.rl: Engineers at IISc studying flapping-wing drones compare bird and insect wings: analogous solutions to the same problem of flight.

topics.h: Factory smoke in 19th-century England changed the colour of moths within decades, a rare chance to watch evolution happen.
p: Industrial melanism: in England, moth collections from the 1850s (before industrialisation) had more white-winged than dark-winged (melanised) moths on tree trunks. Collections from the same area in 1920 (after industrialisation) had more dark-winged moths. (The peppered moth, Biston betularia, is the classic example.)

Explanation: after industrialisation, tree trunks became dark with smoke and soot, and lichens did not grow. White-winged moths stood out and were picked off by predators; dark-winged moths were camouflaged and survived. Before industrialisation, white lichen-covered trunks hid white moths instead.
Lichens serve as indicators of industrial pollution, since they do not grow in polluted areas.

Anthropogenic action also drives evolution: excess use of herbicides and pesticides has selected resistant varieties in a much shorter time scale. The same is true of microbes against which we use antibiotics.

Humans also use artificial selection in domestication to create new breeds, such as the many breeds of dogs. Evolution by natural selection is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutation in organisms.

ex.q: Explain why dark-winged moths increased in industrial areas of England by 1920.
st: Soot darkened tree trunks and lichens disappeared.
Dark-winged moths were camouflaged; white-winged moths were easily seen by predators.
Dark moths survived and reproduced more, so their proportion rose.
ex.a: Natural selection: camouflaged dark moths survived predation and left more progeny.

topics.rl: Doctors across India warn against unnecessary antibiotics because overuse selects resistant bacteria, the same principle as industrial melanism.

topics.h: One small seed-eating bird reached the Galápagos, and its descendants now include insect-eaters and vegetarians with very different beaks.
p: Adaptive radiation is the evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and literally radiating to other areas of geography (habitats).
Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands: from the original seed-eating features, many other forms with altered beaks arose, enabling them to become insectivorous and vegetarian finches.
Australian marsupials: a number of marsupials, each different from the other, evolved from an ancestral stock, all within the Australian island continent.

When more than one adaptive radiation appears to have occurred in an isolated geographical area (representing different habitats), one can call this convergent evolution. Placental mammals in Australia also show adaptive radiation into varieties, each resembling a corresponding marsupial, e.g. placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf (a marsupial).

ex.q: The placental wolf and the Tasmanian wolf look alike but belong to different mammal groups. Explain.
st: Both lineages underwent adaptive radiation in similar habitats.
Similar habitats led to similar body forms in unrelated lineages.
This similarity between a placental and a marsupial form is convergent evolution.
ex.a: Convergent evolution: placental and marsupial radiations produced similar forms in similar habitats.

topics.rl: India's Western Ghats show adaptive radiation too, with many frog species diversifying into different habitats from a few ancestral lineages.

topics.h: If every bacterium in a flask kept dividing unchecked, it would soon outweigh the planet. Limits create competition, and competition fuels selection.
p: Natural selection is based on heritable variation leading to differential reproduction. The fittest (those leaving more progeny) are selected; nature selects for fitness, and fitness is based on characteristics that are inherited.
The two key concepts of Darwinian theory of evolution are branching descent and natural selection.

Darwin's factual observations: natural resources are limited; populations are stable in size except for seasonal fluctuation; members of a population vary in characteristics (no two are alike); most variations are inherited.

Theoretically, population size would grow exponentially if everybody reproduced maximally (as in a growing bacterial population). In reality it is limited, so there is competition for resources; only some survive and grow at the cost of others.

Darwin's insight: heritable variations that make resource use better for a few (adapted better) let those few reproduce more and leave more progeny. Over many generations this leads to change in population characteristics and new forms appear.

ex.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with one cell and unlimited resources, how many cells would there be after 2 hours?
st: 2 hours = 120 minutes = 6 divisions.
Cells = 2⁶ = 64.
ex.a: 64 cells

topics.rl: Food-safety officers in India insist on refrigeration because bacteria in warm food can multiply exponentially, just as Darwin's reasoning assumes.

topics.t: Mutation theory and the mechanism of evolution
topics.h: Evening primrose plants with suddenly very different forms convinced Hugo de Vries that evolution could leap, not just crawl.
p: Hugo de Vries, working on evening primrose (Oenothera lamarckiana), proposed mutations: large differences arising suddenly in a population. He believed mutation, not the minor heritable variations Darwin described, causes evolution.
Mutations are random and directionless, while Darwinian variations are small and directional.
For Darwin evolution was gradual; de Vries believed mutation caused speciation in a single step and called it saltation (single-step large mutation).

Studies in population genetics later brought clarity: variation due to mutation, recombination during gametogenesis, gene flow or genetic drift changes allele frequencies; coupled with reproductive success through natural selection, populations change and may form new species (speciation).

ex.q: Compare Darwin's and de Vries' views on variation and the pace of evolution.
st: Darwin: small, directional, heritable variations; gradual evolution.
de Vries: large, sudden, random, directionless mutations; single-step speciation (saltation).
ex.a: Darwin: small directional variations, gradual; de Vries: large random mutations, saltation.

topics.rl: Plant breeders at Bhabha Atomic Research Centre have released crop varieties developed using induced mutations, a practical use of the idea that mutations create new variation.

topics.h: If you know how many people in a town are colour blind, Hardy–Weinberg lets you estimate how many carriers there are, with just algebra.
p: Hardy–Weinberg principle: allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation. The gene pool (total genes and their alleles in a population) remains constant: genetic equilibrium. The sum of all allele frequencies is 1.
For a gene with alleles A (frequency p) and a (frequency q), p + q = 1. Genotype frequencies are AA = p², Aa = 2pq and aa = q², and p² + 2pq + q² = 1, the binomial expansion of (p + q)².
If measured frequencies differ from expected values, the difference (and its direction) indicates the extent of evolutionary change. A change in allele frequencies is interpreted as evolution.
Numerical method: start from the homozygous recessive frequency q² (the only genotype whose phenotype directly shows it), find q, then p = 1 − q, then 2pq and p².

ex.q: In a population, 16 per cent of individuals show a recessive trait (aa). Find p, q, and the frequency of heterozygotes.
ex.a: p = 0.6, q = 0.4, heterozygotes = 0.48 (48%)

topics.rl: Public-health planners use Hardy–Weinberg estimates to judge how many sickle-cell or thalassemia carriers might be present in a community before planning screening.

topics.t: Factors affecting equilibrium and types of selection
topics.h: When a few people move to a remote island, the island's gene pool can end up very different from the mainland's, purely by chance.
p: Five factors affect Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection.

Gene migration: when a section of a population moves to another place, gene frequencies change in both the original and new populations; repeated migration gives gene flow. Genetic drift: the same change occurring by chance.
Founder effect: sometimes the change in allele frequency in a new sample of population is so different that they become a different species; the original drifted population becomes the founders.

Natural selection can lead to: stabilisation (more individuals acquire the mean character value); directional change (more individuals acquire a value other than the mean, towards one extreme); and disruption (more individuals acquire peripheral values at both ends of the distribution curve).
Microbial experiments show that pre-existing advantageous mutations, when selected, give new phenotypes; over a few generations this would result in speciation.

ex.q: A bird population has beak sizes from small to large. After a drought, only birds with large beaks survive and breed. Which type of natural selection is this?
st: Survival shifts towards one extreme (large beaks).
The mean of the distribution moves in that direction.
ex.a: Directional selection

topics.rl: Indian conservation biologists worry about small, isolated populations such as the Asiatic lions of Gir, where genetic drift and founder effects can reduce genetic diversity.

topics.h: The Tyrannosaurus rex stood about 20 feet tall, and the whole dinosaur group vanished about 65 million years ago.
p: About 2000 million years ago (mya) the first cellular forms appeared. Single-celled organisms slowly became multicellular. By about 500 mya invertebrates were formed and active. Jawless fish probably evolved around 350 mya; seaweeds and a few plants existed around 320 mya. Plants were the first organisms to invade land.

About 350 mya, fish with stout and strong fins could move on land and go back to water. In 1938, a fish caught in South Africa turned out to be a coelacanth, thought to be extinct. These lobefins evolved into the first amphibians. Amphibians evolved into reptiles, which lay thick-shelled eggs that do not dry up in the sun, unlike those of amphibians.

Giant ferns (pteridophytes) were present but fell to form coal deposits. Some land reptiles went back to water as fish-like reptiles about 200 mya (e.g. Ichthyosaurs). The land reptiles were the dinosaurs; the biggest, Tyrannosaurus rex, was about 20 feet tall. About 65 mya dinosaurs suddenly disappeared; some say climatic changes killed them, some say most evolved into birds.

The first mammals were shrew-like. Mammals were viviparous and more intelligent in sensing and avoiding danger. In South America, mammals resembling horse, hippopotamus, bear and rabbit were overridden by North American fauna when the continents joined due to continental drift. The same drift let the pouched mammals of Australia survive because of lack of competition. Evolution of the horse, elephant and dog are special stories of evolution.

Plant evolution (NCERT chart): early vascular plants such as Zosterophyllum and Psilophyton gave rise to lineages leading to ferns and gymnosperms; flowering plants (monocots and dicots) appear later.

ex.q: Arrange in order of appearance: amphibians, jawless fish, first cellular life, reptiles, invertebrates.
st: First cellular life: ~2000 mya.
Invertebrates: ~500 mya.
Jawless fish: ~350 mya.
Lobefins → amphibians; amphibians → reptiles.
ex.a: First cellular life → invertebrates → jawless fish → amphibians → reptiles

topics.rl: Coal mined in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh formed from ancient plant matter, including giant ferns, buried over millions of years.

topics.t: Human evolution: from Dryopithecus to Homo habilis
topics.h: Fossils from Ethiopia and Tanzania suggest that 3 to 4 million years ago, man-like primates walked upright in eastern Africa.
p: About 15 mya, primates called Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus existed. They were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees. Ramapithecus was more man-like, while Dryopithecus was more ape-like.

A few fossils of man-like bones from Ethiopia and Tanzania show hominid features, suggesting that about 3–4 mya man-like primates, probably not taller than 4 feet but walking upright, lived in eastern Africa.
About 2 mya, Australopithecines probably lived in East African grasslands. Evidence shows they hunted with stone weapons but essentially ate fruit.
Some bones among those discovered were different. This creature was called the first human-like being, the hominid, Homo habilis. Its brain capacity was 650–800 cc, and it probably did not eat meat.

ex.q: Which among Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus was more man-like, and when did they live?
st: Both existed about 15 mya and were hairy, walking like gorillas and chimpanzees.
Ramapithecus was more man-like; Dryopithecus more ape-like.
ex.a: Ramapithecus; about 15 million years ago

topics.rl: Fossils of Ramapithecus were found in the Siwalik Hills of north India, making the Himalayan foothills an important site in the story of primate evolution.

topics.t: Human evolution: Homo erectus to Homo sapiens
topics.h: Cave paintings at Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, remind us how long humans have been making art.
p: Fossils discovered in Java in 1891 revealed the next stage, Homo erectus, about 1.5 mya. Homo erectus had a large brain of around 900 cc and probably ate meat.

The Neanderthal man, with a brain size of 1400 cc, lived in the Near East and Central Asian countries between 1,00,000 and 40,000 years ago. They used hides to protect their body and buried their dead.
Homo sapiens arose in Africa and moved across continents. During the ice age between 75,000 and 10,000 years ago, modern Homo sapiens arose.
Pre-historic cave art developed about 18,000 years ago. Agriculture came around 10,000 years ago and human settlements started.

Revision: by brain capacity, Homo habilis (650–800 cc) < Homo erectus (~900 cc) < Neanderthal (1400 cc); by time, Dryopithecus/Ramapithecus → Australopithecines → H. habilis → H. erectus → Neanderthal → H. sapiens.

ex.q: Arrange Homo erectus, Homo habilis and Neanderthal man in increasing order of brain capacity, giving values.
st: Homo habilis: 650–800 cc.
Homo erectus: about 900 cc.
Neanderthal: 1400 cc.
ex.a: H. habilis (650–800 cc) < H. erectus (~900 cc) < Neanderthal (1400 cc)

topics.rl: Archaeological sites such as Bhimbetka rock shelters show long human presence in India, with paintings from very early periods.

topics.t: Health and the kinds of pathogens
topics.h: Health is not just 'not being sick'. A student who is physically fit but anxious and isolated is not fully healthy either.
p: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease. It is affected by genetic disorders (deficiencies one is born with), infections, and life style (food and water, rest and exercise, habits).

Early Greeks like Hippocrates and the Indian Ayurveda system held that health was a balance of certain 'humors'. William Harvey discovered blood circulation by experiment and showed normal body temperature with a thermometer, disproving the 'good humor' hypothesis.

Diseases may be infectious (easily transmitted from one person to another, like the common cold) or non-infectious (like cancer, a major cause of death). AIDS among infectious diseases is fatal. Drug and alcohol abuse also badly affects health.

Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans and helminths. Most parasites are pathogens; they enter the body by various means, multiply and interfere with normal vital activities, causing morphological and functional damage. Pathogens adapt to life in the host, e.g. those entering the gut survive the low stomach pH and resist digestive enzymes.

ex.q: Classify these diseases as infectious or non-infectious: common cold, cancer, typhoid, AIDS.
st: Infectious diseases are transmitted from person to person by pathogens.
Common cold, typhoid and AIDS are caused by pathogens and transmitted.
Cancer is not transmitted from person to person.
ex.a: Infectious: common cold, typhoid, AIDS; non-infectious: cancer

topics.rl: India's Fit India Movement and Ayushman Bharat's Health and Wellness Centres try to promote all three: physical, mental and social well-being.

topics.t: Typhoid, pneumonia and the common cold
topics.h: A cook in early 20th-century New York unknowingly spread typhoid to many people. She was a healthy carrier, and history remembers her as 'Typhoid Mary'.
p: Typhoid: caused by Salmonella typhi, which enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water and migrates to other organs through blood. Symptoms: sustained high fever (39 °C to 40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite. Intestinal perforation and death may occur in severe cases. It is confirmed by the Widal test.
Mary Mallon, nicknamed Typhoid Mary, was a cook and a typhoid carrier who spread typhoid for several years through the food she prepared.

Pneumonia: caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; infects the alveoli of the lungs, which fill with fluid, causing severe breathing problems. Symptoms: fever, chills, cough and headache; in severe cases lips and finger nails turn grey to bluish. Spread by inhaling droplets or aerosols from an infected person, or by sharing glasses and utensils.

Common cold: caused by rhinoviruses that infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs. Symptoms: nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache, tiredness, usually lasting 3–7 days. Spread by droplets from coughs or sneezes, inhaled directly or via contaminated objects like pens, books, cups, doorknobs, computer keyboards or mice.

ex.q: A patient has sustained fever of 39.5 °C, stomach pain and constipation for a week after eating at a roadside stall. Which disease is suspected, and which test confirms it?
st: Sustained high fever with stomach pain after contaminated food suggests typhoid.
Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi.
The Widal test confirms typhoid.
ex.a: Typhoid; Widal test

topics.rl: The typhoid conjugate vaccine introduced in parts of India, and clean-water drives under Jal Jeevan Mission, both attack typhoid at its root.

topics.t: Malaria and the life cycle of Plasmodium
topics.h: The malaria parasite needs two hosts: it reproduces sexually only inside a mosquito, and uses you mostly as a multiplication factory.
p: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a tiny protozoan. Species: P. vivax, P. malariae and P. falciparum. Malignant malaria, caused by P. falciparum, is the most serious and can even be fatal.
Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites (infectious form) through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.

The parasites first multiply in liver cells, then attack red blood cells (RBCs), causing them to rupture. Rupture releases a toxic substance, haemozoin, responsible for the chill and high fever recurring every three to four days.

Sexual stages (gametocytes) develop in RBCs. When a female Anopheles bites an infected person, gametocytes enter the mosquito; fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's gut. Sporozoites formed then move to and are stored in the mosquito's salivary glands, ready to infect the next person.
Plasmodium thus needs two hosts, humans and mosquitoes, to complete its life cycle.

ex.q: Trace the path of Plasmodium from an infected mosquito to a new mosquito.
st: Infected female Anopheles bites, injecting sporozoites.
Parasites multiply in liver cells, then in RBCs, rupturing them (haemozoin causes fever).
Gametocytes form in RBCs and are taken up by another female Anopheles.
Fertilisation in the mosquito gut; sporozoites move to salivary glands.
ex.a: Sporozoites → liver → RBCs → gametocytes → mosquito gut → sporozoites in salivary glands

topics.rl: India's National Framework for Malaria Elimination targets ending malaria by 2030 using bed nets, rapid tests and treatment of every case.

topics.h: Houseflies don't bite, but they can still make you sick by ferrying parasites from faeces to your food.
p: Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery): Entamoeba histolytica, a protozoan parasite of the large intestine. Symptoms: constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, stools with excess mucus and blood clots. Houseflies act as mechanical carriers, moving parasites from faeces to food. Faecal contamination of food and water is the main source.

Ascariasis: Ascaris, the common roundworm, an intestinal parasite. Symptoms: internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage. Eggs leave with faeces and contaminate soil, water and plants; infection is acquired through contaminated water, vegetables and fruits.

Filariasis (elephantiasis): Wuchereria (W. bancrofti and W. malayi), filarial worms. They cause slowly developing chronic inflammation of the organs they live in for years, usually the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs, often also the genital organs, leading to gross deformities. Spread by the bite of female mosquito vectors (such as Culex).

Ringworm: fungi of the genera Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton. Dry, scaly lesions on skin, nails and scalp, with intense itching. Heat and moisture help these fungi grow, so they thrive in skin folds like the groin or between toes. Acquired from soil or by using towels, clothes or even the comb of infected individuals.

ex.q: A child has intense itching with dry, scaly patches between the toes during the monsoon. Name the disease, the type of pathogen and why the monsoon worsens it.
st: Dry scaly itchy lesions in skin folds suggest ringworm.
Ringworm is caused by fungi such as Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton.
Heat and moisture of the monsoon favour fungal growth.
ex.a: Ringworm, a fungal infection; heat and moisture help the fungi grow.

topics.rl: India's mass drug administration campaigns for lymphatic filariasis and school deworming days for roundworm are public-health answers to these parasites.

topics.h: Smallpox, once one of humanity's deadliest diseases, has been completely eradicated thanks to vaccines and immunisation.
p: Personal hygiene: keeping the body clean; consuming clean drinking water, food, vegetables and fruits. Public hygiene: proper disposal of waste and excreta; periodic cleaning and disinfection of water reservoirs, pools, cesspools and tanks; standard hygiene practices in public catering.
For air-borne diseases like pneumonia and common cold, avoid close contact with infected persons and their belongings.

For vector-borne diseases like malaria and filariasis, control vectors and their breeding places: avoid stagnant water, clean household coolers regularly, use mosquito nets, introduce fish like Gambusia that feed on mosquito larvae, spray insecticides in ditches, drains and swamps, and fit doors and windows with wire mesh. This is also crucial for dengue and chikungunya, spread by Aedes mosquitoes.

Vaccines and immunisation have eradicated smallpox and largely controlled polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus. Biotechnology is producing newer, safer vaccines, and antibiotics and other drugs treat infectious diseases effectively.

Revision (match): typhoid–Salmonella typhi; pneumonia–Streptococcus pneumoniae; cold–rhinoviruses; malaria–Plasmodium; amoebiasis–Entamoeba histolytica; ascariasis–Ascaris; filariasis–Wuchereria; ringworm–Microsporum/Trichophyton/Epidermophyton.

ex.q: Suggest four measures a housing society can take during the monsoon to prevent dengue.
st: Dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes breeding in stagnant water.
Remove stagnant water from pots, tyres and coolers; clean coolers regularly.
Use mosquito nets and wire mesh on doors and windows.
Release Gambusia fish in ponds; spray insecticides in drains.
ex.a: Remove stagnant water, clean coolers, use nets and mesh, use Gambusia and insecticides.

topics.rl: Municipal 'dry day' campaigns in Indian cities, where residents empty all standing water once a week, directly target Aedes breeding.

topics.h: The second time you meet a pathogen, your body responds so fast and so strongly that you may never feel sick. That is immune memory.
p: Immunity is the overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system. It is of two types: innate and acquired.

Innate immunity is non-specific and present at birth. Four barriers: physical (skin; mucus coating of epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts traps microbes); physiological (acid in stomach, saliva in mouth, tears from eyes prevent microbial growth); cellular (polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils), monocytes and natural killer lymphocytes in blood and macrophages in tissues phagocytose and destroy microbes); cytokine barriers (virus-infected cells secrete interferons that protect non-infected cells from further viral infection).
Acquired immunity is pathogen-specific and characterised by memory.

The first encounter with a pathogen produces a low-intensity primary response. A later encounter with the same pathogen gives a highly intensified secondary or anamnestic response, because the body remembers the first encounter.

ex.q: Classify: (a) stomach acid, (b) interferons, (c) skin, (d) neutrophils, (e) tears.
st: Skin is a physical barrier.
Stomach acid and tears are physiological barriers.
Neutrophils are a cellular barrier; interferons are a cytokine barrier.
ex.a: (a) physiological (b) cytokine (c) physical (d) cellular (e) physiological

topics.rl: Booster doses in India's Universal Immunisation Programme exploit the anamnestic response, making protection stronger and longer.

topics.h: An antibody looks like the letter Y, with two heavy and two light chains, and each one fits its own target like a key in a lock.
p: Acquired immunity uses two types of lymphocytes: B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes. B-lymphocytes produce an army of proteins called antibodies in response to pathogens. T-cells do not secrete antibodies but help B cells produce them.
Each antibody molecule has four peptide chains: two small light chains and two longer heavy chains, so an antibody is represented as H₂L₂. Types of antibodies include IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG.
Since antibodies are found in the blood, this response is called the humoral immune response.
The second type is the cell-mediated immune response (CMI), mediated by T-lymphocytes.

CMI is responsible for graft rejection: the body can tell 'self' from 'non-self'. Before transplants (heart, eye, liver, kidney), tissue matching and blood group matching are essential, and the patient takes immunosuppressants all his or her life.

ex.q: A kidney transplant patient takes immunosuppressants for life even after tissue matching. Why?
st: The body distinguishes self from non-self.
T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) would attack the graft.
Immunosuppressants reduce this response and prevent rejection.
ex.a: To suppress cell-mediated immunity (T cells) that would reject the non-self graft.

topics.rl: India's organ donation network NOTTO matches donors and recipients by blood group and tissue type to reduce rejection.

topics.h: Snakebite victims across rural India are saved by antivenom, a ready-made dose of antibodies the body did not have to make itself.
p: Active immunity: when the host is exposed to antigens (living or dead microbes or other proteins), it produces its own antibodies. It is slow and takes time to give its full effect. Natural infection or deliberate immunisation induces it.

Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies are given directly. Examples: colostrum, the yellowish fluid secreted by the mother in the initial days of lactation, has abundant antibodies (IgA) to protect the infant; the foetus receives some antibodies from the mother through the placenta.

Vaccination works on the memory of the immune system. A vaccine is a preparation of antigenic proteins of a pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogen. It induces antibodies and also memory B and T cells that recognise the pathogen quickly on later exposure.
For a quick response, as in tetanus, preformed antibodies or antitoxin are injected; in snakebites, the injection contains preformed antibodies against snake venom. This is passive immunisation.
Recombinant DNA technology lets antigenic polypeptides of a pathogen be produced in bacteria or yeast, allowing large-scale production, e.g. the hepatitis B vaccine produced from yeast.

ex.q: Classify each as active or passive immunity: (a) hepatitis B vaccination, (b) anti-tetanus serum after an injury, (c) antibodies in colostrum, (d) recovering from measles.
st: Own antibodies made after antigen exposure = active: (a) and (d).
Ready-made antibodies given = passive: (b) and (c).
ex.a: (a) active (b) passive (c) passive (d) active

topics.rl: India's Universal Immunisation Programme, one of the world's largest, gives free vaccines against diseases such as measles, polio, tetanus and hepatitis B.

topics.t: Allergies, autoimmunity and the lymphoid organs
topics.h: About half of your lymphoid tissue lines your gut, airways and urogenital tract, guarding every doorway into the body.
p: Allergy is an exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens (allergens) in the environment, such as mites in dust, pollen and animal dander. The antibodies produced are of the IgE type. Symptoms include sneezing, watery eyes, running nose and difficulty in breathing.

Allergy is due to release of chemicals like histamine and serotonin from mast cells. Anti-histamines, adrenalin and steroids quickly reduce symptoms. Modern life style has made more children in metro cities of India sensitive, with allergies and asthma.
Autoimmunity: memory-based immunity can tell self from non-self, but sometimes, due to genetic and other unknown reasons, the body attacks self cells. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease.

Primary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus, where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes. Bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced. The thymus, near the heart beneath the breastbone, is large at birth and shrinks with age. Both provide micro-environments for development and maturation of T-lymphocytes.

Secondary lymphoid organs: spleen (filters blood, traps blood-borne microbes, reservoir of erythrocytes), lymph nodes (trap microbes in lymph and tissue fluid), tonsils, Peyer's patches of the small intestine and appendix. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), in the linings of the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts, forms about 50 per cent of lymphoid tissue in the human body.

ex.q: A child sneezes and gets watery eyes every time the house is dusted. Which antibody class and which cells and chemicals are involved, and what drugs help?
st: Dust mites act as allergens.
IgE antibodies are produced.
Mast cells release histamine and serotonin.
Anti-histamines, adrenalin and steroids reduce symptoms.
ex.a: IgE; mast cells releasing histamine and serotonin; treated with anti-histamines, adrenalin, steroids.

topics.rl: Pollution and dust in Indian cities like Delhi are linked to rising childhood asthma and allergies, a public-health concern noted even by NCERT.

topics.t: AIDS: the virus and how it spreads
topics.h: HIV hides inside the very cells meant to fight it, turning macrophages into virus factories.
p: AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is a deficiency of the immune system acquired during an individual's lifetime, so it is not a congenital disease. 'Syndrome' means a group of symptoms. AIDS was first reported in 1981.
AIDS is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), a retrovirus with an envelope enclosing an RNA genome.

Transmission: sexual contact with an infected person; transfusion of contaminated blood and blood products; sharing infected needles (as among intravenous drug abusers); from an infected mother to her child through the placenta. HIV spreads only through body fluids, not by mere touch or physical contact.

Life cycle: HIV enters macrophages, where its RNA genome is copied into viral DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase. This viral DNA gets incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs the cell to produce virus particles. Macrophages keep producing virus and act like an HIV factory.
HIV also enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates and produces progeny viruses, which attack other TH cells, steadily reducing their number.

ex.q: Explain why AIDS is called 'acquired' and why HIV is called a retrovirus.
st: Acquired: the immune deficiency develops during a person's lifetime; it is not inherited or congenital.
Retrovirus: HIV has an RNA genome copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase, the reverse of the usual DNA → RNA flow.
