ex.a: Acquired = develops during lifetime, not congenital; retrovirus = RNA genome reverse-transcribed into DNA.

topics.rl: India's NACO promotes the message that HIV does not spread by touch, hugging, sharing food or utensils, fighting stigma against people living with HIV.

topics.h: HIV is preventable, and NACO's message is simple: don't die of ignorance.
p: There is a time lag between infection and appearance of AIDS symptoms, from a few months to many years (usually 5–10 years).

As helper T cells decrease, the person suffers bouts of fever, diarrhoea and weight loss, and then infections that could otherwise be overcome: bacteria, especially Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and even parasites like Toxoplasma (opportunistic infections). The patient becomes unable to protect against these infections.

The widely used diagnostic test is ELISA (enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay). Treatment with anti-retroviral drugs is only partially effective: they prolong the patient's life but do not cure the infection.

Prevention is the best option. In India, the National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) and NGOs educate people. Measures: safe blood from blood banks, only disposable needles and syringes in hospitals, free distribution of condoms, controlling drug abuse, advocating safe sex and regular HIV check-ups in susceptible populations. The message: 'don't die of ignorance'.
Board link: HIV causes immunodeficiency because it destroys helper T cells, which are needed for B cells to make antibodies and for cell-mediated responses.

ex.q: Explain why a person with AIDS may die from a common infection like tuberculosis.
st: HIV destroys helper T-lymphocytes.
Without TH cells, B cells cannot mount strong antibody responses and cell-mediated immunity weakens.
Opportunistic pathogens like Mycobacterium then overwhelm the body.
ex.a: Loss of helper T cells cripples immunity, so opportunistic infections such as TB become severe.

topics.rl: Under NACO, India provides free anti-retroviral therapy at ART centres across the country, helping people with HIV live longer, healthier lives.

topics.h: Normal cells stop dividing when they touch their neighbours. Cancer cells have lost this 'please stop' signal.
p: Normal cells show contact inhibition: contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth. Cancer cells lose this property, keep dividing and form masses called tumours.

Benign tumours remain confined to their original location and cause little damage. Malignant tumours are masses of proliferating neoplastic (tumour) cells that grow rapidly, invade and damage surrounding tissues and starve normal cells by competing for nutrients. Cells sloughed off reach distant sites through blood and start new tumours: metastasis, the most feared property of malignant tumours.

Carcinogens: physical (ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays; non-ionising UV causes DNA damage), chemical (carcinogens in tobacco smoke are a major cause of lung cancer) and biological (oncogenic viruses with viral oncogenes). Normal cells carry cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto-oncogenes, which, when activated under certain conditions, can cause oncogenic transformation.

Detection: biopsy and histopathological studies (stained thin sections examined by a pathologist); blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts in leukaemias; radiography (X-rays), CT (computed tomography, X-rays to create 3-D images) and MRI (strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation); antibodies against cancer-specific antigens; molecular biology to detect genes for inherited susceptibility.

Treatment: surgery, radiation therapy (tumour cells irradiated lethally while protecting normal tissue), chemotherapy (drugs with side effects like hair loss and anaemia) and immunotherapy. Tumour cells can avoid immune detection, so patients are given biological response modifiers like α-interferon, which activates the immune system to destroy the tumour.

ex.q: Distinguish benign and malignant tumours on two points.
st: Spread: benign stays confined; malignant invades nearby tissues and spreads by metastasis.
Damage: benign causes little damage; malignant grows rapidly, damages tissues and starves normal cells.
ex.a: Benign: confined, little damage. Malignant: invasive, metastasises, damaging.

topics.rl: Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai and India's national cancer screening programmes stress early detection, especially of oral cancers linked to tobacco chewing.

topics.t: Drugs: opioids, cannabinoids, cocaine and tobacco
topics.h: Many substances that are abused started as medicines. The same molecule can heal under a doctor's guidance and harm when misused.
p: Opioids bind to specific opioid receptors in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. Heroin (smack), chemically diacetylmorphine, is a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound obtained by acetylation of morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum. Heroin is a depressant and slows down body functions.

Cannabinoids interact with cannabinoid receptors, mainly in the brain. They are obtained from inflorescences of Cannabis sativa; flower tops, leaves and resin give marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja. They affect the cardiovascular system. Some sportspersons abuse cannabinoids.

Coca alkaloid or cocaine is obtained from Erythroxylum coca, native to South America. It interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine, stimulating the CNS and producing euphoria and increased energy; excessive doses cause hallucinations. Atropa belladonna and Datura also have hallucinogenic properties.

Drugs like barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and LSD, normally used as medicines to help patients cope with mental illnesses like depression and insomnia, are often abused. Morphine is a very effective sedative and painkiller, useful in patients after surgery.

Tobacco contains nicotine, an alkaloid that stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline, raising blood pressure and heart rate. Smoking is associated with cancers of lung, urinary bladder and throat, bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease and gastric ulcer; tobacco chewing with oral cancer. Smoking increases carbon monoxide in blood, reducing haem-bound oxygen.

ex.q: Why does smoking reduce the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood?
st: Smoking increases carbon monoxide (CO) in the blood.
CO binds haemoglobin, reducing the concentration of haem-bound oxygen.
So less oxygen reaches the tissues.
ex.a: CO from smoke binds haemoglobin, lowering haem-bound oxygen.

topics.rl: India's COTPA law bans smoking in public places and requires health warnings on tobacco packs, and the National Tobacco Quitline helps people quit.

topics.t: Adolescence, addiction and prevention of drug abuse
topics.h: Most people who become dependent on drugs or alcohol started in their teens, which is why the teenage years are the best time for prevention.
p: Adolescence is both a period and a process of becoming mature in attitudes and beliefs; roughly 12–18 years of age. Reasons for trying drugs or alcohol include curiosity, need for adventure and excitement, experimentation, escaping problems, academic stress, media influence, unstable or unsupportive family structures and peer pressure.

Addiction is a psychological attachment to effects like euphoria and a temporary feeling of well-being. With repeated use, the tolerance level of receptors increases, so they respond only to higher doses, leading to greater intake. Dependence is the tendency of the body to show an unpleasant withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating) when regular intake is abruptly stopped.

Effects: reckless behaviour, vandalism and violence; excessive doses can cause coma and death from respiratory failure, heart failure or cerebral haemorrhage. Intravenous use risks AIDS and hepatitis B. Chronic alcohol use damages the nervous system and liver (cirrhosis); use in pregnancy harms the foetus. Anabolic steroids in females can cause masculinisation, aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, abnormal menstrual cycles, excess facial and body hair, enlargement of clitoris and deepening of voice; in males, acne, aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, reduced testicle size, decreased sperm production, kidney and liver dysfunction, breast enlargement, premature baldness and prostate enlargement.

Warning signs: drop in academic performance, unexplained absence from school, lack of interest in personal hygiene, withdrawal, isolation, depression, fatigue, aggressive and rebellious behaviour, deteriorating relationships, loss of interest in hobbies, changes in sleeping and eating habits, fluctuations in weight and appetite.

Prevention and control: avoid undue peer pressure; education and counselling; seek help from parents and peers; look for danger signs; seek professional and medical help from psychologists, psychiatrists and de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes.

ex.q: A friend has stopped attending classes, avoids everyone and has lost interest in cricket, which he loved. What could this indicate, and what should you do?
st: Absence, isolation and loss of interest in hobbies are warning signs of possible drug or alcohol abuse (or other distress).
Do not judge or confront aggressively; talk to him with care.
Inform a trusted adult or counsellor so he can get professional help.
ex.a: Possible warning signs of drug abuse; speak kindly and involve parents, teachers or counsellors for professional help.

topics.rl: India's Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan and the national toll-free de-addiction helpline (14446) offer confidential help to anyone affected by drug or alcohol use.

topics.t: Microbes everywhere and lactic acid bacteria
topics.h: The spoonful of old curd your grandmother adds to warm milk holds millions of bacteria, ready to turn tonight's milk into tomorrow's dahi.
p: Microbes are present everywhere: in soil, water, air, inside our bodies and in other animals and plants. They are found even where no other life form could exist, such as deep inside geysers (thermal vents) where temperature may be as high as 100 °C, deep in the soil, under layers of snow several metres thick, and in highly acidic environments.

Microbes are diverse: protozoa, bacteria, fungi, microscopic animal and plant viruses, viroids and prions (proteinaceous infectious agents). Bacteria and many fungi can be grown on nutritive media to form colonies visible to the naked eye.
Lactobacillus and others, called lactic acid bacteria (LAB), grow in milk and convert it to curd. They produce acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins.

A small amount of curd added to fresh milk as inoculum or starter contains millions of LAB, which multiply at suitable temperatures. Curd has better nutritional quality than milk as LAB increase vitamin B₁₂. In our stomach, LAB also check disease-causing microbes.

ex.q: Why does milk set into curd faster on a warm summer day than on a cold winter night, after adding starter?
st: The starter adds LAB to the milk.
LAB multiply faster at suitable warm temperatures.
Faster growth produces acid sooner, coagulating milk proteins sooner.
ex.a: Warm temperature speeds LAB growth and acid production, so curd sets faster.

topics.rl: Dairy cooperatives like Amul use carefully selected LAB starter cultures to make curd and buttermilk of uniform taste across India.

topics.h: The fluffy rise of idli batter overnight and the big holes in Swiss cheese have the same cause: carbon dioxide made by microbes.
p: The dough used for dosa and idli is fermented by bacteria; its puffed-up appearance is due to production of CO₂ gas. Bread dough is fermented using baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Toddy, a traditional drink of some parts of southern India, is made by fermenting sap from palms.
Microbes are also used to ferment fish, soyabean and bamboo shoots to make foods.

Cheese is one of the oldest foods made with microbes. The large holes in Swiss cheese are due to production of a large amount of CO₂ by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii. Roquefort cheese is ripened by growing specific fungi on it, which gives it a particular flavour.

ex.q: Name the microbe and explain the 'holes' in Swiss cheese and the puffing of bread dough.
st: Swiss cheese: Propionibacterium sharmanii produces large amounts of CO₂, forming holes.
Bread: Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments sugars, releasing CO₂ that puffs the dough.
ex.a: Both are due to CO₂: Propionibacterium sharmanii (cheese) and baker's yeast (bread).

topics.rl: North-eastern Indian foods like fermented bamboo shoot (bas tenga, eaten in Assam) and fermented soyabean (axone of Nagaland) rely on microbes, as NCERT notes.

topics.h: Penicillin, the first antibiotic, was found by accident when a mould contaminated an unwashed culture plate.
p: The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, called brewer's yeast in this use, ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol, used for wine, beer, whisky, brandy and rum. Wine and beer are produced without distillation; whisky, brandy and rum are made by distillation of the fermented broth.

Antibiotics are chemical substances produced by some microbes that can kill or retard the growth of other (disease-causing) microbes. 'Anti' means against and 'bio' life; with reference to humans they are pro-life.

Penicillin was the first antibiotic discovered, by chance. Alexander Fleming, working on Staphylococci, saw that they could not grow around a mould in an unwashed culture plate. He named the chemical penicillin after the mould Penicillium notatum.

Its full potential as an antibiotic was established later by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey. It was used extensively to treat American soldiers wounded in World War II. Fleming, Chain and Florey won the Nobel Prize in 1945.
Antibiotics have greatly improved our ability to treat deadly diseases such as plague, whooping cough (kali khansi), diphtheria (gal ghotu) and leprosy (kusht rog).

ex.q: Classify wine, rum, beer and brandy as distilled or non-distilled beverages.
st: Non-distilled: produced directly by fermentation, e.g. wine and beer.
Distilled: fermented broth is distilled, e.g. whisky, brandy and rum.
ex.a: Non-distilled: wine, beer; distilled: rum, brandy

topics.rl: India's National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance urges doctors and patients to use antibiotics only when truly needed, to keep Fleming's gift working.

topics.h: The 'clot buster' given to some heart-attack patients in emergency wards comes from a bacterium.
p: Organic acids: citric acid from Aspergillus niger (a fungus); acetic acid from Acetobacter aceti (a bacterium); butyric acid from Clostridium butylicum (a bacterium); lactic acid from Lactobacillus (a bacterium). Saccharomyces cerevisiae is used for commercial production of ethanol.
Enzymes: lipases are used in detergent formulations to remove oily stains from laundry. Bottled fruit juices are clearer than home-made ones because they are clarified using pectinases and proteases.

Streptokinase, produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering, is used as a 'clot buster' to remove clots from blood vessels of patients who have had a myocardial infarction leading to heart attack.
Cyclosporin A, used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients, is produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum.
Statins, produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus, are blood-cholesterol lowering agents. They act by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for cholesterol synthesis.

ex.q: Name the microbe used for: (a) citric acid, (b) statins, (c) cyclosporin A, (d) streptokinase, (e) Swiss cheese.
st: (a) Aspergillus niger (fungus).
(b) Monascus purpureus (yeast).
(c) Trichoderma polysporum (fungus).
(d) Streptococcus (bacterium); (e) Propionibacterium sharmanii (bacterium).
ex.a: Aspergillus niger, Monascus purpureus, Trichoderma polysporum, Streptococcus, Propionibacterium sharmanii

topics.rl: Indian biotech firms produce enzymes like lipases and proteases for the detergent and juice industries, a major microbial business.

topics.t: Sewage treatment: primary, secondary and BOD
topics.h: A city of a few lakh people produces crores of litres of sewage daily, and microbes clean most of it for free.
p: Sewage is municipal waste-water, mainly human excreta. It contains large amounts of organic matter and microbes, many pathogenic, so it cannot be released directly into rivers. It is treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) to make it less polluting.

Primary treatment is physical removal of particles by filtration and sedimentation. Floating debris is removed by sequential filtration; grit (soil and small pebbles) by sedimentation. Settled solids form the primary sludge, and the supernatant forms the effluent.

Secondary (biological) treatment: the primary effluent goes into large aeration tanks, agitated mechanically with air pumped in. Useful aerobic microbes grow vigorously into flocs: masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments forming mesh-like structures. They consume most of the organic matter, significantly reducing the BOD of the effluent.

BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) is the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria. It measures the rate of oxygen uptake by microbes and indirectly the organic matter present. The greater the BOD, the greater the polluting potential.

ex.q: Water samples have BOD of 8 mg/L (sample A) and 200 mg/L (sample B). Which is more polluted with organic matter, and why?
st: BOD indirectly measures organic matter.
Higher BOD means more organic matter to oxidise.
Sample B has 200/8 = 25 times higher BOD.
ex.a: Sample B is far more polluted (25 times higher BOD).

topics.rl: The Central Pollution Control Board uses BOD as a key indicator to grade river stretches in India, including the Ganga and Yamuna.

topics.t: Activated sludge, anaerobic digesters and river action plans
topics.h: The sludge from a sewage plant can light a stove: anaerobic digesters turn it into biogas.
p: Once BOD is reduced significantly, the effluent passes into a settling tank where bacterial flocs sediment. This sediment is the activated sludge.
A small part of the activated sludge is pumped back to the aeration tank to serve as inoculum. The major remaining part is pumped into large tanks called anaerobic sludge digesters.

In the digesters, bacteria growing anaerobically digest the bacteria and fungi in the sludge, producing a mixture of methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide. These gases form biogas, which is inflammable and can be used as a source of energy.

The effluent from secondary treatment is generally released into natural water bodies like rivers and streams. The Ministry of Environment and Forests initiated the Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan to build many STPs so that only treated sewage is discharged into rivers.
Exam focus: explain primary and secondary treatment, define BOD and interpret BOD data (lower BOD after treatment = success), and describe a biogas plant.

ex.q: What are the two fates of activated sludge, and why is each useful?
st: A small part returns to the aeration tank as inoculum, seeding it with active flocs.
The major part goes to anaerobic sludge digesters.
There anaerobic bacteria digest it, producing biogas for energy.
ex.a: Small part → aeration tank as inoculum; major part → anaerobic digesters → biogas.

topics.rl: Some modern STPs built under Namami Gange capture biogas from sludge digesters to run their own machinery.

topics.h: In thousands of Indian villages, cow dung lights the stove, thanks to microbes living in a cow's stomach.
p: Biogas is a mixture of gases, predominantly methane, produced by microbial activity and used as fuel.

Certain bacteria growing anaerobically on cellulosic material produce large amounts of methane along with CO₂ and H₂. They are called methanogens; a common one is Methanobacterium. They occur in anaerobic sludge of sewage treatment and in the rumen of cattle, where they help break down cellulose and play an important role in cattle nutrition. So cattle dung (gobar) is rich in them, and its biogas is called gobar gas.

A biogas plant has a concrete tank (10–15 feet deep) into which bio-wastes are collected and a slurry of dung is fed. A floating cover over the slurry keeps rising as gas is produced. An outlet pipe supplies biogas to nearby houses. Spent slurry is removed through another outlet and used as fertiliser.

Biogas is used for cooking and lighting. The technology was developed in India mainly through the efforts of the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).

ex.q: Why does cattle dung make good raw material for a biogas plant?
st: Methanogens live in the rumen of cattle.
They help digest the cellulose in cattle food.
So dung is rich in methanogens and cellulosic matter, ideal for anaerobic methane production.
ex.a: Dung is rich in methanogens (from the rumen) and cellulose.

topics.rl: Under the GOBAR-Dhan scheme, Indian villages are setting up community biogas plants to turn cattle dung and farm waste into clean cooking gas and manure.

topics.h: A ladybird beetle can eat many aphids a day. Farmers who welcome ladybirds spray fewer chemicals.
p: Biocontrol is the use of biological methods to control plant diseases and pests. Heavy use of chemical insecticides and pesticides is toxic and extremely harmful to humans, animals and the environment (soil, groundwater, fruits, vegetables, crop plants).

Organic farmers prefer a holistic approach: a biodiversity of organisms in the field, with natural predation as the control. Eradicating all 'pests' is not only impossible but undesirable, because beneficial predators and parasites depend on them. Knowing the life forms in the field, their life cycles, feeding patterns and habitats is key to biological farming.
Natural predators: the ladybird (beetle with red and black markings) controls aphids, and dragonflies control mosquitoes.

Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is used to control butterfly caterpillars. Dried spores in sachets are mixed with water and sprayed on vulnerable plants like brassicas and fruit trees. Insect larvae eat them; the toxin released in the larval gut kills them, leaving other insects unharmed.
Through genetic engineering, B. thuringiensis toxin genes have been introduced into plants, making them resistant to insect pests; Bt-cotton is cultivated in some states of India.

ex.q: Why is spraying Bt spores safer for a farm ecosystem than spraying a broad-spectrum chemical insecticide?
st: Bt toxin acts in the gut of specific insect larvae like caterpillars.
It leaves other insects, including predators and pollinators, unharmed.
Broad-spectrum chemicals kill many non-target organisms and pollute soil and water.
ex.a: Bt is specific to target larvae; chemicals harm non-target organisms and the environment.

topics.rl: Sikkim, declared India's first fully organic state, relies on biological pest control instead of chemical pesticides.

topics.t: Trichoderma, baculoviruses and benefits of biocontrol
topics.h: Some viruses are a farmer's friends: baculoviruses attack only specific insect pests and leave everything else alone.
p: Trichoderma species are free-living fungi, very common in root ecosystems. They are effective biocontrol agents of several plant pathogens.
Baculoviruses are pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods. The majority used as biological control agents are in the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus.
These viruses are excellent candidates for species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticidal applications. They have no negative impacts on plants, mammals, birds, fish or even non-target insects.
This is especially desirable in an overall integrated pest management (IPM) programme, or when an ecologically sensitive area is being treated.

Benefits of biocontrol and biofertilisers over chemicals: less toxic residue in food, soil and water; protection of beneficial organisms and biodiversity; reduced pollution; better long-term soil health; and reduced dependence on costly chemicals.

ex.q: Why are baculoviruses preferred for pest control in an ecologically sensitive area?
st: They are species-specific and narrow-spectrum.
They do not harm plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects.
So they control the pest without disturbing the rest of the ecosystem.
ex.a: They target only specific pests and are harmless to non-target organisms.

topics.rl: Indian agricultural universities sell Trichoderma formulations to farmers for seed and soil treatment against root diseases.

topics.h: Rice farmers in Odisha and Tamil Nadu have long known that blue-green algae in flooded paddy fields act like free fertiliser.
p: Biofertilisers are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of soil, reducing dependence on chemical fertilisers that pollute the environment. Main sources: bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria.
Rhizobium forms root nodules on leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms used by the plant as nutrient (symbiotic).
Free-living soil bacteria Azospirillum and Azotobacter also fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching soil nitrogen.

Mycorrhiza: symbiotic association of fungi with plant roots; many members of the genus Glomus form mycorrhiza. The fungus absorbs phosphorus from soil and passes it to the plant. Such plants also show resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought, and overall increased growth.

Cyanobacteria are autotrophic microbes in aquatic and terrestrial environments; many fix atmospheric nitrogen, e.g. Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria. In paddy fields they are important biofertilisers. Blue-green algae also add organic matter to soil and increase its fertility.

ex.q: A farmer wants to improve phosphorus uptake in his crop and also make it more drought-tolerant. Which biofertiliser suits him, and how does it work?
st: Mycorrhizal fungi (e.g. Glomus) absorb phosphorus and pass it to the plant.
Mycorrhizal plants also show tolerance to drought and salinity.
ex.a: Mycorrhiza (Glomus); the fungus absorbs phosphorus for the plant and increases drought tolerance.

topics.rl: Government schemes promote biofertiliser packets of Rhizobium, Azotobacter and blue-green algae to farmers as part of soil health programmes.

topics.t: What biotechnology is and its two core techniques
topics.h: Your grandmother making curd and a Bengaluru lab making insulin in bacteria are both doing biotechnology, separated by a few thousand years of science.
p: Biotechnology deals with techniques of using live organisms or enzymes from organisms to produce products and processes useful to humans. The European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB) defines it as the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services.

Traditional biotechnology includes making curd, bread or wine using microbes. Modern biotechnology uses genetically modified organisms (GMOs) to produce useful products on a large scale, and includes techniques like in vitro fertilisation, synthesis of a gene, DNA vaccines and correcting a defective gene.

Two core techniques: genetic engineering, which alters the chemistry of genetic material (DNA and RNA), introduces it into host organisms and thus changes their phenotype; and bioprocess engineering, which maintains sterile (microbial contamination-free) conditions to grow only the desired microbe or eukaryotic cell in large quantities for manufacturing products like antibiotics, vaccines and enzymes.

Asexual reproduction preserves genetic information, while sexual reproduction permits variation. Traditional hybridisation often includes and multiplies undesirable genes along with desired ones. Genetic engineering (recombinant DNA, gene cloning and gene transfer) overcomes this by introducing only one or a set of desirable genes.

ex.q: A breeder wants to add a drought-tolerance gene to a rice variety without bringing in any other genes from the donor. Why is genetic engineering better than conventional hybridisation here?
st: Hybridisation mixes whole genomes, carrying undesirable genes along with the desired one.
Genetic engineering can isolate and introduce only the specific desired gene.
ex.a: Genetic engineering transfers only the desired gene; hybridisation brings unwanted genes too.

topics.rl: India's Department of Biotechnology (DBT) funds both traditional fermentation research and modern genetic engineering, from probiotics to recombinant vaccines.

topics.t: Making a recombinant DNA: the first steps
topics.h: In 1972, two scientists stitched an antibiotic-resistance gene into a plasmid and launched the age of genetic engineering.
p: Three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism: (i) identification of DNA with desirable genes; (ii) introduction of the identified DNA into the host; (iii) maintenance of introduced DNA in the host and its transfer to progeny.

An alien piece of DNA cannot multiply by itself in a host. It must be linked to a sequence called the origin of replication (ori), which initiates replication. Making multiple identical copies of any template DNA in this way is called cloning.

Plasmids are autonomously replicating, circular, extra-chromosomal DNA in bacteria. In 1972, Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer made the first recombinant DNA: they cut out a piece of DNA carrying an antibiotic-resistance gene and linked it to a native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium.

Cutting DNA at specific locations became possible with 'molecular scissors', the restriction enzymes. The cut piece was joined to plasmid DNA by DNA ligase, which acts on cut DNA molecules and joins their ends, creating a circular, autonomously replicating recombinant DNA in vitro.

When this recombinant DNA was transferred into Escherichia coli, a bacterium closely related to Salmonella, it replicated using the host's DNA polymerase and made multiple copies: cloning of the antibiotic-resistance gene in E. coli.

ex.q: What role does each play in making recombinant DNA: restriction enzyme, DNA ligase, plasmid, origin of replication?
st: Restriction enzyme cuts DNA at specific sites.
DNA ligase joins the cut ends.
Plasmid acts as the vector carrying the gene into the host.
Ori lets the linked DNA replicate in the host.
ex.a: Cut (restriction enzyme), join (ligase), carry (plasmid vector), replicate (ori).

topics.rl: Indian biotech firms producing recombinant hepatitis B vaccine and insulin all follow the Cohen–Boyer logic of cut, paste and clone.

topics.t: Restriction enzymes and how they are named
topics.h: EcoRI's name is a tiny address label: genus, species, strain and serial number, all packed into five characters.
p: In 1963, two enzymes restricting the growth of bacteriophage in E. coli were isolated: one added methyl groups to DNA, the other cut DNA. The latter was called restriction endonuclease.

The first restriction endonuclease whose function depended on a specific DNA sequence, Hind II, was isolated and characterised five years later. It always cut DNA at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of six base pairs, called its recognition sequence. Today more than 900 restriction enzymes have been isolated from over 230 strains of bacteria.

Naming convention: the first letter is from the genus and the next two from the species of the prokaryote; the fourth letter is from the strain; the Roman numeral shows the order of isolation. EcoRI: E = Escherichia, co = coli, R = strain RY 13, I = first enzyme isolated from that strain.
Restriction enzymes belong to the nucleases. Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA; endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within DNA.

ex.q: Decode the name HindIII using the naming convention, given that it comes from Haemophilus influenzae strain Rd.
st: H = genus Haemophilus; in = species influenzae.
d = strain Rd.
III = third enzyme isolated from this strain.
ex.a: Haemophilus influenzae, strain Rd, third enzyme isolated

topics.rl: Biotech supply companies in India stock dozens of named restriction enzymes; reading the label tells a researcher exactly which bacterium it came from.

topics.h: 'MALAYALAM' reads the same both ways; restriction sites are DNA's version, reading the same on both strands.
p: A palindromic DNA sequence reads the same on the two strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same, e.g. 5′-GAATTC-3′ on one strand and 5′-GAATTC-3′ on the other (3′-CTTAAG-5′ when read backwards).
Each restriction endonuclease inspects DNA, binds to its recognition sequence and cuts each strand at specific points in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

Restriction enzymes cut a little away from the centre of the palindrome, but between the same two bases on the opposite strands. This leaves overhanging single-stranded stretches called sticky ends, which form hydrogen bonds with complementary cut counterparts.

DNA cut by the same restriction enzyme gives fragments with the same kind of sticky ends; these can be joined end-to-end using DNA ligase. Hence the vector and source DNA must be cut with the same enzyme.
Exercise: EcoRI cuts 5′-G^AATTC-3′ between G and A on both strands, leaving 5′-AATT overhangs on each end.

ex.q: Is 5′-GGATCC-3′ palindromic? Check by writing its complementary strand.
st: Complement of 5′-GGATCC-3′ is 3′-CCTAGG-5′.
Reading the complement 5′→3′ gives GGATCC.
Both strands read the same in 5′→3′ direction.
ex.a: Yes, it is palindromic (it is the BamHI site).

topics.rl: Gene-cloning kits used in Indian college labs rely on matching sticky ends; a mismatch means the gene simply won't stick.

topics.h: Running DNA through a gel is like a race through a crowded mela: the smaller ones slip through faster.
p: DNA fragments from restriction digestion are separated by gel electrophoresis. DNA is negatively charged, so in an electric field it moves towards the anode (positive electrode) through a matrix.

The most commonly used matrix is agarose, a natural polymer extracted from seaweeds. Fragments separate according to size by the sieving effect of the gel: the smaller the fragment, the farther it moves.

DNA is visible only after staining with ethidium bromide and exposure to UV radiation, which shows bright orange bands. Bands are cut out and the DNA extracted from the gel piece: elution. Purified fragments are used to construct recombinant DNA. Lab safety: ethidium bromide is a mutagen, so gloves are worn, and UV light needs eye and skin protection.

Restriction digestion is done by incubating purified DNA with the enzyme under optimal conditions; agarose gel electrophoresis is used to check its progress. The vector DNA is cut with the same enzyme, and the gene of interest and the cut vector are mixed with ligase to form recombinant DNA.

ex.q: Fragments of 500 bp, 2000 bp and 1000 bp are loaded in one well. Arrange them from the band nearest the well to the farthest.
st: Smaller fragments move farther through the agarose sieve.
Largest (2000 bp) stays nearest the well; then 1000 bp; smallest (500 bp) moves farthest.
ex.a: 2000 bp (nearest) → 1000 bp → 500 bp (farthest)

topics.rl: Forensic and diagnostic labs across India run agarose gels every day; the orange bands under UV are a familiar sight in a biotech lab.

topics.t: Cloning vectors and selection of recombinants
topics.h: A blue colony means 'no insert here'; a white one says 'I carry your gene'. Colour does the screening.
p: Plasmids and bacteriophages replicate in bacteria independently of chromosomal DNA. Bacteriophages have very high copy numbers; some plasmids have only one or two copies per cell, others 15–100.

Features of a cloning vector: (i) origin of replication (ori), which starts replication and also controls the copy number of linked DNA; (ii) selectable marker, which helps identify and eliminate non-transformants and allows growth of transformants. Genes for resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin are useful markers for E. coli, since normal E. coli cells lack them.

(iii) Cloning (recognition) sites: very few, preferably single, recognition sites for commonly used restriction enzymes, since more sites would give several fragments and complicate cloning. In pBR322, inserting foreign DNA at the BamHI site of the tetracycline-resistance gene (tetʳ) inactivates it. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline; non-recombinants grow on both. pBR322 also has ampʳ, ori and rop (proteins for plasmid replication).

Selection by antibiotic inactivation needs two plates. An easier method uses insertional inactivation of the β-galactosidase gene: with a chromogenic substrate, colonies with plasmids lacking an insert are blue; colonies with an insert (recombinants) produce no colour.

Transformation is the procedure by which a piece of DNA is introduced into a host bacterium. Exam diagram: label pBR322 with ori, rop, ampʳ, tetʳ and sites such as EcoRI, HindIII, BamHI, SalI, PvuI, PstI, ClaI and PvuII.

ex.q: A gene is inserted at the BamHI site of pBR322 and transformed into E. coli. Predict growth of (a) recombinants and (b) non-recombinant transformants on ampicillin and on tetracycline plates.
st: BamHI site lies in tetʳ, so an insert inactivates tetracycline resistance.
(a) Recombinants: ampʳ intact, tetʳ inactivated → grow on ampicillin, not on tetracycline.
(b) Non-recombinants: both genes intact → grow on both.
ex.a: Recombinants: amp yes, tet no. Non-recombinants: grow on both.

topics.rl: Blue-white screening is a staple experiment in Indian university biotech courses, introducing students to insertional inactivation.

topics.t: Vectors for plants and animals and getting DNA into hosts
topics.h: Agrobacterium has been genetically engineering plants for millions of years. Scientists simply borrowed its trick.
p: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants, delivers a piece of DNA called T-DNA that transforms normal plant cells into a tumour and directs them to make chemicals the pathogen needs. Its tumour-inducing (Ti) plasmid has been modified into a cloning vector that is no longer pathogenic but can still deliver genes of interest into many plants.
Similarly, retroviruses can transform normal animal cells into cancerous cells. Disarmed retroviruses are now used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells.

DNA is hydrophilic and cannot pass through cell membranes, so bacteria must first be made competent: treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium, which increases DNA entry through pores in the cell wall. Recombinant DNA is then forced in by incubating cells with rDNA on ice, giving a brief heat shock at 42 °C, and putting them back on ice.

Other methods: micro-injection, where rDNA is injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell; biolistics or gene gun, where plant cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA; and disarmed pathogen vectors that transfer rDNA when they infect a cell.

ex.q: Arrange the steps to make E. coli take up recombinant DNA by heat shock.
st: Treat cells with a divalent cation like Ca²⁺ to make them competent.
Incubate cells with rDNA on ice.
Heat shock briefly at 42 °C.
Put the cells back on ice.
ex.a: Ca²⁺ treatment → ice with rDNA → 42 °C heat shock → back on ice

topics.rl: Indian crop scientists developing GM mustard used Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, while some cereal transformations use the gene gun.

topics.t: Isolating DNA: the first process of rDNA technology
topics.h: You can spool DNA out of crushed fruit using dish soap, salt and ice-cold alcohol in a school lab.
p: The processes of recombinant DNA technology: isolation of DNA; fragmentation of DNA by restriction endonucleases; isolation of the desired DNA fragment; ligation of the fragment into a vector; transferring the recombinant DNA into the host; culturing host cells in a medium at large scale; and extraction of the desired product.
To isolate pure DNA, cells must be broken open to release DNA with RNA, proteins, polysaccharides and lipids. Enzymes used: lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plant cells and chitinase for fungi.
DNA is intertwined with proteins such as histones. RNA is removed by ribonuclease; proteins by protease; other molecules by appropriate treatments.

Purified DNA precipitates out on adding chilled ethanol and is seen as a collection of fine threads in the suspension (spooling). Lab safety: handle ethanol away from flames and wear gloves and goggles.

ex.q: Which enzyme would you use to break open cells of (a) E. coli, (b) a fungus, (c) a spinach leaf? Which enzymes remove RNA and protein afterwards?
st: (a) Bacteria: lysozyme.
(b) Fungus: chitinase.
(c) Plant cells: cellulase.
RNA: ribonuclease; protein: protease.
ex.a: Lysozyme, chitinase, cellulase; then ribonuclease and protease.

topics.rl: DNA extraction kits used in COVID-era labs across India followed the same logic: break cells, remove contaminants, precipitate pure nucleic acid.

topics.h: Starting with a single DNA molecule, PCR can make about a billion copies in a few hours. That's why it can test a tiny swab.
p: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) makes multiple copies of a gene of interest in vitro using two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of DNA) and DNA polymerase.

Each cycle has three steps: denaturation (high temperature separates the double-stranded DNA), annealing (primers bind to the complementary regions), and extension (DNA polymerase extends the primers using nucleotides and the genomic DNA as template).

Repeated cycles amplify the DNA about a billion times (2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 × 10⁹ after 30 cycles). This needs a thermostable DNA polymerase isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus (Taq polymerase), which stays active during high-temperature denaturation. The amplified fragment can be ligated with a vector for further cloning.

Selecting transformants: if rDNA carrying an ampicillin-resistance gene is transferred into E. coli, transformed cells become ampicillin-resistant. On agar plates with ampicillin, only transformants grow; untransformed cells die. Here the ampicillin-resistance gene is the selectable marker.

ex.q: How many double-stranded DNA copies are produced from one molecule after 10 PCR cycles, assuming perfect doubling?
st: Each cycle doubles the number of copies.
After n cycles: 2ⁿ copies.
ex.a: 1024 copies

topics.rl: RT-PCR tests used during COVID-19 across India relied on PCR's exponential amplification to detect tiny amounts of viral genetic material.

topics.h: A bioreactor is like a high-tech pressure cooker for microbes, keeping temperature, pH and oxygen just right for producing medicines.
p: A protein made by a gene expressed in a heterologous (foreign) host is a recombinant protein. Cells with cloned genes may be grown at small scale to extract the protein, or in continuous culture, where used medium is drained from one side and fresh medium added from the other, keeping cells in their most active log/exponential phase for higher yields.

To produce large quantities, bioreactors handling large volumes (100–1000 litres) of culture are needed. A bioreactor is a vessel in which raw materials are biologically converted into specific products using microbial, plant, animal or human cells. It provides optimum growth conditions: temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins and oxygen.

The most common are stirred-tank bioreactors, usually cylindrical or with a curved base to facilitate mixing. A stirrer ensures even mixing and oxygen availability; alternatively, air can be bubbled through (sparged stirred-tank bioreactor, through which sterile air bubbles are sparged). Parts: agitator system, oxygen delivery system, foam control system, temperature control system, pH control system and sampling ports.

Downstream processing: after the biosynthetic stage, the product undergoes separation and purification. It is formulated with suitable preservatives; drugs undergo thorough clinical trials, and strict quality control testing is required. These vary from product to product.

ex.q: List the systems of a stirred-tank bioreactor and state why the base is often curved.
st: Systems: agitator, oxygen delivery, foam control, temperature control, pH control, sampling ports.
A curved base helps mix the reactor contents evenly.
ex.a: Agitator, oxygen delivery, foam control, temperature and pH control, sampling ports; curved base for mixing.

topics.rl: Indian vaccine makers like those in Pune and Hyderabad run huge bioreactors followed by careful downstream processing and quality testing before any batch is released.

topics.t: Applications of biotechnology and options for agriculture
topics.h: The Green Revolution helped India go from importing grain to exporting it, yet scientists say the next jump in food production may need genetic engineering.
p: Biotechnology is applied in therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops for agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment and energy production.

Three critical research areas: (i) providing the best catalyst as an improved organism (usually a microbe) or pure enzyme; (ii) creating optimal conditions through engineering for the catalyst to act; (iii) downstream processing technologies to purify the protein or organic compound.
Three options for increasing food production: agro-chemical based agriculture, organic agriculture and genetically engineered crop-based agriculture.

The Green Revolution tripled food supply, but it is still not enough for the growing population. Yield gains came partly from improved varieties but mainly from better management and agrochemicals (fertilisers and pesticides), which are often too expensive for farmers in the developing world; further gains by conventional breeding are limited. Genetically modified organisms (GMOs), whose genes have been altered by manipulation, offer a possible solution.

ex.q: List the three options for increasing food production and identify which one uses GMOs.
st: Agro-chemical based agriculture.
Organic agriculture.
Genetically engineered crop-based agriculture uses GMOs.
ex.a: Agro-chemical, organic, and GM crop-based agriculture (the third uses GMOs).

topics.rl: Punjab and Haryana were the heartland of India's Green Revolution; today concerns about soil health and groundwater push the search for new options.

topics.h: Golden rice, engineered to make vitamin A precursor, was developed to fight a deficiency that can cause blindness in children.
p: Genetic modification has made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses: cold, drought, salt and heat.
It has reduced reliance on chemical pesticides through pest-resistant crops, and helped reduce post-harvest losses.
It has increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants, preventing early exhaustion of soil fertility.
It has enhanced nutritional value of food, e.g. golden rice, i.e. vitamin A enriched rice.
GM has also been used to create tailor-made plants supplying alternative resources to industries, such as starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals.

ex.q: Match each GM benefit to a problem: (a) salty coastal soils, (b) bollworm attack, (c) vitamin A deficiency.
st: (a) Tolerance to abiotic stress (salt).
(b) Pest-resistant crops reduce pesticide use.
(c) Enhanced nutritional value, e.g. golden rice.
ex.a: (a) Salt-tolerant crops (b) Pest-resistant crops (c) Vitamin A-enriched golden rice

topics.rl: Researchers in India are developing stress-tolerant crop varieties for regions like coastal Odisha, where salinity after cyclones hurts paddy yields.

topics.t: Bt crops: how Bt toxin kills pests
topics.h: Bt cotton's toxin is harmless inside the bacterium that makes it, and switches on only in the alkaline gut of a caterpillar.
p: Bt toxin is produced by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt). The Bt toxin gene has been cloned and expressed in plants to give insect resistance without insecticides, in effect a bio-pesticide. Examples: Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato and soyabean.

Some strains of B. thuringiensis produce proteins that kill certain insects such as lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes). B. thuringiensis forms protein crystals containing a toxic insecticidal protein during a particular phase of growth.

Why the toxin does not kill Bacillus: it exists as an inactive protoxin. Once an insect ingests it, the alkaline pH of the gut solubilises the crystals and converts the protoxin to its active form. The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, causing cell swelling and lysis, and finally death of the insect.

The toxin is coded by cry genes. The choice of gene depends on the crop and target pest, since most Bt toxins are insect-group specific. Proteins encoded by cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms; that of cryIAb controls corn borer.

ex.q: Explain why Bt toxin kills a bollworm but does not kill the Bacillus that produces it.
st: In the bacterium, the toxin is an inactive protoxin.
In the insect's alkaline gut, crystals dissolve and protoxin becomes active.
Active toxin makes pores in midgut epithelial cells, causing swelling, lysis and death.
ex.a: It is inactive (protoxin) in the bacterium and activated only by the alkaline insect gut.

topics.rl: Bt cotton, approved in India in 2002, now covers most of India's cotton area, changing farming in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana.

topics.h: A tobacco plant can be engineered to make a molecule that silences a worm's own gene, so the parasite cannot survive on it.
p: RNA interference (RNAi) takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defence. It silences a specific mRNA by a complementary double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) molecule that binds to the mRNA and prevents its translation.
The complementary RNA may come from infection by viruses with RNA genomes or from mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.
A nematode, Meloidogyne incognita, infects the roots of tobacco plants and greatly reduces yield.

Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into tobacco so that host cells produced both sense and anti-sense RNA. Being complementary, these formed dsRNA, which initiated RNAi and silenced a specific mRNA of the nematode.
As a result, the parasite could not survive in the transgenic host expressing the specific interfering RNA, and the transgenic plant was protected.

ex.q: Arrange the steps by which RNAi protects tobacco from Meloidogyne incognita.
st: Agrobacterium vector introduces nematode-specific genes into tobacco.
Plant cells produce sense and anti-sense RNA.
They pair to form dsRNA, triggering RNAi.
The nematode's specific mRNA is silenced and it cannot survive.
ex.a: Gene transfer → sense + anti-sense RNA → dsRNA → silencing of nematode mRNA → parasite dies

topics.rl: Root-knot nematodes damage vegetables across India; RNAi-based strategies are being studied by Indian scientists as an eco-friendly control method.

topics.h: Before 1983, diabetic patients used insulin from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs. Some patients reacted to this foreign protein.
p: rDNA technology enables mass production of safe and more effective therapeutic drugs. Recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses common with products from non-human sources. About 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use worldwide; in India 12 are being marketed.
Insulin for diabetes was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs; some patients developed allergy or other reactions to the foreign protein.

Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, A and B, linked by disulphide bridges. In mammals it is synthesised as a pro-hormone with an extra stretch, the C peptide, which is removed during maturation. Getting insulin assembled into its mature form was the main challenge.

In 1983, Eli Lilly, an American company, prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them in plasmids of E. coli. Chains A and B were produced separately, extracted and combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin.

ex.q: Why did Eli Lilly produce chains A and B separately instead of producing pro-insulin?
st: Mature insulin has A and B chains linked by disulphide bridges, without the C peptide.
Processing pro-insulin (removing C peptide) was the main challenge in bacteria.
Making A and B separately and joining them by disulphide bonds avoided this problem.
ex.a: To avoid the difficulty of processing pro-insulin; A and B chains were made separately and joined by disulphide bonds.

topics.rl: Indian companies such as Biocon in Bengaluru produce recombinant human insulin at large scale, making it more affordable for millions of diabetics.

topics.h: In 1990 a four-year-old girl became the first person to receive clinical gene therapy, for a disorder that crippled her immune system.
p: Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo. Genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a disease: a normal gene is delivered to take over the function of, and compensate for, the non-functional gene.

The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. ADA is crucial for the immune system to function; the disorder is caused by deletion of the ADA gene.

In some children ADA deficiency can be cured by bone marrow transplantation; in others it can be treated by enzyme replacement therapy (functional ADA given by injection). Neither approach is completely curative.

Gene therapy: lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture; functional ADA cDNA is introduced into them using a retroviral vector; the cells are returned to the patient. Because these cells are not immortal, the patient needs periodic infusion of such engineered lymphocytes.

If the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could be a permanent cure. (Exam outline: production of human insulin and gene therapy for ADA deficiency are favourite long answers.)

ex.q: Why does a patient treated by lymphocyte-based gene therapy for ADA deficiency need repeated infusions?
st: Functional ADA cDNA is introduced into the patient's cultured lymphocytes.
Lymphocytes are not immortal; they die after some time.
New engineered lymphocytes must be infused periodically.
ex.a: The engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so periodic infusions are needed.

topics.rl: Gene therapy for inherited blood disorders is now being tested in India; for example, CMC Vellore has run a clinical trial of gene therapy for haemophilia.

topics.t: Molecular diagnosis: PCR, probes and ELISA
topics.h: PCR can find a virus long before you feel sick, because it multiplies the tiny amount of viral nucleic acid until it can be detected.
p: Early diagnosis is essential for effective treatment. Conventional methods (serum and urine analysis etc.) cannot detect disease early. Recombinant DNA technology, PCR and ELISA serve the purpose of early diagnosis.

By the time disease symptoms appear, pathogen concentration is already high. A very low concentration of bacteria or virus can be detected by amplifying their nucleic acid using PCR. PCR is routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients, mutations in genes in suspected cancer patients, and many other genetic disorders.

A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule (probe) is allowed to hybridise to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells and detected by autoradiography. A clone with a mutated gene will not appear on the photographic film, because the probe will not be complementary to the mutated gene.
ELISA is based on antigen–antibody interaction. Infection can be detected by the presence of pathogen antigens (proteins, glycoproteins etc.) or by detecting antibodies made against the pathogen.

ex.q: A patient was possibly exposed to HIV only a short time ago and shows no symptoms. Which method can detect the virus earliest, and why?
st: Symptoms appear only when pathogen levels are high.
PCR amplifies even very small amounts of viral nucleic acid.
ex.a: PCR, because it can detect very low concentrations of viral nucleic acid before symptoms appear.

topics.rl: India's TB programme uses rapid molecular tests (like CBNAAT, a PCR-based test) to detect TB and drug resistance within hours.

topics.h: In 1997, a cow named Rosie produced milk containing a human protein, 2.4 grams of it in every litre.
p: Transgenic animals have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene. Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, but over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

Uses: (i) Normal physiology and development: studying how genes are regulated and how they affect body functions and development, e.g. complex factors in growth like insulin-like growth factor. (ii) Study of disease: models for human diseases such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's.

(iii) Biological products: transgenic animals can produce useful products, e.g. human protein α-1-antitrypsin used to treat emphysema; similar attempts are being made for PKU and cystic fibrosis. In 1997 the first transgenic cow, Rosie, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre) containing human alpha-lactalbumin, nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk.

(iv) Vaccine safety: transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of polio vaccine; if reliable, they could replace monkeys for testing vaccine batches. (v) Chemical safety testing (toxicity testing): transgenic animals carrying genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances give results in less time.

ex.q: Rosie's milk had 2.4 g of human alpha-lactalbumin per litre. How much of this protein is in 5 litres of her milk?
st: Amount = concentration × volume.

topics.rl: Indian research institutes use transgenic mice as disease models to study cancers and metabolic disorders common in the Indian population.

topics.h: India has 27 documented varieties of Basmati rice, yet in 1997 a foreign company got a patent on 'new' Basmati derived from Indian farmers' varieties.
p: Genetic modification of organisms can have unpredictable results when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem. The Indian Government has set up organisations such as GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee, as named in NCERT; since 2010 it is officially called the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee) to decide on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services.

Patents are being granted for GM crops and other biological resources. Biopiracy is the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment.

In 1997 an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office; the 'new' variety was derived from Indian farmers' varieties (crossed with semi-dwarf varieties). Attempts were also made to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines such as turmeric and neem.

Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, while developing nations are rich in both. There is a need for laws to prevent unauthorised exploitation and to share benefits. The Indian Parliament has cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill to address such issues.

ex.q: A foreign company patents a skin cream based on neem's traditional use in Indian villages, without permission or payment. Is this biopiracy? Explain.
st: Biopiracy: using bio-resources or traditional knowledge without authorisation from the country and people concerned and without compensation.
The neem use is traditional Indian knowledge, used without permission or payment.
ex.a: Yes; it uses Indian bio-resources and traditional knowledge without authorisation or compensation.

topics.rl: India's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) documents ancient remedies so patent offices worldwide can reject claims based on them.

topics.t: Ecology and the idea of a population
topics.h: No tiger lives alone in an ecological sense. It belongs to a population whose births, deaths and movements decide its future.
p: Ecology is the study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical (abiotic) environment.
Ecology deals with four levels of biological organisation: organisms, populations, communities and biomes.

A population is a group of individuals of a species living in a well-defined geographical area, sharing or competing for similar resources, and potentially interbreeding. Examples: all lotus plants in a pond, rats in an abandoned building or teakwood trees in a forest tract. For asexually reproducing organisms, interbreeding is not considered.
Population ecology is important because it links ecology to population genetics and evolution. Natural selection operates at the population level to evolve the desired traits.

ex.q: Which of these is a population: (a) all birds in a forest, (b) all Indian peafowl in Gir National Park, (c) all plants in a garden?
st: A population must be one species in a defined area.
(a) and (c) include many species.
(b) is one species (Pavo cristatus) in a defined area.
ex.a: (b) All Indian peafowl in Gir National Park

topics.rl: Project Tiger, launched in 1973, treats tigers in each reserve as populations to be monitored and managed.

topics.t: Birth rate, death rate and sex ratio
topics.h: If 8 new lotus plants appear in a pond that had 20, the birth rate is 0.4 per lotus per year. Population maths is that direct.
p: A population has attributes that an individual does not: an individual is born and dies, but a population has birth rates and death rates. These are expressed per capita (per individual of the population).
Birth rate example: a pond had 20 lotus plants last year, and 8 new plants were added, making 28. Birth rate = 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year.
Death rate example: in a lab population of 40 fruit flies, 4 died in a week. Death rate = 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week.
Sex ratio is another attribute: an individual is male or female, but a population has a sex ratio, e.g. 60 per cent females and 40 per cent males.

ex.q: A population of 500 deer had 150 births and 50 deaths in a year. Find the per capita birth rate and death rate.
st: Birth rate = births/population = 150/500 = 0.3 per deer per year.
Death rate = deaths/population = 50/500 = 0.1 per deer per year.
ex.a: Birth rate 0.3; death rate 0.1 (per deer per year)

topics.rl: India's Census reports birth rates, death rates and sex ratio, attributes of the population, not of any single person.

topics.t: Age pyramids and measuring population size
topics.h: Census pyramids show why India's working-age population is huge: the shape of the pyramid tells the story of a nation's future.
p: A population at any given time has individuals of different ages. Plotting the age distribution (per cent individuals of a given age or age group) gives an age pyramid. Age groups: pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive. For humans, age pyramids usually show males and females in a combined diagram.
The shape reflects growth status: expanding (triangular, with a broad pre-reproductive base), stable (bell-shaped) and declining (urn-shaped, with fewer pre-reproductive individuals).

Population size (population density, N) is measured in different ways. Total number is often best, but not always meaningful: 200 Parthenium plants versus one huge banyan tree with a large canopy. Here per cent cover or biomass is more meaningful.

If counting is impossible or time-consuming, relative densities can serve, e.g. number of fish caught per trap in a lake. Population sizes are often estimated indirectly: tiger census in national parks and tiger reserves is based on pug marks and faecal pellets.

ex.q: An age pyramid has a very broad base of children and a narrow top of elderly people. What is its shape and what does it show?
st: A broad pre-reproductive base with narrowing upper bars gives a triangle.
Many young individuals will enter the reproductive group.
ex.a: Triangular (expanding) pyramid; the population is growing.

topics.rl: The All India Tiger Estimation uses camera traps along with pug marks and scat surveys, an advanced form of indirect census.

topics.t: Population growth and the exponential model
topics.h: With unlimited food, a few bacteria can outgrow a stadium in days. That is exponential growth.
p: Population density changes due to four basic processes: natality (B), the number of births added; mortality (D), deaths; immigration (I), individuals of the same species coming in; and emigration (E), individuals leaving. Natality and immigration increase density; mortality and emigration decrease it.
If N is density at time t, density at time t + 1 is Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]. Density increases if B + I is more than D + E.

Exponential growth occurs when resources (food and space) are unlimited. If b and d are per capita birth and death rates, dN/dt = (b − d) × N; with r = b − d, dN/dt = rN. In integral form, Nₜ = N₀ eʳᵗ, where e is the base of natural logarithms (2.71828). Plotting N against time gives a J-shaped curve.

r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, an important parameter for assessing biotic or abiotic impacts on population growth. Examples: Norway rat r = 0.015, flour beetle r = 0.12. In 1981, r for India's human population was 0.0205.
Practice type: apply Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)] and dN/dt = rN; draw and interpret age pyramids; calculate per capita birth and death rates.

ex.q: A population of 1000 has 120 births, 30 immigrants, 70 deaths and 20 emigrants in a year. Find the population the next year.
st: Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]

topics.rl: Planners at NITI Aayog use growth-rate models to project India's future population for schools, jobs and healthcare.

topics.h: No population can grow forever. Every habitat has a limit, called the carrying capacity, just as a train compartment has a limit on how many passengers it can safely hold.
p: No population has unlimited resources, so exponential growth cannot continue. Resources are limited, causing competition among individuals and survival of the fittest.
In a given habitat, resources can support a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible: the carrying capacity (K).

A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows an initial lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when population density reaches the carrying capacity. Plotting N against time gives a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve. This is Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth: dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K].
Since resources for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, the logistic growth model is considered more realistic.

Graph comparison: the J-shaped curve (exponential, unlimited resources) keeps rising steeply; the S-shaped curve (logistic) levels off at K. When N is much smaller than K, (K − N)/K is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential.

ex.q: For a population with r = 0.2, K = 1000 and N = 500, calculate dN/dt using the logistic equation.
st: dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K]
ex.a: 50 individuals per unit time

topics.rl: Fisheries departments set catch limits based on carrying capacity so that fish stocks in reservoirs like Hirakud are not overexploited.

topics.h: A bamboo plant may grow for decades, flower once in a spectacular burst and then die, a life-history strategy very different from a mango tree's.
p: Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness, also called Darwinian fitness (high r value), in the habitat where they live.
Under a particular set of selection pressures, organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy.
Some organisms breed only once in their lifetime, like Pacific salmon fish and bamboo; others breed many times during their lifetime, like most birds and mammals.
Some produce a large number of small-sized offspring, like oysters and pelagic fishes; others produce a small number of large-sized offspring, like birds and mammals.
Ecologists suggest life history traits of organisms have evolved in relation to the constraints imposed by the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat in which they live.

ex.q: Classify: (a) bamboo, (b) a pelagic fish, (c) a dog, by breeding frequency or offspring number and size.
st: (a) Bamboo breeds only once in a lifetime.
(b) Pelagic fish produce many small offspring.
(c) Dogs (mammals) breed many times and produce few large offspring.
ex.a: (a) breeds once (b) many small offspring (c) breeds many times, few large offspring

topics.rl: Mass flowering of Melocanna bamboo in Mizoram, about every 48 years, leads to rat population explosions called 'mautam', showing how life history affects whole ecosystems.

topics.h: When prickly pear cactus overran millions of hectares in Australia, the fix was not a chemical but a cactus-eating moth from its native home.
p: Interspecific interactions: mutualism (+, +), competition (−, −), predation (+, −), parasitism (+, −), commensalism (+, 0) and amensalism (−, 0). Both species benefit in mutualism and both lose in competition.

Predation is nature's way of transferring energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels. Predators keep prey populations under control; without them prey could reach very high densities. The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920s spread over millions of hectares and was controlled only after a cactus-feeding moth from its natural habitat was introduced.

Predators help maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey species. When the starfish Pisaster was removed from an enclosed intertidal area in an American experiment, more than 10 invertebrate species became extinct within a year due to interspecific competition. Predators in nature are 'prudent', since overexploiting prey could drive both prey and predator to extinction.

Prey defences: some insects and frogs are cryptically coloured (camouflaged); the monarch butterfly is distasteful to birds due to a chemical acquired by feeding on a poisonous weed as a caterpillar. For plants, herbivores are predators; nearly 25 per cent of insects are phytophagous. Thorns of Acacia and cactus are morphological defences. Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, so cattle and goats do not browse on it. Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are chemicals plants produce as defences against grazers and browsers.

ex.q: Why are cattle and goats rarely seen browsing on Calotropis growing in abandoned fields?
st: Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides.
These chemicals defend the plant against herbivores.
ex.a: Its poisonous cardiac glycosides deter grazing animals.

topics.rl: Wildlife managers in India note that tigers and leopards keep deer and wild boar numbers in check; where predators vanish, crop raiding by herbivores rises.

topics.h: Five kinds of warblers can share one tree without fighting, simply by feeding in different parts of it.
p: Competition is often thought to occur between closely related species for limited resources, but unrelated species can compete too: flamingos and resident fishes in some shallow South American lakes compete for zooplankton. Resources need not be limiting: in interference competition, one species' feeding efficiency drops due to the inhibitory presence of another even when resources are abundant.

Competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured by its r) is significantly lower in the presence of another species. The Abingdon tortoise of the Galapagos became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, apparently due to the goats' greater browsing efficiency.

Competitive release: a species restricted to a small area by a competitively superior species expands its range dramatically when the competitor is removed. Connell's field experiments on rocky sea coasts of Scotland showed that the larger, superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chthamalus (spelt Chathamalus in NCERT).

Gause's competitive exclusion principle: two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually. This may hold if resources are limiting, but not otherwise.

Resource partitioning: competing species can coexist by choosing different times for feeding or different foraging patterns. MacArthur showed five closely related warbler species living on the same tree avoided competition through behavioural differences in foraging.

ex.q: Barnacle species X occupies only the upper rocks; when species Y is removed from the lower rocks, X spreads downward. What is this phenomenon, and which experiment showed it?
st: X was restricted by competitively superior Y.
Removing Y lets X expand its range.
ex.a: Competitive release; Connell's barnacle experiments (Balanus and Chthamalus) in Scotland.

topics.rl: In India's grasslands, invasive species sometimes outcompete native grasses; ecologists use competition theory to plan restoration.

topics.h: A koel lays its eggs in a crow's nest and lets the crow raise its chicks, and its eggs are even coloured to fool the host.
p: Parasitism evolved because it provides free lodging and meals. Many parasites are host-specific (can parasitise only a single species of host), so host and parasite tend to co-evolve: if the host evolves a mechanism to reject the parasite, the parasite must evolve to counter it.
Adaptations of parasites: loss of unnecessary sense organs, adhesive organs or suckers to cling to the host, loss of the digestive system and high reproductive capacity.

Life cycles are often complex. The human liver fluke (a trematode) depends on two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish, to complete its life cycle. The malarial parasite needs a vector (mosquito) to spread. Parasites harm the host: they may reduce survival, growth and reproduction, lower population density and make the host weaker and more vulnerable to predation.

Ectoparasites feed on the external surface of the host: lice on humans, ticks on dogs, copepods on many marine fish. Cuscuta, a parasitic plant on hedge plants, has lost its chlorophyll and leaves and derives nutrition from the host. Endoparasites live inside the host's body (liver, kidney, lungs, red blood cells) and have simplified morphology and anatomy with high reproductive potential.

Brood parasitism in birds: the parasitic bird lays eggs in the host's nest and lets the host incubate them, e.g. the cuckoo (koel) in a crow's nest. The parasite's eggs have evolved to resemble the host's in size and colour, reducing the chance of rejection.

ex.q: Explain how the cuckoo's eggs show co-evolution with the crow.
st: The cuckoo lays eggs in the crow's nest (brood parasitism).
Crows that detect foreign eggs would eject them.
Cuckoo eggs evolved to resemble crow eggs in size and colour, reducing detection.
ex.a: Egg mimicry evolved in response to the host's ability to reject foreign eggs.

topics.rl: The 'kuhoo' call of the Asian koel in Indian summers is familiar; few people realise it is a brood parasite raised by crows.

topics.h: Every fig species has its own wasp partner. Lose the wasp and the fig cannot set seed; lose the fig and the wasp has nowhere to breed.
p: Commensalism (+, 0): one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited. Examples: an orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch; barnacles on the back of a whale; the cattle egret foraging near grazing cattle, which flush out insects; clown fish living among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone for protection, with no apparent benefit to the anemone.

Mutualism (+, +): lichens are an intimate mutualism between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria. Mycorrhizae are associations of fungi with roots of higher plants: fungi help absorb nutrients and plants provide carbohydrates.

Plant–animal mutualisms: plants offer pollen, nectar and fruits as rewards to pollinators and seed dispersers. Many fig species have tight one-to-one relationships with pollinator wasps: the female wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for egg-laying sites, and uses developing seeds to nourish her larvae.

Sexual deceit: the Mediterranean orchid Ophrys has a petal resembling the female bee in size, colour and markings. The male bee pseudocopulates with the flower and gets dusted with pollen, transferring it to another flower. If the female bee's appearance changes even slightly during evolution, the orchid must co-evolve to maintain pollination success.

Exercise type: identify interactions from examples (e.g. cattle egret = commensalism, lichen = mutualism, Cuscuta = parasitism, Balanus vs Chthamalus = competition); list plant defences against herbivores; explain competitive exclusion.

ex.q: Identify the interaction: (a) orchid on a mango branch, (b) lichen, (c) cattle egret and cattle, (d) fig and wasp.
st: (a) Orchid benefits, mango unaffected: commensalism.
(b) Fungus and alga both benefit: mutualism.
(c) Egret benefits, cattle unaffected: commensalism.
(d) Both benefit: mutualism.
ex.a: (a) commensalism (b) mutualism (c) commensalism (d) mutualism

topics.rl: Bagulas (cattle egrets) following tractors and buffaloes in Indian fields are a classic everyday example of commensalism.

topics.h: A village pond and the whole Indian Ocean are both ecosystems. Size changes, but the rules of the game stay the same.
p: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with their surrounding physical environment. Ecosystems vary in size from a small pond to a large forest or sea; many ecologists regard the entire biosphere as a global ecosystem.
Ecosystems are of two basic categories: terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) and aquatic (pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary). Crop fields and an aquarium are man-made ecosystems.
Structure: interaction of biotic and abiotic components gives each ecosystem a characteristic physical structure. Identifying and enumerating plant and animal species gives its species composition.
Stratification is the vertical distribution of different species at different levels. In a forest, trees occupy the top layer, shrubs the second and herbs and grasses the bottom layers.
The components of an ecosystem function as a unit in four ways: productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.

ex.q: Classify: a mangrove estuary, the Thar desert, a rice field, a home aquarium.
st: Estuary: natural aquatic ecosystem.
Thar desert: natural terrestrial ecosystem.
Rice field and aquarium: man-made ecosystems.
ex.a: Estuary aquatic; desert terrestrial; rice field and aquarium man-made
