topics.rl: The Sundarbans mangroves of West Bengal and the grasslands of Kutch are very different Indian ecosystems, yet both run on productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.

topics.h: A small village pond is a complete working ecosystem, with producers, consumers, decomposers and the sun powering it all.
p: A pond is a shallow water body showing all the basic components of an ecosystem. Abiotic components: water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances, and rich soil deposit at the bottom. Solar input, temperature cycle, day length and other climate factors regulate the rate of function of the whole pond.
Autotrophs: phytoplankton, some algae, and floating, submerged and marginal plants at the edges.
Consumers: zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms. Decomposers: fungi, bacteria and flagellates, especially abundant at the bottom.

The pond performs all functions of an ecosystem: autotrophs convert inorganic into organic material using solar energy; heterotrophs consume autotrophs; dead organic matter is decomposed and mineralised for reuse by autotrophs, again and again.
Energy moves in one direction towards higher trophic levels and is dissipated and lost as heat to the environment.

ex.q: Classify these pond components: phytoplankton, zooplankton, bacteria at the bottom, dissolved minerals, sunlight.
st: Phytoplankton: autotroph (producer).
Zooplankton: consumer.
Bottom bacteria: decomposer.
Dissolved minerals and sunlight: abiotic components.
ex.a: Phytoplankton producer; zooplankton consumer; bacteria decomposer; minerals and sunlight abiotic

topics.rl: Traditional village ponds in India, like the johads of Rajasthan, are being revived to recharge groundwater and support local biodiversity.

topics.t: Productivity: GPP, NPP and secondary productivity
topics.h: Oceans cover about 70 per cent of Earth's surface but produce only about a third of its yearly plant biomass.
p: Primary production is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis, expressed as weight (g m⁻²) or energy (kcal m⁻²).
Productivity is the rate of biomass production, expressed as g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or (kcal m⁻²) yr⁻¹, to compare ecosystems.

Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis. A considerable part is used by plants in respiration (R). Net primary productivity: NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers).
Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

Primary productivity depends on plant species, environmental factors, availability of nutrients and photosynthetic capacity, so it varies among ecosystems. Annual NPP of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter; the oceans, despite covering about 70 per cent of the surface, produce only about 55 billion tons, and the rest is produced on land.

ex.q: A grassland has GPP of 2500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ and respiration losses of 900 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. Find NPP.
st: NPP = GPP − R.
ex.a: 1600 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹

topics.rl: Satellites like ISRO's Resourcesat help estimate vegetation productivity across Indian forests and croplands from space.

topics.t: Decomposition: detritus, fragmentation, leaching and catabolism
topics.h: Earthworms are called the farmer's friend: they shred fallen leaves and loosen soil, starting the recycling of nutrients.
p: Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients: decomposition. Earthworms help break down complex organic matter and loosen the soil, which is why they are called the farmer's friend.
Detritus, the raw material for decomposition, consists of dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead remains of animals, including faecal matter.
Fragmentation: detritivores like earthworms break detritus into smaller particles.
Leaching: water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. All these steps operate simultaneously on detritus.

ex.q: A fallen neem leaf is first shredded by earthworms, rain carries its soluble salts into the soil, and fungi digest the remains. Name each step.
st: Shredding by earthworms: fragmentation.
Soluble nutrients washed down: leaching.
Enzymatic breakdown by fungi: catabolism.
ex.a: Fragmentation, leaching, catabolism

topics.rl: Vermicomposting units in Indian villages and cities use earthworms to turn kitchen and farm waste into rich manure.

topics.t: Humification, mineralisation and factors affecting decomposition
topics.h: Leaves decompose in a few weeks in a hot, humid Kerala forest, but may lie almost unchanged for years in a cold Himalayan bog.
p: Humification and mineralisation occur during decomposition in soil. Humification leads to accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance called humus, which is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes at an extremely slow rate. Being colloidal, it serves as a reservoir of nutrients.
Mineralisation: humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients.
Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process. Its rate is controlled by the chemical composition of detritus and by climatic factors.
Under a given climate, decomposition is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quicker if it is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars.

Temperature and soil moisture are the most important climatic factors, acting through their effects on soil microbes. Warm and moist environments favour decomposition; low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it, causing build-up of organic material.

ex.q: Which will decompose faster under the same climate: a pile of nitrogen-rich, sugary vegetable peels or a pile of woody sawdust rich in lignin? Why?
st: Lignin-rich detritus decomposes slowly.
Nitrogen- and sugar-rich detritus decomposes quickly.
ex.a: Vegetable peels, because they are rich in nitrogen and soluble sugars, while sawdust is lignin-rich.

topics.rl: Peat bogs in cold, waterlogged places store huge amounts of carbon because low temperature and lack of oxygen stop decomposition.

topics.h: Plants capture only a tiny fraction of the sunlight that falls on them, yet that sliver powers every living thing you have ever seen.
p: Except for deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth. Of the incident solar radiation, less than 50 per cent is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).

Plants and photosynthetic bacteria (autotrophs) fix the sun's radiant energy to make food from simple inorganic materials. Plants capture only 2–10 per cent of the PAR, and this small amount of energy sustains the entire living world.

Energy flows in one direction: from the sun to producers and then to consumers. Ecosystems also obey the second law of thermodynamics: they need a constant supply of energy to synthesise required molecules and to counteract the universal tendency towards increasing disorderliness.

Green plants are producers. In terrestrial ecosystems the major producers are herbaceous and woody plants; in aquatic ecosystems they are phytoplankton, algae and higher plants. All animals depend directly or indirectly on plants and are consumers (heterotrophs).

Primary consumers feed on producers (herbivores, e.g. insects, birds and mammals on land and molluscs in water). Secondary consumers (primary carnivores) feed on herbivores; tertiary consumers (secondary carnivores) feed on primary carnivores.

ex.q: If 1000 units of solar radiation reach a leaf, at most how much is PAR (taking 50 per cent), and how much might plants capture at 2 per cent and at 10 per cent of this PAR?
st: PAR is less than 50%: up to 500 units.
2% of 500 = 10 units.
10% of 500 = 50 units.
ex.a: PAR up to 500 units; plants capture about 10–50 units.

topics.rl: India's solar power parks convert sunlight to electricity at far higher efficiency than plants, but no solar panel can make food, which is why photosynthesis remains irreplaceable.

topics.t: Food chains, food webs and standing crop
topics.h: In a forest, more energy flows through fallen leaves and the microbes that eat them than through deer and tigers.
p: Grazing food chain (GFC): grass (producer) → goat (primary consumer) → man (secondary consumer). Detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter and is made of decomposers, mainly fungi and bacteria. Decomposers are saprotrophs: they secrete digestive enzymes that break dead matter into simple inorganic materials and absorb them.
In aquatic ecosystems, GFC is the major conduit for energy flow. In terrestrial ecosystems, a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain.
DFC may connect with GFC: some DFC organisms are prey for GFC animals, and some animals like cockroaches and crows are omnivores. This natural interconnection of food chains makes a food web.

Organisms occupy a specific trophic level based on their source of food: producers first, herbivores second, carnivores third. Energy decreases at successive trophic levels. Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time, the standing crop, measured as biomass (fresh or dry weight; dry weight is more accurate) or number per unit area.

Distinctions for exams: GPP vs NPP (NPP = GPP − R); grazing vs detritus food chain (living producers vs dead organic matter); humification vs mineralisation (humus formation vs nutrient release); and pond components (abiotic, producers, consumers, decomposers).

ex.q: Write a grazing food chain from a grassland and name the trophic level of each organism.
st: Grass (producer): first trophic level.
Grasshopper (herbivore): second trophic level.
Frog (primary carnivore): third trophic level; snake (secondary carnivore): fourth.
ex.a: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake (T1 → T2 → T3 → T4)

topics.rl: Crows in Indian cities are omnivores: they eat scraps, insects and carrion, linking grazing and detritus food chains into a food web.

topics.t: The 10 per cent law and trophic levels
topics.h: Of all the energy in the grass a deer eats, only about a tenth ends up in the deer's body. Each step up the chain loses most of the energy.
p: The number of trophic levels in a grazing food chain is restricted because transfer of energy follows the 10 per cent law: only about 10 per cent of the energy is transferred to each trophic level from the lower trophic level.
The rest is used in respiration and other life processes or lost as heat. So energy available decreases sharply at each successive level.
In nature it is possible to have levels like producer, herbivore, primary carnivore and secondary carnivore in a grazing food chain, but rarely many more, because too little energy remains.
Calculation method: energy at the next level = energy at the current level × 10/100. Moving up n levels from producers, energy = producer energy × (1/10)ⁿ.

ex.q: Producers in a grassland fix 20,000 J of energy. Using the 10 per cent law, how much energy reaches the primary carnivores?
st: Producers → herbivores: 20,000 × 10/100 = 2000 J.
Herbivores → primary carnivores: 2000 × 10/100 = 200 J.

topics.rl: This is why a plate of dal-chawal can feed more people per hectare of farmland than meat: eating lower on the food chain loses less energy.

topics.t: Ecological pyramids of number and biomass
topics.h: In a single banyan tree with thousands of insects, a pyramid of numbers stands on its head.
p: An ecological pyramid has producers (first trophic level) at the base and higher levels on top, with top consumers at the apex. The three types are pyramids of number, biomass and energy.

Any calculation of numbers, biomass or energy must include all organisms at that trophic level. A trophic level represents a functional level, not a species: a sparrow is a primary consumer when it eats seeds and a secondary consumer when it eats insects and worms.

Pyramid of number: generally upright, e.g. in a grassland, where producers are most numerous and top carnivores fewest. In a big tree with many insects feeding on it, the pyramid of numbers is inverted (one tree supporting many insects).

Pyramid of biomass: generally upright in terrestrial ecosystems, showing a sharp decrease in biomass at higher levels. In the sea it is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton (at a given time).

ex.q: Why is the pyramid of biomass in the sea generally inverted?
st: Phytoplankton are tiny and short-lived but reproduce very fast.
At any given time, their standing biomass is less than that of the fishes feeding on them.
So the producer bar is smaller than the consumer bars.
ex.a: The biomass of fishes far exceeds the standing biomass of phytoplankton at a given time.

topics.rl: In India's coastal waters, fisheries scientists study phytoplankton and fish biomass to understand why small producers can support large fish catches.

topics.t: Pyramid of energy and limitations of pyramids
topics.h: No matter which ecosystem you choose, the pyramid of energy never stands on its head. Physics forbids it.
p: The pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted, because when energy flows from one trophic level to the next, some energy is always lost as heat at each step. Each bar shows the energy present at that trophic level in a given time or annually per unit area. A primary producer converts only about 1 per cent of the energy in sunlight available to it into NPP.

In most ecosystems all pyramids (number, biomass and energy) are upright: producers exceed herbivores in number and biomass, and herbivores exceed carnivores; energy at a lower level is always more than at a higher level. Exceptions occur for numbers and biomass, but never for energy.

Limitations of ecological pyramids: they do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain, which almost never exists in nature; they do not accommodate a food web; and saprophytes are not given any place even though they play a vital role.
Exam skill: draw pyramids of number, biomass and energy for given ecosystems (grassland, tree, sea), and explain why the energy pyramid is never inverted.
Syllabus note: in the rationalised NCERT book, ecological succession, nutrient cycling (carbon and phosphorus cycles) and ecosystem services are not part of this chapter for the current syllabus.

ex.q: A student draws an inverted pyramid of energy for a lake. Explain why this must be wrong.
st: Energy flows from one trophic level to the next.
At each transfer, some energy is always lost as heat (only about 10% passes on).
So each higher level must have less energy than the one below.
ex.a: An energy pyramid is always upright because energy is lost at every transfer.

topics.rl: Energy-flow studies in Indian wetlands like Chilika Lake help managers decide how many fish can be harvested sustainably.

topics.h: India grows more than 50,000 strains of rice and about 1,000 varieties of mango. That variety within just two species is biodiversity too.
p: Biodiversity is the term popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson to describe the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation. The three most important levels are genetic, species and ecological diversity.

Genetic diversity: a single species can show high diversity at the genetic level over its distributional range. The medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different Himalayan ranges shows genetic variation in the potency and concentration of the active chemical reserpine. India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.
Species diversity: diversity at the species level. For example, the Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.

Ecological diversity: diversity at the ecosystem level. India, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.

ex.q: Classify each as genetic, species or ecological diversity: (a) 1,000 mango varieties, (b) more amphibian species in the Western Ghats than the Eastern Ghats, (c) India having deserts, mangroves and alpine meadows.
st: (a) Variation within one species: genetic diversity.
(b) Number of species compared: species diversity.
(c) Variety of ecosystems: ecological diversity.
ex.a: (a) genetic (b) species (c) ecological

topics.rl: The National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in New Delhi stores thousands of rice and other crop varieties to protect India's genetic diversity.

topics.h: Out of every 10 animal species described on Earth, about 7 are insects.
p: According to the IUCN (2004), the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than 1.5 million. Robert May places the global species diversity at about 7 million.

More than 70 per cent of all recorded species are animals, while plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) make up no more than 22 per cent. Among animals, insects are the most species-rich group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total.
The number of fungi species in the world is more than the combined total of species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.

Prokaryotes are not included in these estimates because conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species, and many species are simply not culturable under laboratory conditions.

India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area but 8.1 per cent of global species diversity, making it one of the 12 mega diversity countries. Nearly 45,000 plant species and twice as many animal species have been recorded. If May's estimate holds (only 22 per cent of species recorded), India probably has more than 1,00,000 plant species and 3,00,000 animal species yet to be discovered.

ex.q: About how many animal species have been recorded from India, according to NCERT?
st: Nearly 45,000 plant species are recorded.
Animal species are about twice as many.
ex.a: About 90,000 animal species

topics.rl: The Zoological Survey of India and Botanical Survey of India describe new species every year, from frogs in the Western Ghats to orchids in the North-East.

topics.h: Colombia near the equator has nearly 1,400 bird species; Greenland, far north, has just 56.
p: Species diversity generally decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles. With few exceptions, tropics (latitudinal range 23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas.

Colombia, near the equator, has nearly 1,400 species of birds; New York at 41° N has 105 and Greenland at 71° N only 56. India, with much land in tropical latitudes, has more than 1,200 bird species. A tropical forest in Ecuador has up to 10 times as many vascular plant species as an equal area of temperate forest in the Midwest of the USA.

The largely tropical Amazonian rain forest has the greatest biodiversity on Earth: more than 40,000 species of plants, 3,000 of fishes, 1,300 of birds, 427 of mammals, 427 of amphibians, 378 of reptiles and more than 1,25,000 invertebrates.

Hypotheses for greater tropical diversity: (a) speciation is a function of time; tropics stayed relatively undisturbed for millions of years (unlike temperate regions with frequent glaciations), giving long evolutionary time; (b) tropical environments are less seasonal, more constant and predictable, promoting niche specialisation; (c) more solar energy in the tropics gives higher productivity, which may indirectly support more diversity.

ex.q: How many times more bird species does Colombia have than Greenland, using NCERT's figures?
st: Colombia ≈ 1,400; Greenland = 56.
ex.a: About 25 times

topics.rl: India's tropical regions, like the Western Ghats and the North-East, are among its richest biodiversity areas, in line with the latitudinal gradient.

topics.h: Explore a bigger patch of forest and you find more species, but each extra hectare adds fewer new ones. Humboldt noticed this two centuries ago.
p: The German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit.

For many taxa (angiosperms, birds, bats, freshwater fishes), the relation between species richness and area is a rectangular hyperbola. On a logarithmic scale it is a straight line: log S = log C + Z log A, where S = species richness, A = area, Z = slope of the line (regression coefficient) and C = Y-intercept.
Z values lie in the range 0.1 to 0.2 regardless of taxonomic group or region (plants in Britain, birds in California or molluscs in New York state).

For very large areas like entire continents, the slope is much steeper, with Z values of 0.6 to 1.2. For frugivorous (fruit-eating) birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents, the slope is 1.15.

ex.q: For a region, log C = 1.2 and Z = 0.15. Find log S for an area with log A = 4.
st: log S = log C + Z log A
ex.a: log S = 1.8

topics.rl: Conservation planners use species–area relationships to estimate how many species might be lost when a forest is cleared, as in debates over mining in Indian forests.

topics.t: Why species diversity matters: stability and rivets
topics.h: Ecologist Paul Ehrlich compared species to rivets in an airplane: pop a few and the plane flies; pop the wrong ones and it falls.
p: Communities with more species generally tend to be more stable. A stable community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year, should be resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances (natural or man-made), and should resist invasion by alien species.

David Tilman's long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots showed that plots with more species had less year-to-year variation in total biomass. Increased diversity also contributed to higher productivity.
Rich biodiversity is not only essential for ecosystem health but imperative for the very survival of humans on Earth.

Rivet popper hypothesis (Paul Ehrlich, Stanford ecologist): in an airplane (ecosystem), parts are joined by thousands of rivets (species). If passengers pop rivets to take home (species go extinct), flight safety (ecosystem functioning) may not be affected at first, but as more rivets go, the plane becomes dangerously weak.
Which rivet is removed also matters: losing rivets on the wings (key species driving major ecosystem functions) is a far bigger threat than losing a few rivets on seats or windows.

ex.q: In the rivet popper analogy, what do the airplane, rivets and wing rivets represent?
st: Airplane: the ecosystem.
Rivets: species.
Wing rivets: key species that drive major ecosystem functions.
ex.a: Airplane = ecosystem; rivets = species; wing rivets = key species

topics.rl: Losing pollinators such as bees would hit Indian crops like mustard and fruit orchards hard, a real-world 'wing rivet'.

topics.t: Loss of biodiversity: extinctions and effects
topics.h: The dodo of Mauritius is gone forever, and so are three subspecies of tiger: Bali, Javan and Caspian.
p: The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species (including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years. Recent examples: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia) and three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan and Caspian). The last twenty years alone saw the disappearance of 27 species.

Extinctions are not random: some groups like amphibians appear more vulnerable. More than 15,500 species worldwide face extinction. At present 12 per cent of bird species, 23 per cent of mammal species, 32 per cent of amphibian species and 31 per cent of gymnosperm species face the threat of extinction.

Earth has had five episodes of mass extinction. The 'sixth extinction' now in progress differs: current extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and humans are primarily responsible. Nearly half of all species on Earth might be wiped out within the next 100 years.

Effects of biodiversity loss in a region: decline in plant production; lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought; increased variability in ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use and pest and disease cycles.

ex.q: Of the 784 extinctions listed in the IUCN Red List (2004), 338 are vertebrates and 87 are plants. How many are invertebrates?
st: Invertebrates = 784 − 338 − 87.
ex.a: 359 invertebrates

topics.rl: The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952; its reintroduction at Kuno National Park in 2022 shows how hard it is to undo a loss.

topics.t: Causes of biodiversity loss: the Evil Quartet
topics.h: Introducing one fish, the Nile perch, into Lake Victoria led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish.
p: The four major causes of accelerated extinction are called the 'Evil Quartet'. (i) Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause. Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 per cent of Earth's land surface but now cover no more than 6 per cent. The Amazon rain forest, called the 'lungs of the planet', is being cleared for soya beans and for grassland to raise beef cattle. Fragmentation especially harms mammals and birds needing large territories and animals with migratory habits; pollution also degrades habitats.

(ii) Over-exploitation: Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon became extinct in the last 500 years due to over-exploitation by humans. Many marine fish populations are over-harvested, endangering commercially important species.

(iii) Alien species invasions: the Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria in East Africa led to extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish. Invasive weeds like carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) threaten native species. Illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture threatens indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers.

(iv) Co-extinctions: when a species becomes extinct, species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct. When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites meets the same fate. In co-evolved plant–pollinator mutualism, extinction of one invariably leads to extinction of the other.
Exam focus: list the Evil Quartet with an example of each; distinguish in situ and ex situ conservation; explain the rivet popper hypothesis.

ex.q: Name the Evil Quartet cause in each case: (a) Nile perch in Lake Victoria, (b) passenger pigeon, (c) clearing Amazon forest for soya beans, (d) parasites dying with their host fish.
st: (a) Alien species invasion.
(b) Over-exploitation.
(c) Habitat loss and fragmentation.
(d) Co-extinction.
ex.a: (a) alien species (b) over-exploitation (c) habitat loss (d) co-extinction

topics.rl: Lantana and Parthenium have spread widely across Indian forests and farmlands, crowding out native plants, a home-grown example of alien species invasion.

topics.h: More than a quarter of the medicines sold worldwide come from plants, and thousands of plant species are used in traditional medicine.
p: Narrowly utilitarian reasons: humans get countless direct economic benefits from nature: food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and medicinal products. More than 25 per cent of drugs sold worldwide are derived from plants, and 25,000 plant species contribute to traditional medicines of native peoples.
Bioprospecting is exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance. Nations rich in biodiversity can expect to reap enormous benefits.

Broadly utilitarian reasons: biodiversity plays a major role in ecosystem services. The Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in Earth's atmosphere. Pollination by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats gives us fruits and seeds. There are also intangible aesthetic pleasures: walking through thick woods, watching spring flowers in bloom or waking up to a bulbul's song.

Ethical reasons: every species has intrinsic value, even if it has no current economic value to us. We have a moral duty to care for their well-being and pass on our biological legacy in good order to future generations.

ex.q: Classify each reason for conservation: (a) neem used for medicines, (b) bees pollinating mango trees, (c) a species has a right to exist.
st: (a) Direct economic product: narrowly utilitarian.
(b) Ecosystem service: broadly utilitarian.
(c) Intrinsic value: ethical.
ex.a: (a) narrowly utilitarian (b) broadly utilitarian (c) ethical

topics.rl: India's AYUSH systems use thousands of plant species; protecting forests also protects this pharmacy of the future.

topics.t: In situ conservation: hotspots, protected areas and sacred groves
topics.h: Some forests in Meghalaya have been protected for centuries not by law but by communities, and they shelter rare plants found almost nowhere else.
p: In situ (on site) conservation protects the whole ecosystem, so biodiversity at all levels is protected: we save the entire forest to save the tiger.

Biodiversity hotspots are regions with very high species richness and a high degree of endemism (species found only there). Initially 25 were identified; nine more were added, making 34. They are also regions of accelerated habitat loss. Three cover India's high-biodiversity regions: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya. All hotspots together cover less than 2 per cent of Earth's land area, but strict protection could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent.

In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries. As per NCERT, India has 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks and 448 wildlife sanctuaries. (These are the book's older figures; current official counts are higher, but use NCERT's numbers in board answers.)

Sacred groves are tracts of forest set aside and protected by communities for religious and cultural reasons, with all trees and wildlife venerated. They are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas (described under Madhya Pradesh in NCERT). In Meghalaya, sacred groves are the last refuges for many rare and threatened plants.

ex.q: How many biodiversity hotspots are there in the world, and which three cover India's high-biodiversity regions?
st: 25 initially + 9 added = 34 hotspots.
India's three: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya.
ex.a: 34; Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya

topics.rl: Mawphlang sacred forest near Shillong is a well-known sacred grove where community traditions protect ancient trees and rare species.

topics.t: Ex situ conservation and international efforts
topics.h: Seeds of thousands of crop varieties sit frozen in seed banks, insurance against the day a disease or disaster wipes out a field.
p: Ex situ (off site) conservation: threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and placed in special settings for protection and special care, e.g. zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks. Many animals extinct in the wild continue to be maintained in zoos. It is desirable when a species is endangered or threatened and needs urgent measures.

Advanced ex situ methods: gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods by cryopreservation; eggs can be fertilised in vitro; plants can be propagated by tissue culture; seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks.

International efforts: the Earth Summit held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 called upon all nations to take measures to conserve biodiversity and sustainably use its benefits (Convention on Biological Diversity). At the World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg, South Africa, in 2002, 190 countries pledged to achieve by 2010 a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss.

Related tools: Ramsar sites are wetlands of international importance designated under the Ramsar Convention (signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971). The IUCN Red Data Book (Red List) documents the conservation status of species and lists those threatened with extinction.

ex.q: Classify as in situ or ex situ: (a) a national park, (b) a seed bank, (c) a sacred grove, (d) cryopreserved gametes, (e) a botanical garden.
st: In situ protects species in their natural habitat: (a) and (c).
Ex situ protects them outside their habitat: (b), (d) and (e).
ex.a: In situ: (a), (c); ex situ: (b), (d), (e)

topics.rl: India's ex situ efforts include the gharial breeding programme and vulture conservation breeding centres such as at Pinjore, Haryana.

qa.q: How many microsporangia are present in a typical dithecous angiosperm anther?
qa.e: A bilobed anther has two theca per lobe, and each theca has one microsporangium, giving four in all, one at each corner of the tetragonal section.

qa.q: Which layer of the microsporangium wall nourishes the developing pollen grains?
qa.e: The tapetum is the innermost wall layer; its cells, with dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus, nourish the developing pollen.

qa.q: Tapetal cells are characterised by
qa.a: dense cytoplasm and generally more than one nucleus
qa.e: Tapetal cells are metabolically very active nourishing cells, so they have dense cytoplasm and are often multinucleate.

qa.q: Which statement about pre-fertilisation events is correct?
qa.a: Hormonal and structural changes lead to the differentiation of a floral primordium well before the flower is seen
qa.e: Pre-fertilisation events begin long before a flower appears: hormonal and structural changes initiate differentiation of the floral primordium.

qa.q: The outer three wall layers of a microsporangium (epidermis, endothecium, middle layers) mainly
qa.a: protect the sporangium and help in dehiscence of the anther to release pollen
qa.e: The outer three layers perform protection and help in dehiscence; nourishment is the job of the tapetum, and pollen arises from sporogenous tissue.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The male reproductive organ of a flower is the androecium. Reason (R): The androecium is a whorl of stamens.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The androecium, a whorl of stamens that produce pollen, represents the male reproductive organ; R defines it and so explains A.

qa.q: In a T.S. of a mature anther, the tetragonal outline is because
qa.a: the four microsporangia lie one at each corner
qa.e: The anther is bilobed, but its four microsporangia sit at the four corners, giving a four-cornered (tetragonal) section.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of the social and cultural value of flowers rather than their reproductive role?
qa.a: Exchanging flower garlands at a wedding
qa.e: Garland exchange is a cultural use of flowers; the other options are reproductive functions.

qa.q: How many pollen grains are produced from 25 microspore mother cells?
qa.e: Each microspore mother cell gives a tetrad of four microspores by meiosis, and each microspore becomes one pollen grain.

qa.q: The exine of the pollen grain is made of
qa.e: Exine is made of sporopollenin, an extremely resistant organic material; cellulose and pectin make the intine.

qa.q: Pollen grains are well preserved as fossils because
qa.a: sporopollenin in the exine resists high temperature, strong acids and alkalis and enzyme attack
qa.e: Sporopollenin is among the most resistant organic materials and no enzyme is known to degrade it, so the exine survives for ages.

qa.q: In what percentage of angiosperms are pollen grains shed at the 2-celled stage, according to NCERT?
qa.e: Pollen in over 60 per cent of angiosperms is shed at the 2-celled stage (vegetative + generative cell); the rest at the 3-celled stage.

qa.q: Germ pores on a pollen grain are
qa.a: regions of the exine where sporopollenin is absent
qa.e: Germ pores are apertures in the exine lacking sporopollenin; the pollen tube emerges through one of them.

qa.q: Which statement about the two cells of a mature pollen grain is correct?
qa.a: The vegetative cell is larger with abundant food reserve; the generative cell is small and spindle-shaped
qa.e: The generative cell (not the vegetative cell) divides mitotically to give two male gametes; the vegetative cell is the big food-rich cell.

qa.q: The division that converts a microspore mother cell into a microspore tetrad is
qa.e: Microspore mother cells are diploid and form haploid microspores, so the division must be meiosis.

qa.q: The male gametes in a 3-celled pollen grain arise from
qa.a: mitotic division of the generative cell
qa.e: The haploid generative cell divides by mitosis to form two haploid male gametes; no meiosis happens inside the pollen grain.

qa.q: At what temperature (in °C) is pollen cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen?
qa.e: Liquid nitrogen boils at about −196 °C, the standard cryopreservation temperature for pollen banks.

qa.q: Pollen grains of rice and wheat generally lose viability within about
qa.e: NCERT cites rice and wheat as cereals whose pollen loses viability within 30 minutes of release.

qa.q: Which weed, known as carrot grass, is a major cause of pollen allergy in India?
qa.e: Parthenium (carrot grass) came with imported wheat and its pollen triggers allergies and asthma.

qa.q: The main purpose of a pollen bank is to
qa.a: store viable pollen for long periods for use in crop breeding
qa.e: Pollen banks cryopreserve pollen so breeders can use it later, even when parents flower at different times or places.

qa.q: Pollen viability refers to
qa.a: the period for which pollen retains its ability to germinate and fertilise
qa.e: Viability is how long pollen remains alive and functional after release.

qa.q: Some members of which family can keep pollen viable for months?
qa.e: Some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae retain pollen viability for months, unlike rice and wheat.

qa.q: A student with asthma finds symptoms worsen in the flowering season of roadside weeds. The most likely cause is
qa.e: Pollen of many plants, especially Parthenium, triggers allergic and bronchial disorders like asthma.

qa.q: Two factors that mainly affect the viability of pollen are
qa.e: The period of viability is highly variable and depends on prevailing temperature and humidity.

qa.q: How many functional megaspores are typically formed from one megaspore mother cell in most flowering plants?
qa.e: Meiosis gives four megaspores, but in most angiosperms only one survives; three degenerate.

qa.q: Papaver has a multicarpellary gynoecium with fused pistils. This condition is called
qa.e: Fused pistils make a syncarpous gynoecium; Michelia, with free pistils, is apocarpous.

qa.q: The stalk by which an ovule is attached to the placenta is the
qa.e: The funicle is the stalk; the hilum is only the junction point between ovule body and funicle.

qa.q: The megaspore mother cell differentiates in which region of the nucellus?
qa.e: Ovules generally have a single MMC in the micropylar region of the nucellus.

qa.q: The nucellus is best described as
qa.a: a mass of cells with reserve food enclosed by the integuments, holding the embryo sac
qa.e: Nucellus cells have abundant food and the embryo sac lies within the nucellus.

qa.q: Which fruit develops from an ovary containing a single ovule?
qa.e: Wheat, paddy and mango have a single ovule per ovary; papaya, watermelon and orchids have many.

qa.q: If the nucellus of an ovule has 2n = 16, the chromosome number in a functional megaspore will be
qa.e: The functional megaspore forms by meiosis of the diploid MMC, so it is haploid: 16 ÷ 2 = 8.

qa.q: The opening at the tip of the ovule, left uncovered by the integuments, is the
qa.e: Integuments enclose the ovule except at the micropyle, the usual entry point of the pollen tube.

qa.q: How many mitotic divisions does the functional megaspore nucleus undergo to form the 8-nucleate embryo sac?
qa.e: Each mitosis doubles the nuclei: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8, which takes three divisions.

qa.q: The egg apparatus of a typical embryo sac consists of
qa.a: two synergids and one egg cell
qa.e: The three micropylar cells are two synergids and the egg; antipodals are at the chalazal end.

qa.q: The filiform apparatus is present on the
qa.a: synergids, and it guides the pollen tube
qa.e: The filiform apparatus is a set of cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip of the synergids that guides the pollen tube into the synergid.

qa.q: A typical angiosperm embryo sac at maturity is
qa.e: The central cell contains two polar nuclei, so 8 nuclei are housed in 7 cells.

qa.q: Development of the embryo sac from a single megaspore is called
qa.e: When only one functional megaspore forms the embryo sac, the method is monosporic.

qa.q: In a plant with 2n = 20, what is the chromosome number in an antipodal cell?
qa.e: Antipodals are cells of the female gametophyte, which is haploid: 20 ÷ 2 = 10.

qa.q: Which pair contains two diploid structures?
qa.e: Nucellus and MMC are sporophytic tissue (2n); the others are gametophytic (n).

qa.q: Free-nuclear divisions in embryo sac development means that
qa.a: nuclear divisions occur without immediate cell wall formation
qa.e: Up to the 8-nucleate stage, nuclei divide without walls; cells organise only afterwards.

qa.q: Transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of another flower on the same plant is called
qa.e: Geitonogamy involves two flowers of the same plant, so it is functionally cross-pollination but genetically like selfing.

qa.q: Which type of pollination brings genetically different pollen grains to the stigma?
qa.e: Only xenogamy moves pollen between genetically different plants.

qa.q: Cleistogamous flowers ensure assured seed set because
qa.a: they are autogamous and do not need pollinators
qa.e: Closed flowers have anthers dehiscing right onto the stigma, so seeds set even when pollinators are absent.

qa.q: Which plant bears both chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers?
qa.e: Viola, Oxalis and Commelina produce both flower types.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Geitonogamy is genetically similar to autogamy. Reason (R): In geitonogamy, the pollen comes from the same plant.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Pollen from the same plant carries the same genes, which is exactly why geitonogamy is genetically like autogamy.

qa.q: A disadvantage of cleistogamy is that it
qa.a: prevents cross-pollination and so reduces genetic variation
qa.e: Since closed flowers self-pollinate, no foreign pollen enters, limiting variation; seed set itself is assured.

qa.q: In autogamy, pollen is transferred
qa.e: Autogamy means pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower that produced it.

qa.q: For autogamy to occur in an open (chasmogamous) flower, it requires
qa.a: synchrony in pollen release and stigma receptivity, with anthers and stigma close together
qa.e: Self-pollination in an open flower needs the anthers and stigma to be near each other and ready at the same time.

qa.q: The silky threads on a corn cob, called tassels in NCERT, are
qa.a: the stigma and style, which trap wind-borne pollen
qa.e: The silky threads that NCERT calls tassels are long styles with stigmas that wave in the wind to catch pollen (botanists call them corn silk).

qa.q: Which is a water-pollinated marine plant?
qa.e: Zostera is a marine sea-grass; Vallisneria is a fresh-water example, and the last two are not water-pollinated.

qa.q: Pollen grains of water-pollinated plants are protected from wetting by
qa.e: A mucilaginous covering keeps the pollen from getting wet.

qa.q: In Vallisneria, pollination takes place when
qa.a: male flowers or pollen released on the water surface reach female flowers held at the surface on long stalks
qa.e: Female flowers rise on long stalks; male flowers or pollen float passively on the surface to them.

qa.q: Which feature is typical of wind-pollinated flowers?
qa.e: A feathery stigma provides a big surface to trap airborne pollen; colour, scent and nectar are for animals.

qa.q: Wind-pollinated flowers often have a single ovule in each ovary and are packed into an inflorescence. This is because
qa.a: chance landing of pollen is low, so many flowers each needing one pollen grain improve seed set
qa.e: Wind pollination is chancy; packing many single-ovuled flowers raises the odds that pollen fertilises enough ovules.

qa.q: Water pollination is found in about how many genera, according to NCERT?
qa.e: Pollination by water is quite rare and limited to about 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons.

qa.q: Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Among abiotic pollinating agents, wind is more common than water
qa.e: Most flowering plants use animals; of the abiotic agents, wind is commoner than water.

qa.q: The dominant biotic pollinating agents are
qa.e: Bees are the most important animal pollinators.

qa.q: In the Yucca plant and its moth partner,
qa.a: neither can complete its life cycle without the other
qa.e: The moth lays eggs in the ovary locule and pollinates the flower; the larvae feed on developing seeds, so the two are mutually dependent.

qa.q: Flowers pollinated by flies and beetles often
qa.a: secrete foul odours to attract the animals
qa.e: Flies and beetles are attracted by foul smells, so such flowers secrete them.

qa.q: An insect that eats nectar from a flower without touching the anthers or stigma is a
qa.e: Pollen or nectar robbers take the floral rewards but do not pollinate.

qa.q: Which set of features is typical of insect-pollinated flowers?
qa.e: Insect flowers advertise with size, colour and scent and reward with nectar.

qa.q: Approximately how tall is the Amorphophallus flower mentioned in NCERT?
qa.e: The tall Amorphophallus flower is about 6 feet and offers insects a site to lay eggs.

qa.q: Why do small flowers often occur clustered into an inflorescence in insect-pollinated plants?
qa.a: To make them conspicuous to pollinators
qa.e: Grouping makes small flowers visible as a big target for insects.

qa.q: Which bird is a pollinator in addition to the sunbird?
qa.e: Sunbirds and hummingbirds are well-known bird pollinators that feed on nectar.

qa.q: Papaya prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy because it is
qa.e: Dioecious plants bear male and female flowers on different plants, so neither selfing route is possible.

qa.q: In maize, which is monoecious, which type of pollination is still possible?
qa.e: Unisexual flowers prevent autogamy, but pollen can still move to another flower on the same plant.

qa.q: Self-incompatibility is
qa.a: a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen from fertilising ovules by blocking germination or tube growth
qa.e: It is a genetic block that stops self-pollen (or pollen of the same plant) from completing fertilisation.

qa.q: Emasculation in artificial hybridisation refers to
qa.a: removal of anthers from a flower bud before they dehisce
qa.e: Emasculation removes the anthers so the flower cannot self-pollinate; bagging is a separate step.

qa.q: Why is an emasculated flower bagged?
qa.a: To prevent contamination of its stigma with unwanted pollen
qa.e: Bagging with butter paper keeps out stray pollen so only the chosen pollen reaches the stigma.

qa.q: The pollen tube usually enters the ovule and then the embryo sac through
qa.a: the micropyle and then a synergid via the filiform apparatus
qa.e: The tube grows through the style, enters through the micropyle and is guided into a synergid by the filiform apparatus.

qa.q: In a unisexual plant, a breeder wants to cross-pollinate the female flowers. Which step is NOT needed?
qa.e: Female flowers have no anthers, so there is nothing to emasculate; bagging is still needed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The pistil can accept compatible pollen and reject incompatible pollen. Reason (R): The pistil recognises pollen through chemical components produced by pollen interacting with those of the pistil.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Recognition of pollen, followed by acceptance or rejection, is mediated by chemical interaction between pollen and pistil.

qa.q: If the leaf cells of a plant have 24 chromosomes, how many chromosomes will its endosperm cells have?
qa.e: Leaf cells are 2n = 24, so n = 12 and endosperm is 3n = 36.

qa.q: Triple fusion involves the fusion of
qa.a: one male gamete with two polar nuclei
qa.e: The second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei of the central cell, giving the 3n PEN.

qa.q: Double fertilisation is the combination of
qa.e: One male gamete does syngamy and the other does triple fusion; both together are double fertilisation.

qa.q: Double fertilisation is a characteristic feature of
qa.e: Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms.

qa.q: Tender coconut water represents
qa.e: Coconut water contains thousands of free nuclei; the white kernel around it is cellular endosperm.

qa.q: Which of these seeds has its endosperm completely consumed during development?
qa.e: In pea, groundnut and beans the embryo absorbs the endosperm; castor, coconut and cereals keep it.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Endosperm development precedes embryo development. Reason (R): The developing embryo needs a supply of nourishment.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Endosperm forms first because it stores the food the developing embryo will draw on.

qa.q: After double fertilisation, the central cell becomes the
qa.e: The central cell, now containing the 3n PEN, is the primary endosperm cell.

qa.q: The single cotyledon of a monocot (grass) embryo is called the
qa.e: The scutellum is the shield-like cotyledon lying to one side of the embryonal axis.

qa.q: The coleorhiza is
qa.a: an undifferentiated sheath enclosing the radicle and root cap in monocot embryos
qa.e: The coleorhiza covers the radicle and root cap; the coleoptile covers the shoot apex.

qa.q: In a dicot embryo, the portion of the embryonal axis above the level of the cotyledons is the
qa.e: Epi- means above: the epicotyl ends in the plumule; the hypocotyl lies below and ends in the radicle.

qa.q: The correct sequence of embryo development is
qa.e: The zygote gives rise to the proembryo, then globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo.

qa.q: The embryo develops at which end of the embryo sac?
qa.e: The zygote is formed at the micropylar end where the egg sits, so the embryo develops there.

qa.q: Most zygotes divide only after a certain amount of endosperm is formed. This is an adaptation to
qa.a: provide assured nutrition to the developing embryo
qa.e: The endosperm stores food, so it must exist before the embryo starts growing fast.

qa.q: In the dicot embryo, the hypocotyl terminates at its lower end in the
qa.e: The hypocotyl ends in the radicle (root tip) covered with a root cap.

qa.q: While labelling an anatropous ovule, the basal part opposite the micropyle should be labelled
qa.e: The chalaza is the basal part of the ovule opposite the micropylar end.

qa.q: A seed about 10,000 years old that germinated was of
qa.e: The lupine seed from the Arctic tundra germinated after about 10,000 years of dormancy; the date palm seed was about 2000 years old.

qa.q: The residual, persistent nucellus in seeds of black pepper and beet is called
qa.e: Perisperm is leftover nucellus; endosperm is the 3n tissue from triple fusion.

qa.q: Which is a false fruit?
qa.e: In apple the thalamus contributes to the fruit, making it a false fruit.

qa.q: Banana is an example of a parthenocarpic fruit because it
qa.a: develops without fertilisation and is seedless
qa.e: Parthenocarpic fruits form without fertilisation, so they lack seeds.

qa.q: The water content of mature seeds is generally about
qa.e: Maturing seeds dry to 10–15 per cent moisture, slowing metabolism and allowing dormancy.

qa.q: After fertilisation, the micropyle of the seed coat
qa.a: remains as a small pore that allows entry of oxygen and water during germination
qa.e: The micropyle persists as a pore for O₂ and water to reach the embryo.

qa.q: Which seed is albuminous?
qa.e: Castor retains endosperm in the mature seed; pea, groundnut and beans have it consumed.

qa.q: Which is NOT an advantage of seeds to angiosperms?
qa.a: Seeds make pollination dependent on water
qa.e: Seed-bearing angiosperms have pollination and fertilisation independent of water; that independence is an advantage.

qa.q: Apomixis is
qa.e: Apomixis gives seeds asexually; fruits without fertilisation is parthenocarpy.

qa.q: Apomixis has been reported in some species of
qa.e: NCERT mentions apomixis in some species of Asteraceae and grasses.

qa.q: In citrus and mango, extra embryos can develop from
qa.a: nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac
qa.e: Some nucellar cells divide, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.

qa.q: Polyembryony is commonly seen in
qa.e: Orange seeds often contain more than one embryo due to nucellar embryony.

qa.q: Why are hybrid seeds expensive for farmers?
qa.a: Hybrid progeny segregate, so fresh hybrid seed must be bought every year
qa.e: Seeds harvested from a hybrid crop do not keep hybrid characters because of segregation, so farmers rebuy.

qa.q: Making hybrids into apomicts would help farmers because
qa.a: there is no segregation, so hybrid characters are maintained in saved seed
qa.e: Apomictic seeds are clones, so a hybrid's traits pass unchanged to the next generation.

qa.q: An embryo formed from a diploid egg cell that developed without meiosis and without fertilisation will be
qa.a: genetically identical to the mother plant
qa.e: No reduction division and no fertilisation means the egg carries exactly the mother's genome.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction. Reason (R): In apomixis, seeds are formed after fusion of male and female gametes.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Apomixis is asexual precisely because no fusion of gametes occurs, so R is false.

qa.q: The scrotum keeps the temperature of the testes lower than the internal body temperature by about
qa.e: The scrotum maintains testicular temperature 2–2.5 °C below body temperature, which is necessary for spermatogenesis.

qa.q: The androgen-secreting cells of the testis are the
qa.e: Leydig cells in the interstitial spaces synthesise and secrete androgens; Sertoli cells nourish germ cells.

qa.q: Sertoli cells are found
qa.a: lining the inside of the seminiferous tubules, providing nutrition to germ cells
qa.e: Sertoli cells line the tubule together with spermatogonia and nourish the germ cells.

qa.q: How many testicular lobules are present in each testis, approximately?
qa.e: Each testis has about 250 lobules, each with one to three seminiferous tubules.

qa.q: Which sequence of reproductive events is correct?
qa.a: Gametogenesis → insemination → fertilisation → implantation → gestation → parturition
qa.e: Gametes form first, are brought together by insemination, fuse at fertilisation; the blastocyst implants, develops through gestation and is delivered at parturition.

qa.q: Which statement about age-related changes is correct?
qa.a: Sperm formation continues even in old age, but formation of ova ceases around fifty years
qa.e: In men spermatogenesis can continue into old age, while women's ovarian cycles stop around fifty (menopause).

qa.q: Assertion (A): Testes are located outside the abdominal cavity. Reason (R): Spermatogenesis requires a temperature lower than the normal internal body temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The extra-abdominal scrotum keeps the testes 2–2.5 °C cooler, as required for spermatogenesis.

qa.q: Humans are described as viviparous because they
qa.e: Viviparous animals develop the embryo inside the mother and give birth to young ones.

qa.q: Seminal plasma is rich in
qa.e: Secretions of the seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands form seminal plasma rich in fructose, calcium and enzymes.

qa.q: The vas deferens opens into the urethra as the
qa.e: After receiving the duct of the seminal vesicle, the vas deferens opens into the urethra as the ejaculatory duct.

qa.q: The epididymis is located
qa.a: along the posterior surface of each testis
qa.e: The vasa efferentia open into the epididymis, which lies along the posterior surface of each testis.

qa.q: Which male accessory glands are paired?
qa.e: There are paired seminal vesicles and paired bulbourethral glands, but a single prostate.

qa.q: Secretions of the bulbourethral glands also help in
qa.e: Besides adding to seminal plasma, bulbourethral secretions lubricate the penis.

qa.q: The enlarged end of the penis is called the
qa.e: The glans penis is the enlarged end; it is covered by a loose fold of skin, the foreskin.

qa.q: In the T.S. of a seminiferous tubule, the cells located in the spaces between tubules are
qa.e: Interstitial cells lie outside the tubules; the other cells lie within the tubule.

qa.q: The urethra originates from the
qa.a: urinary bladder and runs through the penis to the urethral meatus
qa.e: The urethra starts at the urinary bladder and opens to the outside through the urethral meatus.

qa.q: Which layer of the uterus shows strong contractions during delivery of the baby?
qa.e: The myometrium is a thick layer of smooth muscle that contracts strongly during parturition.

qa.q: The finger-like projections at the edge of the infundibulum are called
qa.e: Fimbriae help collect the ovum after ovulation.

qa.q: The birth canal is formed by
qa.a: the cervical canal and the vagina
qa.e: The cavity of the cervix (cervical canal) together with the vagina forms the birth canal.

qa.q: The approximate length of each fallopian tube is
qa.e: Each oviduct is about 10–12 cm long, from the ovary periphery to the uterus; 2–4 cm is the ovary's length.

qa.q: The ovarian stroma is divided into
qa.a: a peripheral cortex and an inner medulla
qa.e: A thin epithelium covers the ovary, enclosing the stroma made of cortex and medulla.

qa.q: Which part of the oviduct joins the uterus?
qa.e: The isthmus, with a narrow lumen, is the last part of the oviduct that joins the uterus.

qa.q: The ovaries are called primary female sex organs because they
qa.a: produce the female gamete and ovarian hormones
qa.e: Primary sex organs produce gametes and sex hormones; the ovaries do both.

qa.q: The endometrium is described as
qa.a: the inner glandular layer that undergoes cyclical changes during the menstrual cycle
qa.e: The endometrium lines the uterine cavity and is built up and shed in each menstrual cycle.

qa.q: The glandular tissue of each breast is divided into how many mammary lobes?
qa.e: Each breast has 15–20 mammary lobes containing alveoli.

qa.q: Milk is secreted by the cells of the
qa.e: Alveolar cells secrete milk, which is stored in their lumens before flowing out through the duct system.

qa.q: The correct order of milk flow is
qa.a: alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary duct → mammary ampulla → lactiferous duct
qa.e: Milk moves from the tiny alveoli to progressively larger tubules and ducts, then out via the lactiferous duct.

qa.q: Which statement about the hymen is correct according to NCERT?
qa.a: Its presence or absence is not a reliable indicator of virginity or sexual experience
qa.e: The hymen can tear for many non-sexual reasons or may persist after coitus.

qa.q: The mons pubis is
qa.a: a cushion of fatty tissue covered by skin and pubic hair
qa.e: The mons pubis is the fatty cushion at the front of the external genitalia.

qa.q: The clitoris is located
qa.a: at the upper junction of the two labia minora, above the urethral opening
qa.e: The clitoris is a tiny finger-like structure at the upper junction of the labia minora.

qa.q: Several mammary ducts join to form the
qa.e: Mammary ducts join to form the wider mammary ampulla, which leads to the lactiferous duct.

qa.q: Besides glandular tissue, mammary glands contain
qa.e: Mammary glands are paired structures with glandular tissue and a variable amount of fat.

qa.q: How many sperms are produced from 100 secondary spermatocytes?
qa.e: Each secondary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis II to give 2 spermatids, which become 2 sperms.

qa.q: The number of chromosomes in a human secondary spermatocyte is
qa.e: Secondary spermatocytes are formed by meiosis I, so they are haploid with 23 chromosomes.

qa.q: The transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa is called
qa.e: Spermiogenesis is the shaping of spermatids into sperms; spermiation is their release from the tubule.

qa.q: LH acts on which cells of the testis?
qa.e: LH targets Leydig cells to produce androgens; FSH targets Sertoli cells.

qa.q: Spermatogenesis starts at puberty due to a significant increase in the secretion of
qa.e: The rise in GnRH at puberty triggers LH and FSH release, which drive spermatogenesis.

qa.q: Which division is called the reduction division in spermatogenesis?
qa.a: Meiosis I, converting primary into secondary spermatocytes
qa.e: The first meiotic division halves the chromosome number, so it is the reduction division.

qa.q: Release of sperms from the seminiferous tubules is called
qa.e: After spermiogenesis, sperm heads embedded in Sertoli cells are released by spermiation.

qa.q: Spermatogonia multiply by
qa.e: Spermatogonia (2n) increase in number by mitosis before some become primary spermatocytes and enter meiosis.

qa.q: A sample has 200 million sperms. What is the minimum number (in millions) that must show vigorous motility for normal fertility?
qa.e: At least 40 per cent must show vigorous motility: 40% of 200 million = 80 million.

qa.q: The enzymes that help a sperm enter the ovum are present in the
qa.e: The cap-like acrosome on the head contains enzymes that help the sperm penetrate the ovum.

qa.q: The middle piece of a sperm contains numerous
qa.a: mitochondria that provide energy for tail movement
qa.e: Mitochondria in the middle piece produce energy for motility.

qa.q: According to NCERT, how many sperms (in millions) does a human male ejaculate during coitus?
qa.e: About 200–300 million sperms are released per ejaculation.

qa.q: For normal fertility, at least what percentage of sperms must have normal shape and size?
qa.e: At least 60 per cent must be normal in shape and size, and at least 40 per cent must be vigorously motile.

qa.q: Semen consists of
qa.e: Semen is the combination of sperms and the seminal plasma from accessory glands.

qa.q: Maturation and motility of sperms depend on secretions of the
qa.a: epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle and prostate
qa.e: These male accessory ducts and glands provide secretions essential for maturation and motility.

qa.q: In a diagram of a blastocyst, the outer layer of cells should be labelled
qa.e: The outer layer is the trophoblast; the inner cell mass is attached to it on the inside.

qa.q: At puberty, the number of primary follicles left in each ovary is about
qa.e: Of the couple of million oogonia formed in the foetal ovary, many follicles degenerate; about 60,000–80,000 remain in each ovary at puberty.

qa.q: Primary oocytes are temporarily arrested at
qa.e: Oogonia start meiosis, enter prophase I and arrest there as primary oocytes until puberty-driven follicle growth.

qa.q: The first meiotic division of the primary oocyte produces
qa.a: a large secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body
qa.e: Meiosis I in oogenesis is unequal; the bulk of cytoplasm goes to the secondary oocyte.

qa.q: The fluid-filled cavity of a tertiary follicle is called the
qa.e: The antrum is the characteristic fluid-filled cavity of the tertiary follicle.

qa.q: The zona pellucida is formed
qa.a: around the secondary oocyte in the Graafian follicle
qa.e: The secondary oocyte forms this new membrane in the Graafian follicle.

qa.q: How many ova are formed from 40 primary oocytes?
qa.e: Each primary oocyte gives one ovum; the other products are polar bodies.

qa.q: Which statement correctly contrasts spermatogenesis and oogenesis?
qa.a: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty, whereas oogenesis begins during embryonic development
qa.e: Oogonia form before birth; spermatogenesis starts only at puberty.

qa.q: At ovulation, the cell released from the Graafian follicle is the
qa.e: The ruptured Graafian follicle releases the secondary oocyte; meiosis II completes only after sperm entry.

qa.q: The first menstruation that begins at puberty is called
qa.e: Menarche is the first menstruation; menopause is the end of cycles around 50 years.

qa.q: The menstrual phase typically lasts
qa.e: Menstrual flow due to breakdown of the endometrium usually lasts 3–5 days.

qa.q: During the follicular phase,
qa.a: primary follicles grow into a mature Graafian follicle and the endometrium regenerates
qa.e: Follicle growth and endometrial proliferation, under rising LH, FSH and oestrogen, define the follicular phase.

qa.q: Menstrual cycles are found in
qa.a: primates such as monkeys, apes and humans
qa.e: Menstrual cycles are a feature of female primates; other mammals have different (oestrous) cycles.

qa.q: Menstruation occurs only if
qa.a: the released ovum is not fertilised
qa.e: Without fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and the endometrium is shed.

qa.q: During the follicular phase, the secretion of oestrogens is increased by
qa.a: growing follicles stimulated by LH and FSH
qa.e: Rising gonadotropins stimulate follicle growth, and the growing follicles secrete oestrogens.

qa.q: The average length of a human menstrual cycle according to NCERT is
qa.e: The cycle repeats on average every 28/29 days.

qa.q: Cyclic menstruation between menarche and menopause indicates
qa.e: Regular cycles between menarche and menopause indicate the normal reproductive phase.

qa.q: Ovulation is induced by
qa.a: the LH surge around the middle of the cycle
qa.e: A rapid rise of LH to a maximum around day 14 causes the Graafian follicle to rupture.

qa.q: The corpus luteum secretes large amounts of
qa.e: The corpus luteum, formed from the ruptured follicle, secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrium.

qa.q: In the absence of fertilisation, what happens to the corpus luteum?
qa.a: It degenerates, causing disintegration of the endometrium
qa.e: Without pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates; progesterone falls and menstruation follows.

qa.q: In a 28-day cycle, ovulation occurs at about day
qa.e: The LH surge and ovulation happen around the middle of the cycle, about day 14.

qa.q: On a graph, which hormone is highest during the luteal phase?
qa.e: Progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum dominates the luteal (secretory) phase.

qa.q: Why does menstruation stop during pregnancy?
qa.a: Progesterone levels stay high, maintaining the endometrium, and the cycle's events stop
qa.e: During pregnancy hormonal support keeps the endometrium intact, so no menstruation occurs.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The endometrium is maintained during the luteal phase. Reason (R): The corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Progesterone from the corpus luteum is essential for maintenance of the endometrium.

qa.q: The luteal phase is also called the
qa.e: In the luteal (secretory) phase, the endometrium is maintained by progesterone; 'proliferative' is the follicular phase.

qa.q: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the
qa.a: ampullary region of the fallopian tube
qa.e: Sperms and ovum meet in the ampullary region of the oviduct.

qa.q: What is the probability that a human zygote is male?
qa.e: Half the sperms carry Y; combining with an X ovum gives XY.

qa.q: The sex of a human baby is determined by
qa.a: the type of sperm (X or Y) that fertilises the ovum
qa.e: Ova always carry X, so the X or Y of the sperm decides the sex.

qa.q: Polyspermy is prevented because
qa.a: contact of a sperm with the zona pellucida changes the membrane, blocking other sperms
qa.e: Changes induced in the zona pellucida after first contact block additional sperms.

qa.q: The second meiotic division of the secondary oocyte results in
qa.a: a haploid ovum (ootid) and a second polar body
qa.e: Meiosis II is unequal, giving a large haploid ovum and a small second polar body.

qa.q: Why do not all copulations lead to fertilisation?
qa.a: The ovum and sperms must reach the ampullary region at the same time
qa.e: Fertilisation needs the ovum and sperms to be transported simultaneously to the ampulla.

qa.q: The secretions that help a sperm pass through the zona pellucida and plasma membrane of the ovum come from the
qa.e: Acrosomal enzymes help the sperm enter the ovum's cytoplasm.

qa.q: A human zygote has how many chromosomes?
qa.e: Haploid sperm (23) and haploid ovum (23) fuse to give a diploid zygote.

qa.q: An embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a
qa.e: The morula is the 8–16 cell stage; it then develops into a blastocyst.

qa.q: The inner cell mass of the blastocyst
qa.e: The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium and the inner cell mass gives rise to the embryo.

qa.q: Cleavage divisions are
qa.e: Cleavage involves rapid mitotic divisions producing blastomeres.

qa.q: The embedding of the blastocyst in the endometrium is called
qa.e: Implantation is the embedding of the blastocyst into the uterine lining, leading to pregnancy.

qa.q: The layer of the blastocyst that attaches to the endometrium is the
qa.e: The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium; later, chorionic villi appear on it.

qa.q: How many blastomeres are formed after three rounds of synchronous cleavage of a zygote?
qa.e: Each round doubles the number: 2³ = 8.

qa.q: Cleavage begins as the zygote moves through the
qa.a: isthmus of the oviduct towards the uterus
qa.e: Mitotic division starts as the zygote moves through the isthmus towards the uterus.

qa.q: The correct sequence is
qa.e: Cleavage gives a morula, which becomes a blastocyst that then implants.

qa.q: Which hormone is NOT secreted by the placenta?
qa.e: Relaxin is secreted by the ovary in the later phase of pregnancy; the others are placental.

qa.q: The placenta is formed by
qa.e: Chorionic villi from the trophoblast interdigitate with uterine tissue to form the placenta.

qa.q: Which set includes hormones produced in women only during pregnancy?
qa.e: hCG, hPL and relaxin are produced only during pregnancy; the others are present outside pregnancy too.

qa.q: A function of the placenta is to
qa.a: remove carbon dioxide and wastes produced by the embryo
qa.e: The placenta supplies O₂ and nutrients and removes CO₂ and excretory wastes.

qa.q: The structure connecting the placenta to the embryo is the
qa.e: The umbilical cord transports substances between the placenta and the embryo.

qa.q: Chorionic villi first appear on the
qa.e: After implantation, finger-like chorionic villi develop from the trophoblast.

qa.q: During pregnancy, the levels of which of the following increase in maternal blood?
qa.e: NCERT lists increased oestrogens, progestogens, cortisol, prolactin and thyroxine during pregnancy.

qa.q: The placenta acts as an endocrine tissue because it
qa.a: produces hormones such as hCG, hPL, oestrogens and progestogens
qa.e: Hormone production makes the placenta an endocrine tissue.

qa.q: By the end of which week is the first trimester complete, with most major organ systems formed?
qa.e: By the end of 12 weeks most major organ systems are formed; this marks the first trimester.

qa.q: The first movements of the foetus and the appearance of hair on the head are usually observed during the
qa.e: NCERT places first movements and head hair in the fifth month.

qa.q: By the end of the second month of pregnancy, the foetus develops
qa.e: Limbs and digits appear by the end of the second month.

qa.q: The germ layer that appears between the ectoderm and endoderm is the
qa.e: Ectoderm and endoderm form first; mesoderm soon appears between them.

qa.q: The heart of a human foetus is formed
qa.e: The heart forms after one month, and its sound can be heard by a stethoscope.

qa.q: Stem cells of the inner cell mass are special because they
qa.a: have the potency to give rise to all tissues and organs
qa.e: Stem cells can differentiate into any tissue or organ of the body.

qa.q: By the end of 24 weeks of pregnancy,
qa.a: the body is covered with fine hair, eyelids separate and eyelashes are formed
qa.e: These features mark the end of the second trimester.

qa.q: The average human gestation period is about
qa.e: Human pregnancy lasts about 9 months.

qa.q: The mild uterine contractions induced by signals from the foetus and placenta are called the
qa.e: Signals from the mature foetus and placenta cause mild contractions called the foetal ejection reflex.

qa.q: During parturition, oxytocin is released from the
qa.e: The foetal ejection reflex triggers oxytocin release from the mother's pituitary.

qa.q: Colostrum is especially important for the newborn because it
qa.a: contains antibodies that help develop resistance
qa.e: Colostrum, the early milk, is rich in antibodies (notably IgA), providing passive immunity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Oxytocin release during labour keeps increasing. Reason (R): Uterine contractions caused by oxytocin stimulate further oxytocin secretion.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: This is positive feedback: contractions trigger more oxytocin, which triggers stronger contractions.

qa.q: Parturition is induced by a
qa.e: Nerves and hormones together (foetal ejection reflex and oxytocin) induce parturition.

qa.q: The production of milk by the mammary glands is called
qa.e: Lactation is milk production, which begins towards the end of pregnancy.

qa.q: Oxytocin acts on which part of the uterus?
qa.e: Oxytocin causes contraction of the smooth muscle of the uterus.

qa.q: The milk produced during the initial few days of lactation is called
qa.e: The first milk is colostrum, rich in antibodies.

qa.q: According to WHO, reproductive health means
qa.a: total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social
qa.e: WHO's definition covers physical, emotional, behavioural and social well-being in reproduction.

qa.q: India launched its national family planning programme in the year
qa.e: India was among the first countries to start such a programme, in 1951.

qa.q: RCH stands for
qa.e: The improved programmes are called Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes.

qa.q: Why is sex education in schools encouraged?
qa.a: To give the young correct information and discourage belief in myths and misconceptions
qa.e: Correct, age-appropriate information protects adolescents from myths and unsafe practices.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a strategy for improving reproductive health listed in NCERT?
qa.e: NCERT stresses the importance of breastfeeding; discouraging it is not a strategy.

qa.q: A reproductively healthy society has people with
qa.a: normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in sex-related aspects
qa.e: Healthy reproductive organs plus healthy emotional and behavioural interactions define reproductive health.

qa.q: Who can play an important role in giving reproductive-health information, according to NCERT?
qa.a: Parents, close relatives, teachers and friends
qa.e: Besides agencies and media, family, teachers and friends are important sources of correct information.

qa.q: The family planning programme of India is now implemented in an improved form called
qa.e: Family planning evolved into Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes covering wider areas.

qa.q: Amniocentesis is a test based on
qa.a: the chromosomal pattern in the amniotic fluid surrounding the embryo
qa.e: Cells in the amniotic fluid reveal the foetal chromosomal pattern, helping detect genetic disorders.

qa.q: Why is there a statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination in India?
qa.a: To legally check the rise in female foeticide
qa.e: The ban targets misuse that led to abortion of female foetuses.

qa.q: The oral contraceptive Saheli was developed by scientists at
qa.e: Saheli was developed at the Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow.

qa.q: Which is an indicator of improved reproductive health in society?
qa.a: Decreased maternal and infant mortality rates
qa.e: Better post-natal care and assisted deliveries reduce maternal and infant mortality.

qa.q: Massive child immunisation and the ban on sex-determination tests are both examples of
qa.a: steps taken under reproductive and child health programmes
qa.e: NCERT lists them among the major tasks carried out under RCH programmes.

qa.q: A positive outcome of reproductive health programmes is
qa.a: an increased number of couples with small families
qa.e: More couples choosing small families is one of the gains listed by NCERT.

qa.q: The legitimate medical use of amniocentesis is to
qa.a: detect genetic disorders in the developing foetus
qa.e: It reveals chromosomal abnormalities, which is the allowed medical purpose.

qa.q: Research to find new reproduction-related methods is supported by
qa.e: NCERT notes that research is encouraged by governmental and non-governmental agencies.

qa.q: According to NCERT, the legal marriageable age in India is
qa.a: 18 years for females and 21 years for males
qa.e: The statutory marriageable age is 18 for females and 21 for males.

qa.q: Which is NOT a cause of the population explosion?
qa.a: An increase in maternal mortality rate
qa.e: Population rises when MMR falls, not when it increases.

qa.q: India's population at the time of Independence was approximately
qa.e: About 350 million people lived in India in 1947.

qa.q: The 2011 census reports India's growth rate as less than 2 per cent. This equals less than how many people per 1000 per year?
qa.e: 2 per cent of 1000 = 20.

qa.q: A town of 80,000 people grows at 20 per 1000 per year. How many people are added in one year?
MMR and IMR stand for
qa.a: maternal mortality rate and infant mortality rate
qa.e: MMR = maternal mortality rate; IMR = infant mortality rate; declines in both raised population.

qa.q: The slogan 'Hum Do Hamare Do' promotes
qa.e: It encouraged couples to have small families.

qa.q: A direct consequence of uncontrolled population growth is
qa.a: scarcity of basic requirements like food, shelter and clothing
qa.e: More people with the same resources leads to scarcity of basic needs.

qa.q: In the periodic abstinence method, couples avoid coitus from day
qa.e: Days 10–17 make up the fertile period when ovulation is expected.

qa.q: Lactational amenorrhea is theoretically effective for a maximum of how many months after parturition?
qa.e: It works only while the mother breastfeeds fully, and only up to a maximum of six months after delivery.

qa.q: Which is NOT a feature of an ideal contraceptive?
qa.a: It should permanently prevent conception in everyone
qa.e: An ideal contraceptive must be reversible, not permanent.

qa.q: Coitus interruptus means
