qa.a: the male partner withdraws before ejaculation
qa.e: In withdrawal (coitus interruptus), the penis is withdrawn before ejaculation to avoid insemination.

qa.q: Lactational amenorrhea works because
qa.a: ovulation and the menstrual cycle do not occur during intense lactation
qa.e: During intense breastfeeding after delivery, ovulation is suppressed, so conception chances are almost nil.

qa.q: A major disadvantage of natural methods of contraception is
qa.e: Natural methods have almost no side effects but fail more often.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Periodic abstinence avoids coitus from day 10 to 17. Reason (R): Ovulation is expected during this period, so chances of fertilisation are very high.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The window is chosen because ovulation, and hence fertilisation, is most likely then.

qa.q: An ideal contraceptive should NOT
qa.a: interfere with the sexual drive, desire or the sexual act
qa.e: NCERT lists non-interference with sexual drive as a key requirement.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-medicated IUD?
qa.e: Lippes loop is non-medicated; the others release copper or hormones.

qa.q: Copper ions released by copper IUDs
qa.a: suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity
qa.e: Cu ions act on sperms, reducing motility and fertilising capacity.

qa.q: Which contraceptive also protects against STIs and AIDS?
qa.e: Condoms are physical barriers that block exchange of body fluids, protecting against STIs.

qa.q: Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults are
qa.a: reusable rubber barriers that cover the cervix during coitus
qa.e: They are inserted to cover the cervix and are reusable.

qa.q: IUDs are considered ideal for women who
qa.a: want to delay pregnancy and/or space children
qa.e: IUDs are reversible, long-acting and suit spacing; they do not protect against STIs.

qa.q: Hormone-releasing IUDs act by
qa.a: making the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms
qa.e: Progestasert and LNG-20 release hormones that change the uterus and cervix.

qa.q: A general action of all IUDs is to
qa.a: increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus
qa.e: IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus; copper and hormones add extra effects.

qa.q: Spermicidal creams, jellies and foams are used along with diaphragms to
qa.e: Spermicides kill sperms that escape the barrier, raising efficiency.

qa.q: Oral contraceptive pills are usually taken daily for a period of
qa.e: Pills are taken for 21 days, then a 7-day gap during which menstruation occurs.

qa.q: Emergency contraceptives are effective if used within how many hours of coitus?
qa.e: Hormones or IUDs used within 72 hours of coitus act as emergency contraceptives.

qa.q: Saheli, the oral contraceptive, is
qa.e: Saheli contains a non-steroidal preparation and is taken once a week.

qa.q: In vasectomy, a small part of the
qa.a: vas deferens is removed or tied up
qa.e: Vasectomy blocks the vas deferens so sperms cannot reach the semen.

qa.q: Oral pills prevent conception by
qa.a: inhibiting ovulation and implantation and altering cervical mucus
qa.e: Progestogen-based pills act on ovulation, implantation and cervical mucus.

qa.q: The main drawback of surgical methods of contraception is
qa.e: Sterilisation is highly effective but hard to reverse.

qa.q: Which is a possible side effect of contraceptives listed by NCERT?
qa.e: NCERT lists nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular menstrual bleeding and even breast cancer.

qa.q: Progestogens can also be given as
qa.a: injections or implants under the skin
qa.e: Injections and implants of progestogens act like pills but over a longer period.

qa.q: MTP is considered relatively safe during
qa.e: MTPs are relatively safe up to 12 weeks (first trimester).

qa.q: Approximately how many MTPs are performed worldwide each year, according to NCERT?
qa.e: NCERT states nearly 45 to 50 million MTPs per year worldwide, about one-fifth of conceived pregnancies.

qa.q: As per NCERT's description of the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017, a pregnancy within the first 12 weeks may be terminated on the opinion of
qa.e: Up to 12 weeks, one registered medical practitioner's opinion suffices; two are needed beyond that up to 24 weeks.

qa.q: Which of these is a valid ground for MTP mentioned in NCERT?
qa.a: Continuing the pregnancy would risk the woman's life or cause grave injury to her health
qa.e: Risk to the mother or substantial risk of serious abnormality in the child are the legal grounds.

qa.q: Why is the government strict about the conditions for MTP?
qa.a: To prevent misuse such as female foeticide and unsafe abortions
qa.e: Strict conditions curb female foeticide and illegal, unsafe procedures.

qa.q: India first legalised MTP in the year
qa.e: The first MTP legislation came in 1971; 1951 was the family planning programme.

qa.q: Illegal MTPs performed by unqualified quacks are dangerous because they
qa.a: are unsafe and could be fatal
qa.e: Unsafe procedures by unqualified persons risk the woman's life.

qa.q: Using MTP in place of contraception is
qa.a: risky, because MTP should not be treated as a routine birth-control method
qa.e: MTP is a medical procedure with risks; contraception and counselling are the safer approach.

qa.q: Which STI is NOT completely curable even if detected early, according to NCERT?
qa.e: Except hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV, the listed STIs are completely curable with early treatment.

qa.q: Hepatitis-B and HIV can be transmitted by
qa.a: sharing injection needles, blood transfusion and from infected mother to foetus, besides sexual contact
qa.e: These two also spread through blood and needles and vertically from mother to child.

qa.q: Which complication can result from untreated STIs?
qa.e: Untreated STIs can cause PID, abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility or reproductive tract cancer.

qa.q: The age group in which STIs are most common, according to NCERT, is
qa.e: NCERT notes very high incidence among persons in the 15–24 age group.

qa.q: Why do many STIs remain undetected in females?
qa.a: Infected females may often be asymptomatic, and stigma delays treatment
qa.e: Lack of symptoms plus social stigma prevents timely detection.

qa.q: Which is the best set of preventive measures for STIs?
qa.a: Avoid sex with unknown or multiple partners, use condoms, and consult a qualified doctor early if in doubt
qa.e: NCERT's three simple principles prevent and control STIs; pills do not protect against infection.

qa.q: Early symptoms of STIs often include
qa.a: itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swellings in the genital region
qa.e: Early symptoms are often minor and local to the genital region.

qa.q: PID stands for
qa.e: Pelvic inflammatory disease is a complication of untreated STIs.

qa.q: In ZIFT, the zygote or early embryo with up to how many blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube?
qa.e: ZIFT transfers a zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres; larger embryos go to the uterus by IUT.

qa.q: IUT involves the transfer of
qa.a: embryos with more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus
qa.e: IUT = intra uterine transfer of embryos with more than 8 blastomeres.

qa.q: IVF stands for
qa.e: In vitro means 'in glass': fertilisation outside the body, in the lab.

qa.q: In a 'test tube baby' programme, fertilisation takes place
qa.a: outside the body in the laboratory, followed by embryo transfer
qa.e: The zygote forms in the lab; the embryo is then transferred to the woman's body to develop.

qa.q: Which set lists possible causes of infertility mentioned by NCERT?
qa.a: Physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological, psychological
qa.e: NCERT lists a wide range of causes, from physical to psychological.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In IVF, the zygote is formed outside the woman's body. Reason (R): In vitro fertilisation means fertilisation in laboratory conditions similar to those in the body.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: In vitro ('in glass') fertilisation happens in the lab under simulated body conditions, which is why the zygote forms outside the body.

qa.q: An embryo at the 16-blastomere stage should be transferred by
qa.e: Embryos with more than 8 blastomeres are transferred into the uterus by IUT.

qa.q: ART stands for
qa.e: ART refers to the special techniques like IVF, ZIFT, IUT, GIFT, ICSI and IUI that help infertile couples.

qa.q: In ICSI,
qa.a: a sperm is directly injected into the ovum
qa.e: ICSI = intra cytoplasmic sperm injection: one sperm is injected into the ovum's cytoplasm.

qa.q: GIFT involves
qa.a: transfer of an ovum collected from a donor into the fallopian tube of another female
qa.e: In GIFT a gamete (ovum) is transferred so that fertilisation can occur in the recipient's tube.

qa.q: Artificial insemination is advised when
qa.a: the male partner cannot inseminate or has a very low sperm count
qa.e: AI introduces semen from the husband or a donor into the vagina or uterus.

qa.q: Semen artificially introduced into the uterus is called
qa.e: IUI is intra-uterine insemination, a form of artificial insemination.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of ART mentioned by NCERT?
qa.a: It needs specialised professionals and expensive instruments, so it is available in few centres
qa.e: High precision, cost and limited centres restrict access; emotional, religious and social factors also deter.

qa.q: NCERT suggests which alternative for couples looking for parenthood?
qa.e: Legal adoption gives care to orphaned and destitute children and parenthood to couples.

qa.q: Which of these ARTs involves fertilisation occurring inside the female body?
qa.e: In GIFT, the donor ovum is placed in the fallopian tube where fertilisation can occur; the others involve lab fertilisation.

qa.q: Which ART uses embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation?
qa.a: Embryo transfer to a female who cannot conceive
qa.e: Embryos formed in vivo (within a female) can be transferred to help females who cannot conceive.

qa.q: For how many years did Mendel conduct his hybridisation experiments on garden peas?
qa.e: He worked from 1856 to 1863, which is seven years.

qa.q: How many true-breeding pea varieties did Mendel select?
qa.e: He chose 7 pairs of varieties, each pair differing in one character, so 14 varieties.

qa.q: In pea, which trait is dominant for pod colour?
qa.e: Green pod is dominant over yellow pod; note that for seed colour, yellow is dominant.

qa.q: True-breeding lines are those that
qa.a: show stable trait inheritance over several generations through continuous self-pollination
qa.e: True-breeding plants breed true: their progeny show the same trait generation after generation.

qa.q: The Sahiwal cows of Punjab are an example of
qa.a: artificial selection and domestication using natural variation
qa.e: Humans selected desirable variants over generations to produce such breeds.

qa.q: Which feature gave credibility to Mendel's data?
qa.a: Large sample sizes and statistical analysis
qa.e: Counting many plants and analysing them mathematically made his conclusions reliable.

qa.q: Genetics is the branch of biology that deals with
qa.e: Genetics studies how characters are inherited and how variation arises.

qa.q: In Mendel's pea, which flower position is dominant?
qa.e: Axial flower position is dominant over terminal.

qa.q: In an F2 generation of a monohybrid cross between tall and dwarf pea, 800 plants were raised. About how many would be dwarf?
qa.e: Dwarf plants are 1/4 of the F2: 800 × 1/4 = 200.

qa.q: The F2 genotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross is
qa.e: TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1, which collapses to 3 : 1 phenotypically when T is dominant.

qa.q: A test cross is a cross between
qa.a: an organism with the dominant phenotype and the recessive parent
qa.e: Crossing with the homozygous recessive reveals the unknown genotype of the dominant-phenotype organism.

qa.q: If a test cross produces all dominant-phenotype progeny, the tested organism is
qa.e: TT × tt gives only Tt offspring, all showing the dominant phenotype.

qa.q: Among 600 tall plants in an F2 generation, how many are expected to be heterozygous (Tt)?
qa.e: Among tall F2 plants (TT and Tt in 1 : 2 ratio), 2/3 are heterozygous: 600 × 2/3 = 400.

qa.q: The term 'allele' refers to
qa.a: alternative forms of a gene coding for a pair of contrasting traits
qa.e: Alleles are slightly different forms of the same gene, such as T and t.

qa.q: The Punnett square was developed by
qa.e: British geneticist Reginald C. Punnett devised this graphical method.

qa.q: A plant with genotype Tt is described as
qa.e: Tt has two different alleles (heterozygous), and T is dominant, so it is tall.

qa.q: In snapdragon, the F2 phenotypic ratio of a cross between red and white flowered plants is
qa.e: With incomplete dominance, each genotype has its own phenotype, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1.

qa.q: The law of segregation states that
qa.a: the two alleles of a pair separate during gamete formation so each gamete gets only one
qa.e: Segregation ensures gametes are pure for a trait.

qa.q: A pink snapdragon is crossed with a white one. What fraction of the progeny will be pink?
qa.e: Rr × rr gives Rr : rr = 1 : 1, i.e. pink : white = 1 : 1.

qa.q: Which statement best explains why an allele is recessive?
qa.a: It often produces a non-functional or less efficient product, or no product
qa.e: The allele producing a functional enzyme usually masks the one producing a non-functional or less efficient product.

qa.q: Which law is also called the 'law of purity of gametes' in many books, and states that gametes carry one allele?
qa.e: Segregation means each gamete is pure, carrying only one allele of a pair.

qa.q: The F1 of a cross between red (RR) and white (rr) snapdragons is pink. This shows that
qa.a: R is not completely dominant over r
qa.e: An intermediate F1 shows incomplete dominance; the alleles reappear unchanged in F2, so there is no blending.

qa.q: Number of kinds of gametes produced by a plant of genotype TT is
qa.e: A homozygous plant produces only one kind of gamete (T).

qa.q: According to the law of dominance, factors
qa.a: occur in pairs, and in a dissimilar pair one dominates the other
qa.e: Discrete factors occur in pairs; one member of a dissimilar pair is dominant.

qa.q: How many genotypes are possible for the human ABO blood groups?
qa.e: Three alleles give 3 homozygous + 3 heterozygous combinations = 6 genotypes (4 phenotypes).

qa.q: Blood group AB is an example of
qa.e: Both Iᴬ and Iᴮ are fully expressed together.

qa.q: A child has blood group O. Which parental pair could NOT have produced this child?
qa.e: An AB parent (IᴬIᴮ) has no i allele, so every child gets Iᴬ or Iᴮ and cannot be ii.

qa.q: Parents with genotypes Iᴬi and Iᴮi have a child. What is the probability that the child has blood group O?
qa.e: Each parent passes i with probability 1/2; 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

qa.q: Multiple allelism can be observed only when
qa.a: population studies are made, as an individual has only two alleles
qa.e: More than two alleles exist in the population, but each diploid individual carries just two.

qa.q: In pea seeds with genotype Bb, the seeds are
qa.e: For seed shape B is dominant (round), but starch grain size is intermediate.

qa.q: The number of phenotypes of the ABO blood group system is
qa.e: Phenotypes: A, B, AB and O.

qa.q: A woman of group AB marries a man of group O. What fraction of their children will have group A?
qa.e: IᴬIᴮ × ii gives Iᴬi (A) and Iᴮi (B) in a 1 : 1 ratio.

qa.q: In a dihybrid cross of RrYy × RrYy, what fraction of the progeny will be wrinkled and yellow?
qa.e: Wrinkled (rr) = 1/4 and yellow (Y_) = 3/4, so 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16.

qa.q: How many types of gametes does a plant of genotype RrYy produce?
qa.e: Independent assortment gives RY, Ry, rY and ry.

qa.q: In the F2 of a dihybrid cross, 960 seeds were obtained. How many are expected to be round and yellow?
The law of independent assortment states that
qa.a: segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair when two pairs are combined in a hybrid
qa.e: Each gene pair segregates independently of other gene pairs (for genes on different chromosomes).

qa.q: What is the probability of getting an RRYY plant in the F2 of a dihybrid cross?
The F2 ratio for seed shape alone (round : wrinkled) in a dihybrid cross is
How many different genotypes appear in the F2 of a dihybrid cross?
qa.e: Each gene gives 3 genotypes (e.g. RR, Rr, rr), and 3 × 3 = 9.

qa.q: RrYy is test-crossed with rryy. The expected phenotypic ratio is
qa.e: RrYy makes four gamete types equally, each combining with ry, giving four phenotypes in equal ratio.

qa.q: Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900 by
qa.a: de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak
qa.e: These three scientists independently rediscovered Mendel's results in 1900.

qa.q: The chromosomal theory of inheritance was proposed by uniting chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles. The scientist credited with this union is
qa.e: Sutton and Boveri noted the parallel; Sutton united chromosomal segregation with Mendel's principles.

qa.q: Experimental verification of the chromosomal theory was done by
qa.a: Thomas Hunt Morgan using Drosophila melanogaster
qa.e: Morgan's work on fruit flies verified the theory experimentally.

qa.q: Which is NOT a reason for using Drosophila in genetics?
qa.a: It has a life cycle of about two years
qa.e: Drosophila's life cycle is about two weeks, not two years.

qa.q: The parallel between genes and chromosomes is that both
qa.a: occur in pairs and segregate during gamete formation
qa.e: Like Mendel's factors, homologous chromosomes occur in pairs and separate at meiosis.

qa.q: In how many years after Mendel published (1865) was his work rediscovered (1900)?
One reason Mendel's work was not recognised for a long time was that
qa.a: his idea of discrete factors that did not blend contradicted the then belief in continuous variation
qa.e: Communication was poor, and his concept of non-blending factors and his mathematical approach were not accepted at the time.

qa.q: Homologous chromosomes separate during
qa.a: meiosis (anaphase I), so only one of each pair goes to a gamete
qa.e: Separation of homologues in meiosis I mirrors Mendel's segregation of alleles.

qa.q: In Morgan's experiments, the recombination between the genes for yellow body and white eye was
qa.e: Yellow body and white eye were tightly linked with only 1.3 per cent recombination; white eye–miniature wing showed 37.2 per cent.

qa.q: Genes that show very low recombination are
qa.a: tightly linked and located close together
qa.e: The closer two genes are, the less often crossing over separates them.

qa.q: Who used the frequency of recombination to map positions of genes on a chromosome?
qa.e: Sturtevant, Morgan's student, made the first genetic maps.

qa.q: The term linkage was coined by
qa.e: Morgan coined 'linkage' for the physical association of genes on a chromosome.

qa.q: Morgan's F2 ratios deviated from 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 because
qa.a: the two genes were on the same chromosome and did not segregate independently
qa.e: Linked genes on the X chromosome tend to be inherited together, breaking independent assortment.

qa.q: Recombination refers to
qa.a: the generation of non-parental gene combinations
qa.e: Recombinants carry new combinations not found in either parent.

qa.q: Two genes show 37.2 per cent recombination. This suggests they are
qa.a: loosely linked, being relatively far apart
qa.e: A high recombination frequency suggests the genes are far apart on the chromosome.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly distinguished?
qa.a: Aneuploidy: gain or loss of chromosomes; polyploidy: increase in whole sets of chromosomes
qa.e: Aneuploidy involves individual chromosomes; polyploidy involves whole sets. Linkage keeps genes together; crossing over separates them.

qa.q: Human skin colour is an example of
qa.e: Several genes with additive effects, plus environment, control skin colour.

qa.q: Phenylketonuria is an example of pleiotropy because
qa.a: a single gene mutation causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation
qa.e: One defective gene affects a metabolic pathway, giving multiple phenotypic effects.

qa.q: In PKU, the enzyme that is lacking normally converts
qa.e: Without this enzyme, phenylalanine accumulates and forms phenylpyruvic acid.

qa.q: In the three-gene model, how many dominant alleles does the genotype AaBbCc carry?
qa.e: One dominant allele from each of the three genes: A, B and C.

qa.q: Polygenic traits show
qa.e: Additive effects of many genes produce a smooth range of phenotypes.

qa.q: PKU is inherited as
qa.e: PKU is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism.

qa.q: How many dominant alleles are present in the darkest genotype AABBCC?
qa.e: Each of the three genes contributes two dominant alleles: 3 × 2 = 6.

qa.q: In PKU, phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives are also excreted in urine because of
qa.a: their poor absorption by the kidney
qa.e: They accumulate and, being poorly absorbed by the kidney, appear in urine.

qa.q: In birds, sex determination is of which type?
qa.e: Female birds are ZW and male birds are ZZ.

qa.q: In grasshoppers, males have
qa.a: only one X chromosome besides autosomes (XO)
qa.e: In the XO type, males lack a second sex chromosome.

qa.q: The X body was first observed by
qa.e: Henking observed it during spermatogenesis of some insects in 1891.

qa.q: Male heterogamety means that
qa.a: males produce two different kinds of gametes with respect to sex chromosomes
qa.e: In XO and XY systems, sperms either carry X or not (XO) or carry X or Y (XY).

qa.q: Which organism shows female heterogamety?
qa.e: Birds such as pigeons follow the ZW system, where females produce two kinds of eggs.

qa.q: Half the sperms of a grasshopper carry an X chromosome. The other half
qa.e: In XO males, meiosis gives sperms with or without the X.

qa.q: In the ZW system, a ZZ individual is
qa.e: ZZ is male and ZW is female in birds.

qa.q: Chromosomes that are not involved in sex determination are called
qa.e: Autosomes are all chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes.

qa.q: In honey bees, an unfertilised egg develops into a
qa.e: Unfertilised eggs develop parthenogenetically into haploid males.

qa.q: The chromosome number of a male honey bee is
qa.e: Males are haploid: half of the female's 32.

qa.q: Male honey bees produce sperms by
qa.e: Since drones are haploid, they form sperms by mitosis.

qa.q: Why is it wrong to blame the mother for the sex of a human child?
qa.a: All ova carry X; the sex depends on whether an X or Y sperm fertilises the ovum
qa.e: The father's gamete (X or Y) determines the sex.

qa.q: The probability of a male child in each human pregnancy is
qa.e: Half the sperms carry Y, and every ovum carries X.

qa.q: How many autosomes does a human somatic cell contain?
qa.e: 22 pairs of autosomes = 44; plus 2 sex chromosomes gives 46.

qa.q: A drone in a honey bee colony has
qa.e: The drone's mother (queen) came from a fertilised egg, so her father is the drone's grandfather.

qa.q: The sex-determination system in honey bees is called
qa.e: Sex depends on the number of chromosome sets: diploid females, haploid males.

qa.q: Sickle-cell anaemia results from substitution of
qa.a: glutamic acid by valine at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain
qa.e: A single base change (GAG → GUG) in the sixth codon replaces Glu with Val in the beta chain.

qa.q: The change in the codon responsible for sickle-cell anaemia is
qa.e: GAG codes glutamic acid and GUG codes valine.

qa.q: Two carriers of sickle-cell trait have a child. What is the probability that the child is unaffected and not a carrier?
qa.e: HbᴬHbᴬ forms in 1 of 4 combinations.

qa.q: Insertion or deletion of a base pair in a gene causes a
qa.e: Adding or removing bases shifts the reading frame of all downstream codons.

qa.q: Which is a physical mutagen?
qa.e: UV radiation is a physical agent that induces mutation.

qa.q: Chromosomal aberrations are commonly observed in
qa.e: Cancer cells often show deletions, duplications and other chromosomal changes.

qa.q: Under what condition do RBCs of a sickle-cell patient become sickle-shaped?
qa.e: The mutant haemoglobin polymerises at low oxygen tension, distorting RBCs into sickles.

qa.q: Mutation is defined as
qa.a: an alteration of DNA sequences that changes the genotype and phenotype
qa.e: Mutations alter DNA sequence and are a source of variation besides recombination.

qa.q: In pedigree analysis, a double line between a male and a female represents
qa.e: A double line indicates a mating between blood relatives.

qa.q: Myotonic dystrophy is inherited as an
qa.e: NCERT gives myotonic dystrophy as an example of an autosomal dominant pedigree.

qa.q: β thalassemia is controlled by
qa.a: a single gene HBB on chromosome 11
qa.e: β globin is coded by HBB on chromosome 11; α globin by HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16.

qa.q: Thalassemia differs from sickle-cell anaemia in that thalassemia is a
qa.a: quantitative problem of synthesising too few globin molecules
qa.e: Thalassemia reduces the amount of globin made; sickle-cell makes a faulty globin.

qa.q: Two unaffected parents have an affected son and an unaffected daughter. The trait could be
qa.e: Unaffected parents with an affected child point to a recessive allele; an affected son fits both autosomal and X-linked recessive.

qa.q: Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by
qa.a: alteration or mutation in a single gene
qa.e: Single-gene changes cause Mendelian disorders; chromosome number changes cause chromosomal disorders.

qa.q: In α thalassemia, how many genes in total (from both parents) control α globin production?
qa.e: Two closely linked genes (HBA1 and HBA2) on chromosome 16 of each parent: 2 × 2 = 4.

qa.q: A trait appears in every generation, and each affected child has at least one affected parent. The trait is most likely
qa.e: Dominant traits rarely skip generations because one copy of the allele is enough.

qa.q: A colour-blind man marries a woman with normal vision who is not a carrier. What is the probability that their son will be colour blind?
qa.e: Sons get their X from the mother, who has two normal X chromosomes, so no son is colour blind; all daughters will be carriers.

qa.q: A carrier woman (XᴴXʰ) marries a normal man. What fraction of their sons is expected to be haemophilic?
qa.e: Each son receives one of the mother's two X chromosomes; half receive Xʰ.

qa.q: Colour blindness occurs in about what percentage of human females?
qa.e: About 8 per cent of males but only about 0.4 per cent of females are colour blind.

qa.q: Haemophilia affects
qa.a: a single protein that is part of the cascade of proteins involved in blood clotting
qa.e: A defective clotting protein makes even small cuts bleed for long.

qa.q: Why is a haemophilic female extremely rare?
qa.a: Her mother must be at least a carrier and her father must be haemophilic
qa.e: Both her X chromosomes must carry the allele, so she needs a carrier/affected mother and an affected father.

qa.q: A colour-blind man and a carrier woman have a daughter. What is the probability that she is colour blind?
qa.e: Daughter gets the father's Xᶜ (colour-blind allele) for sure, and the mother's Xᶜ with probability 1/2.

qa.q: Colour blindness is caused by a defect in
qa.a: either the red or the green cone of the eye
qa.e: A mutation in X-linked genes affects red or green cones, causing failure to discriminate red from green.

qa.q: From the cross XᴴXʰ × XᴴY, what fraction of daughters will be carriers?
qa.e: Daughters receive Xᴴ from the father and Xᴴ or Xʰ from the mother, so half are XᴴXʰ carriers.

qa.q: The karyotype of a person with Turner's syndrome is
qa.e: Turner's syndrome results from the absence of one X chromosome.

qa.q: Down's syndrome is caused by
qa.e: An additional copy of chromosome 21 causes Down's syndrome.

qa.q: Gynaecomastia is a feature of
qa.e: Klinefelter's males (47, XXY) show overall masculine development with some feminine features like breast development.

qa.q: Down's syndrome was first described by
qa.e: Langdon Down described it in 1866.

qa.q: Failure of cytokinesis after telophase of cell division leads to
qa.e: An entire set of chromosomes is added when the cell fails to divide after nuclear division.

qa.q: Total number of chromosomes in a person with Klinefelter's syndrome is
qa.e: 44 autosomes + XXY = 47.

qa.q: Failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division resulting in gain or loss of a chromosome is called
qa.e: Aneuploidy is the gain or loss of individual chromosomes.

qa.q: Females with Turner's syndrome are sterile because
qa.e: Rudimentary ovaries and lack of secondary sexual characters are hallmarks of Turner's syndrome.

qa.q: The length of a DNA molecule is 1.36 mm. How many base pairs does it have? (distance between bp = 0.34 nm)
qa.e: Number of bp = length ÷ 0.34 nm = 1.36 × 10⁻³ m ÷ 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m = 4 × 10⁶.

qa.q: A DNA segment has 1000 base pairs. What is its length in nm?
qa.e: Length = 1000 × 0.34 nm = 340 nm.

qa.q: Which bond links a nitrogenous base to the pentose sugar?
qa.e: Base and sugar are joined by an N-glycosidic linkage at the 1′C to form a nucleoside.

qa.q: Uracil is present in
qa.e: RNA has uracil instead of thymine; cytosine is common to both.

qa.q: The 5′ end of a polynucleotide chain carries
qa.a: a free phosphate group on the 5′ carbon of the sugar
qa.e: One end has a free phosphate at the 5′C (5′ end); the other has a free 3′-OH (3′ end).

qa.q: How many base pairs are present in the genome of bacteriophage lambda?
qa.e: λ phage has 48502 bp; φX174 has 5386 nucleotides; E. coli 4.6 × 10⁶ bp; human haploid 3.3 × 10⁹ bp.

qa.q: 'Nuclein', the acidic substance in the nucleus, was first identified by
qa.e: Friedrich Meischer identified it in 1869; it was later recognised as DNA.

qa.q: An additional –OH group at the 2′ position of the sugar is found in
qa.e: Ribose in RNA carries a 2′-OH, which makes RNA more reactive than DNA.

qa.q: A double-stranded DNA has 30 per cent guanine. What is the percentage of thymine?
How many hydrogen bonds hold a G–C base pair together?
qa.e: G pairs with C by three hydrogen bonds; A–T has two.

qa.q: A DNA segment has 100 bp, of which 40 are A–T pairs and the rest G–C. How many hydrogen bonds are there in total?
qa.e: A–T pairs: 40 × 2 = 80; G–C pairs: 60 × 3 = 180; total 260.

qa.q: The pitch of the DNA helix is
qa.e: One full turn is 3.4 nm and holds about 10 bp, each 0.34 nm apart.

qa.q: 'Antiparallel' strands in DNA means that
qa.a: one strand runs 5′→3′ and the other runs 3′→5′
qa.e: The two chains have opposite polarity.

qa.q: The central dogma of molecular biology was proposed by
qa.e: Crick proposed DNA → RNA → protein as the flow of genetic information.

qa.q: Besides hydrogen bonds, which feature gives stability to the DNA double helix?
qa.a: Stacking of base-pair planes over one another
qa.e: Base stacking, in addition to H-bonds, stabilises the helix.

qa.q: Reverse transcription (RNA → DNA) occurs in
qa.e: In some viruses, such as retroviruses, information flows from RNA to DNA.

qa.q: Histones are rich in which amino acids?
qa.e: Lysine and arginine carry positive charges in their side chains, making histones basic.

qa.q: How many histone molecules make up a histone octamer?
qa.e: 'Octa' means eight.

qa.q: A typical nucleosome contains how many base pairs of DNA?
qa.e: NCERT states a typical nucleosome contains 200 bp of DNA helix.

qa.q: The DNA of E. coli, held by positively charged proteins, lies in a region called the
qa.e: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus; their DNA is organised in the nucleoid.

qa.q: Which statement about heterochromatin is correct?
qa.a: It is densely packed, stains dark and is transcriptionally inactive
qa.e: Dense packing makes heterochromatin dark-staining and inactive.

qa.q: Packaging of chromatin at a higher level requires
qa.e: NHC proteins are needed for packaging beyond the nucleosome level.

qa.q: Why does DNA bind strongly to histones?
qa.a: DNA is negatively charged and histones are positively charged
qa.e: Opposite charges attract: phosphates of DNA bind the basic histones.

qa.q: If a cell has 4 × 10⁶ nucleosomes of 200 bp each, the total bp packaged is
In the Hershey–Chase experiment, radioactive sulphur (³⁵S) was used to label
qa.a: the protein coat of the phage
qa.e: Proteins contain sulphur but DNA does not, so ³⁵S labels protein.

qa.q: Griffith observed that mice died when injected with
qa.a: heat-killed S strain mixed with live R strain
qa.e: The live R strain was transformed by material from the dead S strain into virulent S.

qa.q: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that transformation was inhibited by
qa.e: Only the DNA-digesting enzyme stopped transformation, so DNA is the transforming principle.

qa.q: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, bacteria infected with ³²P-labelled phages were radioactive because
qa.e: ³²P labels DNA; radioactive bacteria showed that DNA is injected into the host.

qa.q: The organism used by Griffith was
qa.e: Griffith worked with S and R strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae in mice.

qa.q: Which is NOT a criterion that a genetic material must fulfil?
qa.a: It must be unable to change at all
qa.e: Genetic material should allow slow changes (mutation) needed for evolution.

qa.q: The purpose of the blender in the Hershey–Chase experiment was to
qa.a: remove the viral coats from the surface of the bacteria
qa.e: Blending detached phage coats; centrifugation then separated bacteria from free coats.

qa.q: Griffith's experiment was performed in the year
qa.e: Griffith reported transformation in 1928; Hershey–Chase was 1952.

qa.q: The reactive group that makes RNA labile and easily degradable is
qa.e: Every RNA nucleotide carries a 2′-OH, which makes RNA reactive and unstable.

qa.q: DNA is preferred over RNA for storage of genetic information because it is
qa.a: chemically less reactive and structurally more stable
qa.e: DNA's stability suits long-term storage; RNA's reactivity suits transmission.

qa.q: For transmission of genetic information, RNA is better because it
qa.a: can directly code for the synthesis of proteins
qa.e: RNA can be translated directly; DNA needs RNA as an intermediate.

qa.q: The first genetic material is believed to be
qa.e: The RNA world hypothesis holds that RNA was the first genetic material.

qa.q: DNA evolved from RNA mainly to gain
qa.e: Chemical modifications made DNA more stable than its RNA ancestor.

qa.q: Why do RNA viruses mutate faster than DNA organisms?
qa.a: RNA is unstable and mutates at a faster rate
qa.e: RNA's instability leads to more frequent mutations, and short life spans speed evolution.

qa.q: Which life processes evolved around RNA, according to NCERT?
qa.e: NCERT says essential processes such as metabolism, translation and splicing evolved around RNA.

qa.q: Assertion (A): DNA is more stable than RNA. Reason (R): RNA has a reactive 2′-OH group on every nucleotide.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The 2′-OH makes RNA labile; its absence in deoxyribose contributes to DNA's stability.

qa.q: In the Meselson–Stahl experiment, after two generations in ¹⁴N medium, the DNA consisted of
qa.a: equal amounts of hybrid and light DNA
qa.e: Semi-conservative replication gives 2 hybrid and 2 light molecules after two generations.

qa.q: After three generations of semi-conservative replication starting from one ¹⁵N DNA molecule in ¹⁴N medium, how many hybrid molecules are present?
qa.e: The two original ¹⁵N strands are always in two hybrid molecules; all others are light.

qa.q: DNA polymerase can polymerise nucleotides only in the
qa.e: This is why one strand is made continuously and the other discontinuously.

qa.q: The discontinuously synthesised fragments on the lagging strand are joined by
qa.e: DNA ligase seals the gaps between fragments.

qa.q: The heavy isotope used by Meselson and Stahl was
qa.e: ¹⁵N is a heavy, non-radioactive isotope distinguished by density.

qa.q: In eukaryotes, DNA replication takes place in the
qa.a: S phase of the cell cycle
qa.e: DNA is synthesised in the S (synthesis) phase.

qa.q: The deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates in replication serve as
qa.a: both substrates and sources of energy
qa.e: Their two terminal phosphates are high-energy, like ATP.

qa.q: Semi-conservative replication in chromosomes of Vicia faba was shown by Taylor and colleagues using
qa.e: They traced newly synthesised DNA in chromosomes with radioactive thymidine.

qa.q: The coding strand of a DNA segment is 5′-ATGCTAG-3′. The mRNA transcribed from this gene is
qa.e: mRNA has the same sequence and polarity as the coding strand, with U replacing T.

qa.q: A template strand reads 3′-TACGGT-5′. The mRNA formed is
qa.e: Pair each template base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, T→A … and the mRNA runs 5′→3′.

qa.q: Which strand of DNA has the same sequence as the mRNA (except T for U)?
qa.e: The coding strand matches the mRNA; the template strand is its complement.

qa.q: The promoter of a transcription unit is located
qa.a: upstream, towards the 5′ end of the structural gene (coding strand)
qa.e: The promoter is upstream and provides the RNA polymerase binding site.

qa.q: One reason why both DNA strands are not transcribed for the same gene is that
qa.a: the two RNAs would be complementary and form double-stranded RNA that cannot be translated
qa.e: Complementary RNAs would pair up, preventing translation and making transcription futile.

qa.q: The template strand of DNA in a transcription unit has which polarity?
qa.e: RNA is made 5′→3′, so the template is read in the 3′→5′ direction.

qa.q: How many nucleotides will an mRNA have if its gene's transcribed region is 300 bp long?
qa.e: Each base of the template gives one ribonucleotide.

qa.q: The terminator in a transcription unit
qa.a: defines the end of transcription and lies towards the 3′ end of the coding strand
qa.e: The terminator is downstream and marks where transcription stops.

qa.q: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes the precursor of mRNA (hnRNA)?
qa.e: Pol II makes hnRNA; Pol I makes most rRNAs; Pol III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs.

qa.q: 5S rRNA and tRNA are transcribed by
qa.e: Pol III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs.

qa.q: In capping, the nucleotide added to the 5′ end of hnRNA is
qa.e: An unusual nucleotide, methyl guanosine triphosphate, forms the 5′ cap; adenylates form the 3′ tail.

qa.q: Split genes contain
qa.e: Coding exons are separated by non-coding introns, which are removed by splicing.

qa.q: In bacteria, transcription and translation can be coupled because
qa.a: there is no nuclear membrane separating them and mRNA needs no processing
qa.e: In prokaryotes both occur in the same compartment, so translation can start before transcription ends.

qa.q: The factor that helps bacterial RNA polymerase terminate transcription is
qa.e: σ helps initiation; ρ helps termination.

qa.q: Structural genes in bacteria are mostly
qa.e: Bacterial transcription units often code several polypeptides; eukaryotic ones are mostly monocistronic.

qa.q: About how many adenylate residues are added during tailing?
qa.e: Tailing adds 200–300 adenylate residues at the 3′ end in a template-independent manner.

qa.q: How many codons code for amino acids?
qa.e: Of 64 codons, 3 are stop codons, leaving 61 that code for amino acids.

qa.q: Which scientist developed the chemical method of synthesising RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases?
qa.e: Khorana's chemical synthesis of defined RNAs was key to deciphering the code.

qa.q: The genetic code is said to be degenerate because
qa.a: some amino acids are coded by more than one codon
qa.e: Degeneracy means multiple codons for one amino acid; the code is still unambiguous.

qa.q: The mRNA 5′-AUG CCC UGA GGG-3′ will produce a polypeptide of how many amino acids?
qa.e: AUG (Met) and CCC are translated; UGA is a stop codon, so translation ends there.

qa.q: Insertion of one base into a gene's coding region usually causes
qa.a: a frame-shift mutation that changes all downstream codons
qa.e: Adding one base shifts the reading frame from the point of insertion.

qa.q: Insertion of three bases (one codon) into a gene results in
qa.a: the addition of one amino acid with the reading frame unaltered after that point
qa.e: Three bases add one codon, keeping the downstream frame intact.

qa.q: AUG has a dual function: it codes for methionine and
qa.e: AUG is both the start codon and the codon for methionine.

qa.q: Gamow proposed a triplet code because
qa.a: 4 bases taken three at a time give 64 combinations, enough for 20 amino acids
qa.e: 4² = 16 is too few for 20 amino acids; 4³ = 64 is sufficient.

qa.q: How many peptide bonds are present in a polypeptide of 50 amino acids?
qa.e: n amino acids in a chain are joined by n − 1 peptide bonds.

qa.q: The secondary structure of tRNA looks like
qa.e: The secondary structure is clover-leaf; the actual 3-D structure is an inverted L.

qa.q: Which rRNA acts as the enzyme (ribozyme) for peptide bond formation in bacteria?
qa.e: NCERT gives 23S rRNA in bacteria as the ribozyme.

qa.q: The process of linking an amino acid to its tRNA using ATP is called
qa.e: Amino acids are activated with ATP and attached to their cognate tRNA.

qa.q: Translation terminates when
qa.a: a release factor binds to the stop codon
qa.e: No tRNA reads stop codons; a release factor ends translation.

qa.q: Untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNA are present
qa.a: at both the 5′ end (before the start codon) and the 3′ end (after the stop codon)
qa.e: UTRs flank the coding region and help efficient translation.

qa.q: The anticodon on the tRNA for the codon 5′-GCA-3′ is
qa.e: The anticodon is complementary and antiparallel: codon 5′-GCA-3′ pairs with anticodon 3′-CGU-5′, which is 5′-UGC-3′.

qa.q: Translation begins when
qa.a: the small ribosomal subunit encounters the mRNA
qa.e: Ribosomal subunits stay separate when inactive; translation starts when the small subunit meets mRNA.

qa.q: The z gene of the lac operon codes for
qa.e: z codes β-galactosidase, which hydrolyses lactose into galactose and glucose.

qa.q: In the lac operon, the inducer is
qa.e: Lactose (allolactose) binds and inactivates the repressor, switching the operon on.

qa.q: In the absence of lactose, the lac operon is switched off because
qa.a: the repressor binds to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase
qa.e: The repressor, made constitutively from the i gene, binds the operator when no inducer is present.

qa.q: Regulation of the lac operon by the repressor is an example of
qa.e: A repressor turning genes off is negative regulation.

qa.q: The lac operon was first explained by
qa.e: Jacob and Monod described the first transcriptionally regulated system.

qa.q: The y gene product increases the permeability of the cell to
qa.e: Permease (y) lets β-galactosides like lactose enter the cell.

qa.q: In prokaryotes, gene expression is mainly regulated at the level of
qa.e: Prokaryotes control mainly how often transcription starts; splicing and nuclear transport do not apply.

qa.q: How many structural genes are present in the lac operon?
qa.e: z, y and a are the three structural genes; i is regulatory.

qa.q: The Human Genome Project was completed in
qa.e: It was launched in 1990 and completed in 2003.

qa.q: At US $3 per bp, what would be the estimated cost of sequencing 3 × 10⁹ bp?
qa.e: 3 × 10⁹ bp × $3 = $9 × 10⁹ = 9 billion dollars.

qa.q: The HGP aimed to identify approximately how many human genes?
qa.e: The goal stated 20,000–25,000 genes; 3 billion is the number of base pairs.

qa.q: ELSI in the context of HGP stands for
qa.e: HGP aimed to address the ethical, legal and social issues arising from the project.

qa.q: The HGP was coordinated by
qa.a: the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institute of Health
qa.e: These two U.S. agencies coordinated it; the Wellcome Trust was a major partner.

qa.q: The approach that identifies all genes expressed as RNA is called
qa.e: ESTs target expressed genes; annotation sequences everything and assigns function later.

qa.q: Which free-living, non-pathogenic nematode's genome was sequenced alongside HGP?
qa.e: C. elegans is a model organism; the others are parasites.

qa.q: How many years did the HGP take, from launch to completion?
Which human chromosome has the most genes?
qa.e: Chromosome 1 has the most genes and Y has the fewest.

qa.q: What percentage of the human genome codes for proteins?
qa.e: Less than 2 per cent codes for proteins; repeated sequences make up a large portion.

qa.q: The automated sequencers used in HGP worked on the principle of the method developed by
qa.e: Sanger developed the DNA sequencing method; Jeffreys developed DNA fingerprinting.

qa.q: The largest known human gene is
qa.e: Dystrophin is the largest at 2.4 million bases; the average gene has 3000 bases.

qa.q: BAC and YAC are
qa.a: vectors used to clone DNA fragments in bacteria and yeast
qa.e: Bacterial and yeast artificial chromosomes carried DNA fragments for amplification.

qa.q: How many base pairs differ between two humans, if 99.9 per cent of 3 × 10⁹ bp are identical?
qa.e: 0.1 per cent of 3 × 10⁹ = 3 × 10⁶.

qa.q: Genetic and physical maps of the genome were generated using
qa.a: polymorphism of restriction endonuclease recognition sites and microsatellites
qa.e: Restriction-site polymorphisms and microsatellite repeats served as map markers.

qa.q: The total number of genes in the human genome is estimated by NCERT at about
qa.e: NCERT gives an estimate of 30,000 genes.

qa.q: DNA fingerprinting was initially developed by
qa.e: Jeffreys used VNTR probes to develop the technique.

qa.q: The probe used by Alec Jeffreys in DNA fingerprinting was
qa.e: VNTRs, a mini-satellite class showing high polymorphism, served as the probe.

qa.q: The size of VNTRs varies from
qa.e: NCERT states VNTR size ranges from 0.1 to 20 kb.

qa.q: Satellite DNA appears in density gradient centrifugation as
qa.a: small peaks separate from the major peak of bulk DNA
qa.e: Bulk DNA forms the major peak; repetitive DNA forms minor satellite peaks.

qa.q: Transferring separated DNA fragments from the gel to a nitrocellulose or nylon membrane is called
qa.e: Blotting moves the fragments onto a membrane before hybridisation with the probe.

qa.q: The use of DNA fingerprinting in paternity testing is possible because
qa.a: polymorphisms are inherited from parents to children
qa.e: Inherited VNTR bands let a child's pattern be traced to each parent.

qa.q: Which step comes immediately after electrophoresis in DNA fingerprinting?
qa.e: After separation by electrophoresis, fragments are blotted, then hybridised, then detected.

qa.q: The sensitivity of DNA fingerprinting has been increased by
qa.e: PCR amplifies DNA so that even a single cell can be enough.

qa.q: According to NCERT, Earth was formed about
qa.e: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago in the solar system of the Milky Way galaxy.

qa.q: The theory that life came from decaying and rotting matter is called
qa.e: Spontaneous generation was disproved by Louis Pasteur.

qa.q: Louis Pasteur's experiments showed that
qa.a: life comes only from pre-existing life
qa.e: In pre-sterilised flasks, no life arose from killed yeast, disproving spontaneous generation.

qa.q: Life is believed to have appeared on Earth about
qa.e: Life appeared about 500 million years after Earth formed (4.5 billion − 0.5 billion = 4 billion years ago).

qa.q: Panspermia proposes that
qa.a: units of life called spores were transferred to Earth from outer space
qa.e: It is the idea that life arrived from elsewhere in space.

qa.q: The early atmosphere of Earth contained mainly
qa.a: water vapour, methane, carbon dioxide and ammonia
qa.e: These gases were released from the molten mass; free oxygen was not abundant.

qa.q: The theory that explains the origin of the universe as a singular huge explosion is the
qa.e: The Big Bang theory describes the explosion, expansion and cooling of the universe.

qa.q: In the early Earth, UV rays from the sun
qa.a: broke water into hydrogen and oxygen
qa.e: UV split water; lighter hydrogen escaped and oxygen combined with ammonia and methane to form other compounds.

qa.q: Miller's experiment produced
qa.e: Electric discharge through the gas mixture gave amino acids.

qa.q: Which gas was NOT used in Miller's experiment?
qa.e: The mixture was CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour, a reducing atmosphere without free oxygen.

qa.q: The temperature (in °C) in Miller's closed flask was
qa.e: NCERT states CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at 800 °C.

qa.q: The first cellular forms of life originated about
qa.e: Non-cellular forms appeared about 3 billion years ago; cellular forms about 2000 mya.

qa.q: Chemical evolution refers to
qa.a: formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents
qa.e: Oparin and Haldane proposed that chemical evolution preceded life.

qa.q: Miller's experiment was performed in the year
qa.e: S. L. Miller carried out the experiment in 1953.

qa.q: The electric discharge in Miller's experiment represented
qa.e: Sparks simulated the energy of lightning in the early atmosphere.

qa.q: The early atmosphere assumed by Oparin and Haldane was
qa.e: A reducing atmosphere with methane and ammonia favoured formation of organic molecules.

qa.q: Which is NOT a connotation of the theory of special creation?
qa.a: Species have evolved gradually by natural selection
qa.e: Gradual evolution by natural selection is Darwin's idea, which opposed special creation.

qa.q: In Darwinian terms, fitness ultimately refers to
qa.e: The fit are those that leave more progeny.

qa.q: Alfred Wallace came to conclusions similar to Darwin's while working in the
qa.e: NCERT names the Malay Archipelago for Wallace.

qa.q: Darwin's sea voyage was aboard the ship
qa.e: Darwin sailed around the world on H.M.S. Beagle.

qa.q: According to the theory of special creation, the age of Earth is about
qa.e: Special creation claimed Earth is about 4000 years old; science estimates 4.5 billion years.

qa.q: Darwin concluded that existing life forms share similarities with
qa.a: each other and with life forms that existed millions of years ago
qa.e: Similarities among living and extinct forms suggested common ancestry.

qa.q: The theory of special creation was strongly challenged in the
qa.e: Observations by Darwin and others in the 1800s challenged it.

qa.q: Assertion (A): According to Darwin, some individuals leave more progeny than others. Reason (R): Characteristics that help some individuals survive better in natural conditions allow them to outbreed others.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Better-adapted individuals reproduce more; this differential reproduction is natural selection.

qa.q: Embryological support for evolution was proposed by
qa.e: Haeckel proposed it based on features like vestigial gill slits in embryos; von Baer disproved it.

qa.q: Haeckel's embryological evidence was disproved by
qa.e: Von Baer noted that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.

qa.q: The age of fossils is determined by
qa.e: Radioactive dating estimates the age of rocks and fossils.

qa.q: Similarities in proteins and genes among diverse organisms are evidence of
qa.e: Shared molecular features point to common descent.

qa.q: Vestigial gill slits behind the head are seen in
qa.a: the embryos of all vertebrates, including humans
qa.e: They appear in all vertebrate embryos but are functional only in fish.

qa.q: The study of fossils is called
qa.e: Palaeontological evidence comes from fossils in rock layers.

qa.q: Fossils of dinosaurs show that
qa.a: some life forms that once existed are now extinct
qa.e: Extinct forms in older layers show that life changed over time.

qa.q: Von Baer's key observation was that
qa.a: embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals
qa.e: This undermined Haeckel's claim that embryos recapitulate ancestral adults.

qa.q: Wings of a butterfly and of a bird are examples of
qa.e: They perform the same function but have different structures and origins.

qa.q: Thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita represent
qa.e: They share the same basic origin but perform different functions.

qa.q: Homologous organs are a result of
qa.e: The same structure diverged to suit different needs.

qa.q: Sweet potato and potato are analogous because
qa.a: sweet potato is a modified root and potato is a modified stem, but both store food
qa.e: Different origins, same storage function: analogy.

qa.q: Which bones are common to the forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human?
qa.a: Humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges
qa.e: Forelimbs of these mammals share the same set of bones, showing homology.

qa.q: Flippers of penguins and dolphins are an example of
qa.e: A bird and a mammal evolved flippers independently for swimming.

qa.q: Convergent evolution occurs when
qa.a: different structures evolve for the same function due to similar habitats
qa.e: Similar environments push unrelated lineages to similar solutions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The eye of an octopus and the eye of a mammal are analogous. Reason (R): They perform the same function but are not anatomically similar in origin.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Similar function with different origins is the definition of analogy.

qa.q: In England, after industrialisation (by 1920), which moths were more common?
qa.e: Dark moths were camouflaged on soot-covered trunks and escaped predators.

qa.q: Lichens are used as indicators of
qa.e: Lichens do not grow in polluted areas.

qa.q: Herbicide-resistant weeds becoming common after heavy herbicide use is an example of
qa.e: Human action selected resistant varieties in a short time.

qa.q: White-winged moths declined in industrial areas because
qa.a: they were easily spotted and eaten by predators on dark trunks
qa.e: Selection by predators removed conspicuous moths.

qa.q: The appearance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria is explained by
qa.a: natural selection of pre-existing resistant variants
qa.e: Resistant mutants survive the antibiotic and multiply.

qa.q: Evolution by natural selection is described by NCERT as
qa.a: a stochastic process based on chance events and chance mutation
qa.e: Evolution depends on chance variation acted on by selection.

qa.q: The collections of moths compared in England were made in the 1850s and in
qa.e: Collections from the 1850s were compared with those from 1920.

qa.q: New breeds of dogs are produced through
qa.e: Breeders select parents with desired traits over generations.

qa.q: Darwin's finches are a classic example of
qa.e: Many finch species with different beaks evolved from one seed-eating ancestor.

qa.q: The original diet of the ancestral Galápagos finch was
qa.e: Altered beaks later allowed insectivorous and vegetarian forms.

qa.q: Placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf are an example of
qa.e: Unrelated lineages (placental and marsupial) evolved similar forms.

qa.q: Adaptive radiation is the evolution of
qa.a: different species in a given area starting from a point and radiating to other habitats
qa.e: Starting from a common ancestor, species spread into different habitats.

qa.q: Australian marsupials evolved
qa.a: from an ancestral stock within the Australian island continent
qa.e: All these marsupials radiated from a common stock in Australia.

qa.q: When more than one adaptive radiation in an isolated area produces similar forms, it is called
qa.e: Similar habitats lead separate radiations to similar forms.

qa.q: The Tasmanian wolf is a
qa.e: It is the marsupial counterpart of the placental wolf.

qa.q: Which feature changed most in Darwin's finches during adaptive radiation?
qa.e: Beaks adapted for seeds, insects and plant food.

qa.q: The two key concepts of Darwinian theory are
qa.e: Darwin proposed common descent with branching, and natural selection as its mechanism.

qa.q: A bacterial cell divides every 30 minutes. With unlimited resources, how many cells will be present after 3 hours, starting from one cell?
qa.e: 3 hours = 6 divisions; 2⁶ = 64.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of Darwin's factual observations?
qa.a: All variations in a population are acquired during life and not inherited
qa.e: Darwin observed that most variations are inherited.

qa.q: Natural selection acts on
qa.a: heritable variation, leading to differential reproduction
qa.e: Only inherited differences pass on, so only they can be selected.

qa.q: Why is there competition among members of a population?
qa.a: Population sizes are limited by limited resources
qa.e: If everyone reproduced maximally, resources would run out, so individuals compete.

qa.q: Theoretically, if every individual reproduced maximally, population size would grow
qa.e: Unlimited reproduction gives exponential growth, as in a bacterial culture.

qa.q: Darwin's novel insight was that
qa.a: heritable variations that make resource use better let some individuals reproduce more
qa.e: Better-adapted variants leave more progeny, shifting the population over time.

qa.q: Natural selection can act only on characteristics that are
qa.e: Selection works on inherited traits; acquired ones are not passed on.

qa.q: Hugo de Vries proposed the mutation theory based on his work on
qa.e: He studied Oenothera lamarckiana, the evening primrose.

qa.q: Saltation refers to
qa.e: de Vries used saltation for sudden, large evolutionary jumps.

qa.q: According to de Vries, mutations are
qa.e: Mutations occur by chance in any direction.

qa.q: Darwin's variations differ from de Vries' mutations in being
qa.e: Darwin described minor heritable variations that accumulate gradually.

qa.q: The scientific name of the evening primrose used by de Vries is
qa.e: de Vries worked on Oenothera lamarckiana.

qa.q: Which two processes are major sources of variation according to population genetics?
qa.e: New alleles arise by mutation; recombination shuffles them into new combinations.

qa.q: For Darwin, evolution was
qa.e: Darwin saw evolution as gradual accumulation of small changes.

qa.q: The formation of new species is called
qa.e: Speciation is the origin of new species; saltation is one proposed mode of it.

qa.q: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the recessive allele is 0.3. What is the frequency of heterozygotes?
If 36 per cent of a population is homozygous recessive (aa), what is the frequency of the dominant allele A?
The Hardy–Weinberg equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1 is the binomial expansion of
qa.e: Squaring (p + q) gives p² + 2pq + q².

qa.q: According to the Hardy–Weinberg principle, in the absence of disturbing factors, allele frequencies
qa.a: remain constant from generation to generation
qa.e: The gene pool stays constant: genetic equilibrium.

qa.q: In a population of 1000 individuals, 90 show the recessive phenotype. Assuming equilibrium, how many are expected to be heterozygous?
If p = 0.8, what is the expected frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype?
The total genes and their alleles in a population make up the
qa.e: The gene pool is the sum of all genes and alleles in the population.

qa.q: A change in allele frequencies in a population is interpreted as
qa.e: Departure from Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium indicates evolutionary change.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the five factors affecting Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?
qa.e: The five factors are gene migration/flow, genetic drift, mutation, recombination and natural selection.

qa.q: When change in allele frequency occurs by chance, it is called
qa.e: Drift is random change in allele frequencies, especially in small populations.

qa.q: When the original drifted population becomes the founders of a new species, it is called
qa.e: NCERT calls this the founder effect.

qa.q: In disruptive selection, more individuals acquire
qa.a: peripheral character values at both ends of the distribution
qa.e: Disruption favours both extremes over the average.

qa.q: Stabilising selection results in
qa.a: more individuals acquiring the mean character value
qa.e: The average phenotype is favoured.

qa.q: When a section of a population migrates repeatedly to another population, causing gene frequency changes, it is called
qa.e: Repeated gene migration is gene flow.

qa.q: A population of insects shows medium body size being eaten most by a predator, while small and large ones survive. This is
qa.e: Both extremes are favoured over the mean.

qa.q: How many factors affect Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, according to NCERT?
qa.e: Gene migration, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection.

qa.q: Lobefins such as the coelacanth evolved into the first
qa.e: Fish with stout fins (lobefins) gave rise to the first amphibians.

qa.q: Reptiles were better adapted to land than amphibians because they
qa.a: lay thick-shelled eggs that do not dry up in the sun
qa.e: Shelled eggs freed reptiles from water for reproduction.

qa.q: Dinosaurs suddenly disappeared from Earth about
qa.e: NCERT gives about 65 mya; the true reason is not known.

qa.q: The first mammals were
qa.e: Their fossils are small-sized and resemble shrews.

qa.q: Jawless fish probably evolved around
qa.e: NCERT dates jawless fish to about 350 mya.

qa.q: The height of Tyrannosaurus rex, the biggest dinosaur according to NCERT, was about
qa.e: It was about 20 feet tall with dagger-like teeth.

qa.q: Pouched mammals of Australia survived because
qa.a: continental drift isolated them, and there was a lack of competition from other mammals
qa.e: Isolation meant no competition, unlike South American mammals overrun by North American fauna.

qa.q: In NCERT's chart of plant evolution, which plants appear most recently?
qa.e: Angiosperms (monocots and dicots) are the most recent; Zosterophyllum and Psilophyton are early vascular plants.

qa.q: The brain capacity of Homo habilis was
qa.e: Homo habilis had a brain of 650–800 cc; Homo erectus about 900 cc; Neanderthal 1400 cc.

qa.q: Which primate, existing about 15 mya, was more man-like?
qa.e: Ramapithecus was more man-like, Dryopithecus more ape-like.

qa.q: Australopithecines are believed to have
qa.a: hunted with stone weapons but essentially eaten fruit
qa.e: NCERT notes they hunted with stone weapons but mainly ate fruit.

qa.q: The first human-like being (hominid) was
qa.e: Homo habilis was called the first human-like being.

qa.q: According to NCERT, Homo habilis probably
qa.e: NCERT states Homo habilis probably did not eat meat; Homo erectus probably did.

qa.q: Australopithecines probably lived about
qa.e: NCERT places them about 2 mya in East African grasslands.

qa.q: Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus existed about
qa.e: They lived about 15 mya.

qa.q: Early man-like primates of eastern Africa (3–4 mya) were probably
qa.a: not taller than 4 feet but walked upright
qa.e: NCERT describes them as short but upright.

qa.q: The brain capacity of Neanderthal man was about
qa.e: Neanderthals had a 1400 cc brain; Homo erectus about 900 cc.

qa.q: Fossils of Homo erectus were discovered in Java in the year
qa.e: Java fossils (1891) revealed Homo erectus, about 1.5 mya.

qa.q: Which human ancestor used hides to protect the body and buried their dead?
qa.e: NCERT describes Neanderthals doing both.

qa.q: Neanderthal man lived between
qa.a: 1,00,000 and 40,000 years ago in the Near East and Central Asia
qa.e: NCERT gives these dates and regions for Neanderthals.

qa.q: Agriculture came around
qa.e: Agriculture started about 10,000 years ago; cave art about 18,000 years ago.

qa.q: Homo sapiens arose in
qa.e: Homo sapiens arose in Africa and moved across continents.

qa.q: Which ancestor probably ate meat, according to NCERT?
qa.e: Homo erectus probably ate meat; Homo habilis probably did not.

qa.q: Pre-historic cave art developed about
qa.e: NCERT dates cave art to about 18,000 years ago.

qa.q: According to NCERT, health is
qa.a: a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
qa.e: Health includes physical, mental and social well-being, not just absence of disease.

qa.q: Who disproved the 'good humor' hypothesis by discovering blood circulation experimentally?
qa.e: Harvey's experiments on circulation and body temperature disproved the humor idea.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-infectious disease?
qa.e: Cancer is not transmitted from person to person, though it is a major cause of death.

qa.q: Pathogens that enter the human gut must be able to
qa.a: survive low stomach pH and resist digestive enzymes
qa.e: Pathogens are adapted to the host environment, including the acidic stomach.

qa.q: Which factor affects health according to NCERT?
qa.a: Life style, including food, water, rest, exercise and habits
qa.e: Genetic disorders, infections and life style affect health.

qa.q: Which group of organisms is NOT listed among human pathogens in NCERT?
qa.a: Green algae used in food supplements
qa.e: Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans and helminths.

qa.q: The early Indian system that held health to be a balance of 'humors' is
qa.e: Like Hippocrates, Ayurveda described health as a balance of humors.

qa.q: Diseases easily transmitted from one person to another are called
qa.e: Infectious diseases spread from one person to another.

qa.q: Typhoid fever is confirmed by the
qa.e: The Widal test is used to confirm typhoid.

qa.q: The common cold is caused by
qa.a: rhinoviruses that infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs
qa.e: Rhinoviruses cause the common cold; pneumonia affects the alveoli.

qa.q: In pneumonia, the
qa.a: alveoli of the lungs get filled with fluid
qa.e: Fluid in alveoli causes severe breathing problems in pneumonia.

qa.q: Which pathogens cause pneumonia in humans?
qa.e: NCERT names these two bacteria as causes of pneumonia.

qa.q: Mary Mallon is remembered as 'Typhoid Mary' because she
qa.a: was a carrier who spread typhoid through the food she cooked
qa.e: She showed no illness herself but spread the bacteria for years.

qa.q: The sustained high fever of typhoid is typically in the range of
qa.e: NCERT describes sustained high fever of 39–40 °C.

qa.q: The common cold usually lasts for
qa.e: Cold symptoms usually last 3–7 days.

qa.q: A healthy person can acquire pneumonia by
qa.a: inhaling droplets from an infected person or sharing glasses and utensils
qa.e: Pneumonia spreads via droplets, aerosols and shared utensils.

qa.q: The infectious form of Plasmodium that enters the human body through a mosquito bite is the
qa.e: Sporozoites are injected by the bite of an infected female Anopheles.

qa.q: The chill and high fever in malaria recur every
qa.e: Haemozoin released at RBC rupture causes fever recurring every 3–4 days.

qa.q: Which species causes malignant malaria?
qa.e: P. falciparum causes the most serious, potentially fatal malaria.

qa.q: The toxic substance responsible for the chill and fever in malaria is
qa.e: Haemozoin is released when infected RBCs rupture.

qa.q: In Plasmodium, fertilisation takes place in the
qa.a: gut of the female Anopheles mosquito
qa.e: Gametocytes fuse in the mosquito gut; sporozoites later move to the salivary glands.

qa.q: In the human body, Plasmodium parasites first multiply in the
qa.e: They multiply in liver cells before attacking RBCs.

qa.q: The vector of malaria is the
qa.e: Female Anopheles transmits Plasmodium; Aedes transmits dengue and chikungunya.

qa.q: How many hosts does Plasmodium need to complete its life cycle?
qa.e: It needs humans and mosquitoes.

qa.q: Elephantiasis is caused by
qa.e: Filarial worms of the genus Wuchereria cause filariasis (elephantiasis).

qa.q: Houseflies spread amoebiasis by acting as
qa.a: mechanical carriers of the parasite from faeces to food
qa.e: Flies physically carry Entamoeba from faeces to food; they do not bite.

qa.q: Which of these is a fungal disease?
qa.e: Ringworm is caused by Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton fungi.

qa.q: Internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage are symptoms of
qa.e: These are typical symptoms of roundworm (Ascaris) infection.

qa.q: Entamoeba histolytica lives in the
qa.e: It is a protozoan parasite of the large intestine.

qa.q: Ringworm fungi thrive in skin folds such as the groin because
qa.a: heat and moisture there help the fungi grow
qa.e: Warm, moist conditions favour fungal growth.

qa.q: A healthy person usually acquires Ascaris infection through
qa.e: Eggs passed in faeces contaminate soil, water and plants.

qa.q: Filariasis usually affects the
qa.a: lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs
qa.e: Filarial worms live for years in lymphatic vessels, causing chronic inflammation and swelling.

qa.q: Gambusia fish are introduced into ponds because they
qa.e: Gambusia eats mosquito larvae, reducing vector populations.

qa.q: Dengue and chikungunya are transmitted by
qa.e: NCERT links dengue and chikungunya to Aedes mosquitoes.

qa.q: The disease completely eradicated through vaccines and immunisation programmes is
qa.e: Smallpox has been eradicated; polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus are largely controlled.

qa.q: Which is a measure of public hygiene?
qa.a: Proper disposal of waste and excreta
qa.e: Public hygiene covers community-level measures like waste disposal and water treatment.

qa.q: To prevent air-borne diseases like pneumonia, one should
qa.a: avoid close contact with infected persons and their belongings
qa.e: Air-borne pathogens spread through droplets and shared items.

qa.q: Which pathogen–disease pair is correct?
qa.e: Microsporum is one of the fungi causing ringworm; the other pairs are mismatched.

qa.q: Regular cleaning of household coolers helps prevent
qa.a: mosquito-borne diseases by removing breeding sites
qa.e: Stagnant water in coolers is a mosquito breeding site.

qa.q: Which advance has helped treat many bacterial infectious diseases effectively?
qa.e: Antibiotics and other drugs have enabled effective treatment of many infections.

qa.q: Interferons are secreted by
qa.a: virus-infected cells, protecting non-infected cells from further viral infection
qa.e: Interferons form the cytokine barrier of innate immunity.

qa.q: Acid in the stomach and tears from the eyes are examples of
qa.e: They prevent microbial growth chemically, so they are physiological barriers.

qa.q: The highly intensified response on a second encounter with the same pathogen is called the
qa.e: Memory from the first encounter makes the secondary response strong and quick.

qa.q: Which is a cellular barrier of innate immunity?
qa.e: NK cells, neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages form the cellular barrier.

qa.q: Innate immunity is described as
qa.e: It is the inborn, general defence.

qa.q: The skin is an example of which type of innate barrier?
qa.e: The skin physically prevents entry of microbes.

qa.q: Acquired immunity is characterised by
qa.e: Acquired immunity targets specific pathogens and remembers them.

qa.q: PMNL in the cellular barrier stands for
qa.e: PMNL-neutrophils are polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes that phagocytose microbes.

qa.q: An antibody molecule is represented as
qa.e: Two heavy (H) and two light (L) chains make H₂L₂.

qa.q: How many peptide chains are present in one antibody molecule?
qa.e: Two heavy plus two light chains.

qa.q: Antibodies are produced by
qa.e: B cells produce antibodies; T cells help them.

qa.q: The response mediated by antibodies in the blood is called the
qa.e: 'Humoral' refers to body fluids such as blood.

qa.q: Graft rejection is mainly due to
qa.e: CMI distinguishes self from non-self and rejects grafts.

qa.q: Which is NOT a type of antibody listed by NCERT?
qa.e: The types named are IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG.

qa.q: Even after tissue matching, a transplant patient takes
qa.a: immunosuppressants all his or her life
qa.e: Immunosuppressants are needed to prevent rejection.

qa.q: The role of T-lymphocytes in antibody production is to
qa.e: T cells do not secrete antibodies but help B cells.

qa.q: Colostrum provides the newborn with
qa.e: Ready-made IgA from the mother gives passive protection.

qa.q: Injection of anti-tetanus serum after a deep wound is an example of
qa.e: Preformed antibodies (antitoxin) give immediate protection.

qa.q: Active immunity differs from passive immunity in that it
qa.a: is produced by the host's own antibodies and is slow to develop
qa.e: In active immunity the body makes its own antibodies, taking time but giving memory.

qa.q: The hepatitis B vaccine is produced using recombinant DNA technology in
qa.e: Antigenic polypeptides are produced in yeast for large-scale vaccine supply.

qa.q: Vaccines protect us because they
qa.a: generate memory B and T cells that respond quickly on later exposure
qa.e: Memory cells overwhelm the real pathogen with a massive antibody response.

qa.q: The foetus receives some antibodies from the mother through the
qa.e: Antibodies crossing the placenta give the foetus passive immunity.

qa.q: A patient bitten by a venomous snake is given
qa.e: Antivenom gives immediate passive protection.

qa.q: A vaccine may contain
qa.a: antigenic proteins of a pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogens
qa.e: These antigens trigger an active immune response with memory.

qa.q: Antibodies produced during allergic reactions are of the type
qa.e: Allergic responses involve IgE antibodies.

qa.q: Histamine and serotonin released during allergy come from
qa.e: Mast cells release these chemicals, causing allergy symptoms.

qa.q: Rheumatoid arthritis is an example of
qa.e: In autoimmunity the body attacks its own cells.

qa.q: Which of these is a primary lymphoid organ?
qa.e: Bone marrow and thymus are primary; the others are secondary.

qa.q: MALT constitutes about what percentage of lymphoid tissue in the human body?
qa.e: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue forms about 50 per cent of lymphoid tissue.

qa.q: The spleen acts mainly as a
qa.a: filter of blood that traps blood-borne microorganisms
qa.e: The spleen filters blood and also stores erythrocytes.

qa.q: Which drugs quickly reduce the symptoms of allergy?
qa.e: These counter the effects of histamine and the allergic response.

qa.q: The thymus
qa.a: is large at birth and keeps reducing in size with age
qa.e: The thymus near the heart shrinks to a small size by puberty.

qa.q: AIDS was first reported in
qa.e: AIDS was first reported in 1981.

qa.q: The enzyme that copies the RNA genome of HIV into DNA is
qa.e: Reverse transcriptase makes viral DNA from RNA.

qa.q: HIV mainly attacks which type of lymphocytes?
qa.e: HIV destroys TH cells, causing progressive immunodeficiency.

qa.q: Which is NOT a route of HIV transmission?
qa.e: HIV spreads only through body fluids, not by casual contact.

qa.q: HIV is a member of the group of viruses called
qa.e: HIV is a retrovirus with an envelope enclosing an RNA genome.

qa.q: Why are macrophages described as an 'HIV factory'?
qa.a: They keep producing virus particles after HIV DNA is incorporated in them
qa.e: Infected macrophages continue to release virus.

qa.q: 'Acquired' in AIDS means that the immunodeficiency
qa.a: develops during the lifetime of the individual and is not congenital
qa.e: AIDS is acquired, not congenital.

qa.q: The genetic material of HIV is
qa.e: HIV has an RNA genome enclosed in an envelope.

qa.q: The widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is
qa.e: ELISA detects HIV antibodies or antigens; Widal is for typhoid.

qa.q: The time lag between HIV infection and the appearance of AIDS symptoms is usually
qa.e: It may vary from a few months to many years, usually 5–10 years.

qa.q: AIDS patients suffer from opportunistic infections because
qa.a: the number of helper T-lymphocytes decreases
qa.e: Fewer TH cells mean the body cannot fight infections it would otherwise overcome.

qa.q: Treatment of AIDS with anti-retroviral drugs is
qa.a: only partially effective, prolonging life but not curing the infection
qa.e: ART drugs control the virus and prolong life, but HIV infection is not cured.

qa.q: Which is an opportunistic pathogen in AIDS patients?
qa.e: NCERT lists Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and parasites like Toxoplasma.

qa.q: NACO stands for
qa.e: NACO educates people and runs HIV prevention programmes in India.

qa.q: Which is a recommended measure to prevent spread of HIV?
qa.a: Ensuring use of only disposable needles and syringes in hospitals
qa.e: HIV spreads through blood and body fluids, so safe needles help; casual contact is safe.

qa.q: During early HIV progression, before severe infections, the patient may suffer
qa.a: bouts of fever, diarrhoea and weight loss
qa.e: NCERT lists fever, diarrhoea and weight loss as TH cells decrease.

qa.q: The property lost by cancer cells that normally stops uncontrolled division is
qa.e: Cancer cells lose contact inhibition and keep dividing.

qa.q: Metastasis refers to
qa.a: spread of cancer cells to distant sites through blood, forming new tumours
qa.e: Metastasis is the most feared property of malignant tumours.

qa.q: Which is a non-ionising radiation that can cause DNA damage leading to cancer?
qa.e: X-rays and gamma rays are ionising; UV is non-ionising but still damages DNA.

qa.q: The major cause of lung cancer identified by NCERT is
qa.e: Tobacco smoke carcinogens are a major cause of lung cancer.

qa.q: MRI detects pathological changes using
qa.a: strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation
qa.e: MRI uses magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation; CT uses X-rays.

qa.q: Cancer patients are given α-interferon because it
qa.a: activates the immune system to help destroy the tumour
qa.e: α-interferon is a biological response modifier used in immunotherapy.

qa.q: Genes in normal cells that can cause cancer when activated under certain conditions are called
qa.e: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that can trigger oncogenic transformation when activated.

qa.q: Leukaemia is detected by
qa.a: blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts
qa.e: Leukaemias are blood cancers diagnosed by blood and marrow cell counts.

qa.q: Heroin is chemically
qa.e: Heroin (smack) is obtained by acetylation of morphine.

qa.q: Cocaine interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter
qa.e: NCERT states cocaine interferes with dopamine transport.

qa.q: Opioids bind to specific receptors present in the
qa.a: central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract
qa.e: Opioid receptors are in the CNS and gut.

qa.q: Nicotine raises blood pressure and heart rate because it
qa.a: stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline
qa.e: Adrenal hormones released by nicotine increase BP and heart rate.

qa.q: Smoking reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood because
qa.a: it increases carbon monoxide, reducing haem-bound oxygen
qa.e: CO binds haemoglobin in place of oxygen.

qa.q: Marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja are obtained from
qa.e: These cannabinoids come from the flower tops, leaves and resin of Cannabis sativa.

qa.q: Which plants are known for hallucinogenic properties?
qa.e: NCERT names these as hallucinogenic plants.

qa.q: Tobacco chewing is associated with an increased risk of
qa.e: Chewing tobacco is linked with cancer of the oral cavity.

qa.q: The period of adolescence is generally considered to be
qa.e: NCERT takes 12–18 years as the adolescence period.

qa.q: Withdrawal syndrome is characterised by
qa.a: anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating when regular intake is stopped
