qa.e: Dependence shows as unpleasant withdrawal symptoms after abrupt discontinuation.

qa.q: Why does a drug user need increasing doses over time?
qa.a: The tolerance level of receptors increases with repeated use
qa.e: Receptors respond only to higher doses, driving greater intake.

qa.q: Chronic use of alcohol is known to damage the
qa.e: Alcohol abuse causes liver cirrhosis and nerve damage.

qa.q: Which is a side effect of anabolic steroid abuse in males, according to NCERT?
qa.a: Reduction in size of the testicles and decreased sperm production
qa.e: NCERT lists reduced testicle size, decreased sperm production and more.

qa.q: People who inject drugs with shared needles are at high risk of
qa.e: Shared needles transmit blood-borne infections.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of NCERT's suggested measures for prevention of drug abuse?
qa.a: Giving in to peer pressure to fit in
qa.e: Avoiding undue peer pressure is a prevention measure.

qa.q: Addiction is described as
qa.a: a psychological attachment to effects like euphoria and a temporary feeling of well-being
qa.e: It is a psychological attachment that drives repeated use.

qa.q: The bacteria that convert milk into curd are commonly called
qa.e: Lactobacillus and other LAB convert milk to curd.

qa.q: Curd is nutritionally better than milk partly because LAB increase its content of
qa.e: LAB increase vitamin B₁₂ in curd.

qa.q: LAB convert milk to curd by
qa.a: producing acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins
qa.e: Lactic acid coagulates the proteins.

qa.q: Which of these is listed by NCERT among microbes?
qa.e: Microbes include protozoa, bacteria, fungi, viruses, viroids and prions.

qa.q: A small amount of curd added to milk to make new curd is called the
qa.e: The starter contains millions of LAB that multiply in the milk.

qa.q: Microbes have been found in thermal vents where the temperature (in °C) may be as high as
qa.e: NCERT mentions geysers with temperatures as high as 100 °C.

qa.q: Visible masses of bacteria or fungi grown on nutrient media are called
qa.e: Colonies are visible to the naked eye and useful in studying microbes.

qa.q: Besides making curd, LAB in our stomach are useful because they
qa.e: LAB play a beneficial role in checking harmful microbes.

qa.q: The large holes in Swiss cheese are due to CO₂ produced by
qa.e: Propionibacterium sharmanii produces large amounts of CO₂ in Swiss cheese.

qa.q: Baker's yeast used to make bread is
qa.e: Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments bread dough.

qa.q: The puffed-up appearance of dosa and idli dough is due to
qa.a: CO₂ produced during fermentation by bacteria
qa.e: Bacterial fermentation produces CO₂, which puffs the dough.

qa.q: Toddy is a traditional drink of some parts of southern India made by fermenting
qa.e: Toddy is fermented palm sap.

qa.q: Roquefort cheese gets its particular flavour from
qa.a: specific fungi grown on it during ripening
qa.e: Fungal growth ripens Roquefort cheese.

qa.q: Which foods are mentioned by NCERT as made by microbial fermentation?
qa.e: Microbes are used to ferment fish, soyabean and bamboo shoots.

qa.q: The gas common to the rising of bread dough and holes in Swiss cheese is
qa.e: Both result from CO₂ produced by microbes.

qa.q: Idli and dosa batter is fermented mainly by
qa.e: NCERT states this dough is fermented by bacteria.

qa.q: Penicillin was named after the mould
qa.e: Fleming named the chemical after Penicillium notatum.

qa.q: The full potential of penicillin as an effective antibiotic was established by
qa.e: Chain and Florey developed it into a usable drug; Fleming discovered it.

qa.q: Which beverage is produced by distillation of fermented broth?
qa.e: Whisky, brandy and rum are distilled; wine and beer are not.

qa.q: Fleming, Chain and Florey were awarded the Nobel Prize in
qa.e: They shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

qa.q: Antibiotics are best defined as
qa.a: chemicals produced by some microbes that kill or retard the growth of other microbes
qa.e: Antibiotics come from microbes and act against other microbes.

qa.q: Which disease does NCERT list as treatable with antibiotics?
qa.e: Antibiotics treat bacterial diseases like plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy.

qa.q: The yeast used to ferment malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol is
qa.e: The same yeast used in baking, called brewer's yeast here, produces ethanol.

qa.q: Fleming observed that Staphylococci could not grow around
qa.a: a mould growing on an unwashed culture plate
qa.e: The mould produced a chemical that inhibited the bacteria.

qa.q: Citric acid is produced commercially by
qa.e: The fungus Aspergillus niger produces citric acid.

qa.q: Statins lower blood cholesterol by
qa.a: competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for cholesterol synthesis
qa.e: Statins from Monascus purpureus are competitive inhibitors of cholesterol synthesis.

qa.q: Cyclosporin A, used in organ-transplant patients, is produced by
qa.e: The fungus Trichoderma polysporum produces cyclosporin A, an immunosuppressant.

qa.q: Streptokinase is used as a
qa.a: clot buster for patients who have had myocardial infarction
qa.e: It removes blood clots from vessels.

qa.q: Bottled fruit juices are clearer than home-made ones because they are treated with
qa.e: These enzymes clarify the juice.

qa.q: Lipases are added to detergent formulations to
qa.e: Lipases break down fats and oils.

qa.q: Butyric acid is produced by
qa.e: Clostridium butylicum is the bacterium for butyric acid.

qa.q: Monascus purpureus, the source of statins, is a
qa.e: NCERT describes Monascus purpureus as a yeast.

qa.q: BOD refers to the amount of oxygen consumed if all the organic matter in
qa.a: one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria
qa.e: This is the NCERT definition of biochemical oxygen demand.

qa.q: Primary treatment of sewage involves
qa.a: physical removal of particles by filtration and sedimentation
qa.e: Primary treatment is purely physical.

qa.q: Flocs in secondary treatment are
qa.a: masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments forming mesh-like structures
qa.e: Flocs consume organic matter and reduce BOD.

qa.q: A sewage sample has BOD of 300 mg/L; after secondary treatment it is 30 mg/L. By what factor has BOD been reduced?
qa.e: 300 ÷ 30 = 10 times lower.

qa.q: The greater the BOD of waste water,
qa.a: the more is its polluting potential
qa.e: High BOD means lots of organic matter, i.e. more pollution.

qa.q: In aeration tanks, air is pumped into the effluent to
qa.a: allow vigorous growth of useful aerobic microbes
qa.e: Aerobic microbes need oxygen to grow and consume organic matter.

qa.q: Settled solids in primary treatment form the
qa.e: Primary sludge settles; the supernatant is the effluent.

qa.q: Why can sewage not be discharged directly into rivers?
qa.a: It contains large amounts of organic matter and pathogenic microbes
qa.e: Raw sewage would pollute rivers and spread disease.

qa.q: Activated sludge is
qa.a: the sediment of bacterial flocs in the settling tank after aeration
qa.e: Flocs settle as activated sludge once BOD is lowered.

qa.q: Gases produced in anaerobic sludge digesters include
qa.a: methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide
qa.e: These gases form biogas.

qa.q: A small part of activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank to
qa.e: The returned sludge seeds the tank with active microbes.

qa.q: The Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan were initiated by the
qa.e: NCERT credits the Ministry of Environment and Forests.

qa.q: The main aim of the Ganga and Yamuna Action Plans is to
qa.a: ensure only treated sewage is discharged into the rivers by building STPs
qa.e: More STPs mean cleaner discharge.

qa.q: The bacteria in anaerobic sludge digesters
qa.a: grow without oxygen and digest the bacteria and fungi in the sludge
qa.e: Anaerobic digestion produces biogas.

qa.q: After secondary treatment, the effluent is generally
qa.a: released into natural water bodies like rivers and streams
qa.e: Treated effluent goes into rivers and streams.

qa.q: Biogas produced from sludge can be used as a source of energy because it is
qa.e: Methane-rich biogas burns, so it can be used as fuel.

qa.q: The predominant gas in biogas is
qa.e: Biogas is mainly methane, with CO₂ and H₂ also present.

qa.q: A common methanogenic bacterium is
qa.e: Methanobacterium produces methane.

qa.q: Methanogens are found in the
qa.a: rumen of cattle and anaerobic sludge
qa.e: They live in anaerobic places rich in cellulose.

qa.q: The depth of the concrete tank in a typical biogas plant is about
qa.e: NCERT describes a concrete tank 10–15 feet deep.

qa.q: The floating cover of a biogas plant
qa.a: keeps rising as gas is produced by microbial activity
qa.e: Gas accumulates under the cover and pushes it up.

qa.q: Biogas technology in India was developed mainly by
qa.e: The Indian Agricultural Research Institute and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission developed it.

qa.q: Methanogens produce methane by growing
qa.e: They break down cellulose without oxygen.

qa.q: Spent slurry from a biogas plant is used as
qa.e: Leftover slurry is nutrient-rich and enriches soil.

qa.q: Ladybirds and dragonflies are useful to control
qa.e: Ladybirds eat aphids; dragonflies eat mosquitoes.

qa.q: Bacillus thuringiensis spores are used to control
qa.e: The toxin kills caterpillars in their gut.

qa.q: Biocontrol refers to
qa.a: using biological methods to control plant diseases and pests
qa.e: Biocontrol uses living organisms instead of toxic chemicals.

qa.q: Organic farmers consider complete eradication of pests undesirable because
qa.a: beneficial predators and parasites depend on them for food or as hosts
qa.e: Without pests, beneficial predatory and parasitic insects cannot survive.

qa.q: The Bt toxin kills insect larvae when it is released in their
qa.e: Larvae ingest spores; the toxin acts in their gut.

qa.q: Which crop grown in India carries Bt toxin genes?
qa.e: Bt-cotton is cultivated in some states of India.

qa.q: Bt spore sprays are used on vulnerable plants such as
qa.e: NCERT names brassicas and fruit trees.

qa.q: A major disadvantage of heavy chemical pesticide use is that it
qa.a: is toxic and harmful to humans, animals and the environment
qa.e: Chemical pesticides pollute soil, water and food.

qa.q: Trichoderma is a
qa.a: free-living fungus used as a biocontrol agent of plant pathogens
qa.e: Trichoderma species are common in root ecosystems and control plant pathogens.

qa.q: Most baculoviruses used as biological control agents belong to the genus
qa.e: NCERT names Nucleopolyhedrovirus.

qa.q: Baculoviruses are suitable for IPM because they
qa.a: are species-specific and do not harm non-target organisms
qa.e: Their narrow spectrum makes them ideal for IPM.

qa.q: Baculoviruses have no negative impact on
qa.a: plants, mammals, birds, fish and non-target insects
qa.e: They act only on specific target insects and arthropods.

qa.q: Trichoderma is very common in
qa.e: It is a free-living fungus in root ecosystems.

qa.q: Which is a benefit of biocontrol over chemical pesticides?
qa.a: It reduces toxic residues and protects beneficial organisms
qa.e: Biocontrol is targeted and environmentally safer.

qa.q: Baculoviruses attack
qa.e: They are pathogens of insects and other arthropods.

qa.q: IPM stands for
qa.e: IPM combines several methods, including biocontrol, to manage pests.

qa.q: Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen in
qa.e: Rhizobium forms a symbiotic association in legume root nodules.

qa.q: Many members of which genus form mycorrhiza?
qa.e: Glomus fungi form mycorrhiza and supply phosphorus.

qa.q: The fungal symbiont in mycorrhiza mainly absorbs which nutrient from soil for the plant?
qa.e: Mycorrhizal fungi absorb phosphorus and pass it to the plant.

qa.q: Which cyanobacteria are important biofertilisers in paddy fields?
qa.e: These autotrophic cyanobacteria fix nitrogen in paddy fields.

qa.q: Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil include
qa.e: Azospirillum and Azotobacter fix nitrogen without a host.

qa.q: Plants with mycorrhiza show
qa.a: resistance to root-borne pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought
qa.e: Mycorrhiza gives several benefits besides phosphorus supply.

qa.q: Biofertilisers are
qa.a: organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil
qa.e: They are living organisms, mainly bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria.

qa.q: Besides fixing nitrogen, blue-green algae
qa.a: add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility
qa.e: They increase soil fertility by adding organic matter.

qa.q: The two core techniques that enabled modern biotechnology are
qa.e: Genetic engineering alters DNA; bioprocess engineering grows the desired cells at scale in sterile conditions.

qa.q: Bioprocess engineering is concerned with
qa.a: maintaining sterile conditions to grow only the desired microbe or cell in large quantities
qa.e: It enables manufacture of products like antibiotics, vaccines and enzymes.

qa.q: A limitation of traditional hybridisation is that it
qa.a: often includes and multiplies undesirable genes along with desired ones
qa.e: Whole genomes mix in hybridisation; genetic engineering transfers only the chosen gene.

qa.q: The definition of biotechnology quoted from EFB refers to the
qa.a: integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof and molecular analogues for products and services
qa.e: The European Federation of Biotechnology gave this broad definition.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of traditional biotechnology?
qa.e: Curd making uses microbes in a traditional way.

qa.q: Asexual reproduction is useful for
qa.e: Asexual reproduction gives genetically identical offspring.

qa.q: Which product is manufactured using bioprocess engineering?
qa.e: Antibiotics, vaccines and enzymes are made by growing microbes in sterile conditions.

qa.q: Genetic engineering changes the phenotype of a host organism by
qa.a: introducing altered genetic material into it
qa.e: Altered DNA introduced into a host changes its traits.

qa.q: The first recombinant DNA was constructed by
qa.a: Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer in 1972
qa.e: They linked an antibiotic-resistance gene to a plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium.

qa.q: The native plasmid used in the first recombinant DNA came from
qa.e: The plasmid was from Salmonella typhimurium; the rDNA was then cloned in E. coli.

qa.q: Plasmids are
qa.e: Plasmids replicate independently of the chromosome.

qa.q: An alien DNA piece multiplies in a host only if it is linked to
qa.e: Ori initiates replication of the linked DNA.

qa.q: The enzyme that joins the ends of cut DNA molecules is
qa.e: Ligase seals the sugar-phosphate backbone between fragments.

qa.q: Cloning in biotechnology means
qa.a: making multiple identical copies of a template DNA
qa.e: DNA cloning copies a DNA sequence many times.

qa.q: Restriction enzymes are called 'molecular scissors' because they
qa.e: They recognise specific sequences and cut DNA there.

qa.q: E. coli was a suitable host for Cohen and Boyer's recombinant DNA because it is
qa.a: closely related to Salmonella, and its DNA polymerase could replicate the plasmid
qa.e: The rDNA replicated in E. coli using the host's DNA polymerase.

qa.q: In EcoRI, the letter 'R' stands for
qa.e: The fourth letter shows the strain of the bacterium.

qa.q: In EcoRI, the Roman numeral 'I' indicates
qa.a: the order in which the enzyme was isolated from that strain
qa.e: 'I' means it was the first enzyme isolated from that strain.

qa.q: Hind II cuts DNA by recognising a specific sequence of how many base pairs?
qa.e: Hind II recognises a six base pair recognition sequence.

qa.q: Endonucleases differ from exonucleases in that they
qa.a: make cuts at specific positions within the DNA
qa.e: Exonucleases act at the ends; endonucleases cut within.

qa.q: How many restriction enzymes have been isolated so far, according to NCERT?
qa.e: More than 900 enzymes from over 230 strains of bacteria.

qa.q: The first two letters after the genus initial in a restriction enzyme name come from the
qa.e: E.g. 'co' in EcoRI stands for coli.

qa.q: Restriction enzymes belong to the larger class of enzymes called
qa.e: They hydrolyse nucleic acids.

qa.q: The two enzymes isolated in 1963 restricted the growth of
qa.e: They restricted phage growth: one methylated DNA and the other cut it.

qa.q: Which of the following is a palindromic sequence?
qa.e: Read 5′→3′, both strands of GAATTC give GAATTC.

qa.q: Sticky ends are formed because restriction enzymes cut
qa.a: a little away from the centre of the palindrome, between the same two bases on both strands
qa.e: The staggered cut leaves single-stranded overhangs.

qa.q: Sticky ends are called 'sticky' because they
qa.a: form hydrogen bonds with complementary cut ends
qa.e: Complementary overhangs pair up, aiding DNA ligase.

qa.q: To join a gene into a vector, both should be cut with
qa.e: The same enzyme gives matching sticky ends.

qa.q: The complementary strand of 5′-AAGCTT-3′, read 5′→3′, is
qa.e: The complement is 3′-TTCGAA-5′, which reads AAGCTT from 5′ to 3′, so the site is palindromic.

qa.q: After EcoRI cuts 5′-GAATTC-3′, the single-stranded overhang on each fragment is
qa.e: EcoRI cuts between G and A, leaving 5′-AATT overhangs.

qa.q: Restriction enzymes cut DNA in the
qa.e: They cut backbone bonds on each strand at specific points.

qa.q: A palindromic DNA sequence is one that
qa.a: reads the same on both strands when read in the same orientation
qa.e: DNA palindromes compare the two strands in the same 5′→3′ direction.

qa.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move towards the
qa.a: anode, because DNA is negatively charged
qa.e: Negatively charged DNA migrates to the positive electrode (anode).

qa.q: The commonly used matrix for DNA electrophoresis, agarose, is obtained from
qa.e: Agarose is a natural polymer from seaweeds.

qa.q: DNA bands stained with ethidium bromide appear under UV light as
qa.e: Ethidium bromide fluoresces orange under UV.

qa.q: In a gel, the fragment that moves farthest from the well is the
qa.e: Smaller fragments pass through the agarose sieve more easily.

qa.q: Elution refers to
qa.a: extracting separated DNA from the gel piece
qa.e: The band is cut out and DNA extracted; this is elution.

qa.q: Agarose gel electrophoresis is used during restriction digestion to
qa.a: check the progression of the digestion
qa.e: The gel shows whether DNA has been cut into expected fragments.

qa.q: Why should gloves be worn when handling ethidium bromide?
qa.a: It is a mutagen that can damage DNA
qa.e: Ethidium bromide intercalates in DNA and is mutagenic, so skin contact must be avoided.

qa.q: DNA fragments separate in agarose gel according to their
qa.e: The gel matrix sieves fragments by size.

qa.q: In blue-white screening, recombinant colonies are
qa.a: colourless (white), because the insert inactivates the β-galactosidase gene
qa.e: Insertional inactivation stops β-galactosidase, so no blue colour forms.

qa.q: In pBR322, foreign DNA inserted at the BamHI site inactivates resistance to
qa.e: The BamHI site lies within tetʳ.

qa.q: The origin of replication in a vector also controls
qa.a: the copy number of the linked DNA
qa.e: Ori starts replication and controls how many copies are made.

qa.q: Selectable markers in a vector help to
qa.a: identify and eliminate non-transformants and allow growth of transformants
qa.e: Markers such as antibiotic-resistance genes allow selection.

qa.q: A vector should preferably have a single recognition site for a restriction enzyme because
qa.a: more sites would generate several fragments and complicate cloning
qa.e: One site allows the vector to open at just one place for the insert.

qa.q: Normal E. coli cells are suitable hosts for vectors with antibiotic-resistance markers because they
qa.a: do not carry resistance to these antibiotics
qa.e: Only cells that receive the vector survive on antibiotic plates.

qa.q: Why was blue-white selection developed as an alternative to antibiotic inactivation?
qa.a: Antibiotic inactivation needs simultaneous plating on two antibiotic plates, which is cumbersome
qa.e: Colour screening identifies recombinants on a single plate.

qa.q: The procedure through which a piece of DNA is introduced into a host bacterium is called
qa.e: Transformation introduces DNA into a host cell.

qa.q: The Ti plasmid used as a plant cloning vector comes from
qa.e: The tumour-inducing plasmid of A. tumefaciens has been disarmed for gene delivery.

qa.q: Bacterial cells are made competent to take up DNA by treating them with
qa.a: a divalent cation such as calcium
qa.e: Ca²⁺ increases DNA entry through pores in the cell wall.

qa.q: During heat shock, cells with rDNA are placed briefly at which temperature (in °C)?
qa.e: The ice → 42 °C → ice sequence helps DNA enter.

qa.q: The gene gun (biolistics) method is particularly suitable for
qa.e: High-velocity DNA-coated gold or tungsten particles are shot into plant cells.

qa.q: In micro-injection, recombinant DNA is injected directly into the
qa.e: Micro-injection delivers rDNA straight into the animal cell nucleus.

qa.q: DNA cannot pass through cell membranes on its own because it is
qa.e: Hydrophilic DNA cannot cross the lipid membrane without help.

qa.q: Retroviruses are used as vectors in animals after they are
qa.a: disarmed so they no longer cause disease
qa.e: Disarmed retroviruses deliver genes without making cells cancerous.

qa.q: The particles used in biolistics are made of
qa.e: Micro-particles of gold or tungsten are coated with DNA.

qa.q: To isolate DNA from fungal cells, the cell wall is broken using
qa.e: Fungal walls contain chitin, digested by chitinase.

qa.q: Purified DNA precipitates out on adding
qa.e: Chilled ethanol makes DNA come out of solution as fine threads.

qa.q: Lysozyme is used in DNA isolation to break open
qa.e: Lysozyme digests the bacterial cell wall.

qa.q: RNA contaminating a DNA preparation is removed by treatment with
qa.e: Ribonuclease digests RNA; DNase would destroy the DNA we want.

qa.q: The fine threads of DNA seen after adding chilled ethanol are collected by
qa.e: Spooling winds up the precipitated DNA threads.

qa.q: Proteins such as histones associated with DNA are removed using
qa.e: Protease digests proteins.

qa.q: Which is the correct first step in recombinant DNA technology?
qa.e: DNA must first be isolated before cutting and ligation.

qa.q: Cellulase is used in DNA isolation from
qa.e: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose.

qa.q: Starting from one DNA molecule, how many copies are made after 5 PCR cycles?
qa.e: Each cycle doubles the DNA: 2⁵ = 32.

qa.q: The thermostable DNA polymerase used in PCR is obtained from
qa.e: Taq polymerase stays active at the high denaturation temperatures.

qa.q: The correct sequence of steps in one PCR cycle is
qa.e: Strands separate, primers bind, then polymerase extends them.

qa.q: Primers used in PCR are
qa.a: small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of DNA
qa.e: Primers bind to template regions and give a starting point for polymerase.

qa.q: Taq polymerase is preferred in PCR because it
qa.a: remains active during high-temperature denaturation of DNA
qa.e: It is thermostable, so it is not destroyed in each cycle.

qa.q: Starting with 3 DNA molecules, how many copies are present after 4 PCR cycles?
In selection of transformants, the ampicillin-resistance gene acts as a
qa.e: Only cells carrying it survive on ampicillin plates.

qa.q: If transformed E. coli are spread on ampicillin agar plates, the cells that grow are
qa.a: only those that have taken up the vector with the ampicillin-resistance gene
qa.e: Untransformed cells die because they lack resistance.

qa.q: Bioreactors process culture volumes of about
qa.e: NCERT gives 100–1000 litres for bioreactors.

qa.q: Separation and purification of a product after biosynthesis is called
qa.e: Downstream processing prepares the product for the market.

qa.q: A stirred-tank bioreactor is usually cylindrical or has a curved base to
qa.a: facilitate mixing of the reactor contents
qa.e: Shape aids even mixing.

qa.q: In a sparged stirred-tank bioreactor,
qa.a: sterile air bubbles are sparged through the culture
qa.e: Sparging bubbles sterile air for oxygen supply.

qa.q: Continuous culture keeps cells in their
qa.a: log/exponential phase, giving larger biomass and higher yields
qa.e: Draining used medium and adding fresh medium maintains active growth.

qa.q: A protein produced when a gene is expressed in a heterologous host is called a
qa.e: Expression in a foreign host gives a recombinant protein.

qa.q: Which is NOT a system of a typical stirred-tank bioreactor?
qa.e: Gel electrophoresis is a lab separation method, not part of a bioreactor.

qa.q: Before a recombinant drug is marketed, it must undergo
qa.a: thorough clinical trials and strict quality control
qa.e: Formulated drugs need clinical trials and quality control.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three options for increasing food production listed by NCERT?
qa.e: The three options are agrochemical, organic and GM crop-based agriculture.

qa.q: The Green Revolution increased food supply mainly due to
qa.a: better management practices and use of agrochemicals
qa.e: Improved varieties helped, but management and agrochemicals were the main factors.

qa.q: GMOs are organisms
qa.a: whose genes have been altered by manipulation
qa.e: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals with altered genes are GMOs.

qa.q: Which is one of the three critical research areas of biotechnology?
qa.a: Providing the best catalyst as an improved organism or pure enzyme
qa.e: The others are optimal conditions and downstream processing.

qa.q: The Green Revolution approximately
qa.e: NCERT states it succeeded in tripling food supply.

qa.q: A limitation of agrochemical-based agriculture for farmers in developing countries is that
qa.e: High cost limits their use; conventional breeding has also reached limits.

qa.q: Which of these is an application of biotechnology?
qa.e: Biotechnology applications include bioremediation, waste treatment and energy production.

qa.q: Downstream processing is needed to
qa.a: purify the protein or organic compound produced
qa.e: It separates and purifies the product.

qa.q: Golden rice is genetically modified to be rich in
qa.e: Golden rice is vitamin A-enriched rice.

qa.q: Making crops tolerant to cold, drought, salt and heat refers to tolerance to
qa.e: These are non-living (abiotic) stresses.

qa.q: Which is a benefit of GM plants mentioned by NCERT?
qa.e: GM has helped reduce post-harvest losses.

qa.q: Increased efficiency of mineral usage by GM plants helps to
qa.a: prevent early exhaustion of soil fertility
qa.e: Efficient mineral use conserves soil fertility.

qa.q: Tailor-made GM plants have been used to supply industries with
qa.e: Plants have been engineered to produce such alternative resources.

qa.q: Pest-resistant GM crops reduce
qa.e: Built-in pest resistance cuts pesticide spraying.

qa.q: Drought tolerance in a GM crop is an example of
qa.e: Drought is an abiotic (physical) stress.

qa.q: The main nutritional purpose of golden rice is to address deficiency of
qa.e: It is enriched with vitamin A.

qa.q: Bt toxin becomes active in the insect gut because of
qa.a: the alkaline pH of the gut, which solubilises the crystals
qa.e: Alkaline pH activates the protoxin.

qa.q: Activated Bt toxin kills the insect by
qa.a: binding to midgut epithelial cells and creating pores, causing swelling and lysis
qa.e: Pores in the gut lining cause cell swelling, lysis and death.

qa.q: The protein encoded by cryIAb controls
qa.e: cryIAb controls corn borer; cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms.

qa.q: Bt toxin does not kill Bacillus thuringiensis itself because
qa.a: it exists in the bacterium as an inactive protoxin
qa.e: The protoxin is activated only in the alkaline insect gut.

qa.q: Which insect groups can be killed by proteins of some Bt strains?
qa.e: Bt proteins target certain insects: lepidopterans, beetles and flies/mosquitoes.

qa.q: Bt toxin genes are called
qa.e: The toxins are coded by cry genes.

qa.q: Proteins encoded by which genes control cotton bollworms?
qa.e: These two cry genes are used against bollworms.

qa.q: Bt crops are described as having a built-in
qa.e: The plant makes its own insecticidal protein.

qa.q: RNA interference involves
qa.a: silencing of a specific mRNA by a complementary dsRNA molecule
qa.e: dsRNA binds to and prevents translation of the target mRNA.

qa.q: The nematode that infects the roots of tobacco plants is
qa.e: Meloidogyne incognita is the root-knot nematode of tobacco.

qa.q: In the RNAi strategy against the nematode, the vector used to introduce genes into tobacco was
qa.e: Agrobacterium vectors delivered the nematode-specific genes.

qa.q: In transgenic tobacco, dsRNA was formed because the introduced genes produced
qa.a: both sense and anti-sense RNA, which are complementary
qa.e: Complementary sense and anti-sense RNAs pair to form dsRNA.

qa.q: The source of complementary RNA in natural RNAi could be
qa.a: RNA viruses or transposons that replicate via an RNA intermediate
qa.e: NCERT names these two sources.

qa.q: RNAi takes place in
qa.a: all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defence
qa.e: RNAi is a eukaryotic defence mechanism.

qa.q: The result of RNAi in transgenic tobacco was that
qa.a: the nematode could not survive in the transgenic host
qa.e: Silencing the nematode's mRNA killed the parasite.

qa.q: RNAi prevents the function of target mRNA by
qa.e: dsRNA binding stops the mRNA from being translated.

qa.q: Human insulin consists of
qa.a: two polypeptide chains, A and B, linked by disulphide bridges
qa.e: Mature insulin has A and B chains; the C peptide is removed.

qa.q: In which year did Eli Lilly prepare human insulin using rDNA technology?
qa.e: Eli Lilly produced human insulin chains in E. coli in 1983.

qa.q: Insulin extracted from cattle and pigs was problematic because
qa.a: some patients developed allergy or other reactions to the foreign protein
qa.e: Foreign protein triggered immune reactions in some patients.

qa.q: The C peptide is
qa.a: an extra stretch in pro-insulin that is removed during maturation
qa.e: Pro-insulin contains the C peptide, which is absent from mature insulin.

qa.q: How many recombinant therapeutics are being marketed in India, according to NCERT?
qa.e: About 30 are approved worldwide; 12 are marketed in India.

qa.q: Chains A and B of recombinant insulin were combined by creating
qa.e: Disulphide bridges link the two chains.

qa.q: Recombinant therapeutics are preferred over products from non-human sources because they
qa.a: do not induce unwanted immunological responses
qa.e: Human-identical proteins avoid immune reactions to foreign proteins.

qa.q: The host used by Eli Lilly for producing insulin chains was
qa.e: The A and B DNA sequences were put into plasmids of E. coli.

qa.q: The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 for
qa.e: A 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency received the first gene therapy.

qa.q: ADA deficiency is caused by
qa.a: deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase
qa.e: Deletion of the ADA gene disables a key immune enzyme.

qa.q: In gene therapy for ADA deficiency, functional ADA cDNA is introduced into lymphocytes using a
qa.e: A retroviral vector carries the gene into lymphocytes.

qa.q: Why do patients treated with ADA gene therapy using lymphocytes need periodic infusions?
qa.a: The engineered lymphocytes are not immortal
qa.e: Engineered lymphocytes die over time, so they must be replaced.

qa.q: A permanent cure for ADA deficiency could be possible if
qa.a: the gene from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages
qa.e: Early embryonic cells give rise to all body cells, including immune cells.

qa.q: Enzyme replacement therapy for ADA deficiency involves
qa.a: giving functional ADA to the patient by injection
qa.e: It supplies the enzyme directly but is not completely curative.

qa.q: Gene therapy is defined as
qa.a: correction of a gene defect by delivering a normal gene into the individual or embryo
qa.e: A normal gene compensates for the non-functional gene.

qa.q: The age of the girl who received the first clinical gene therapy in 1990 was
qa.e: She was a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency.

qa.q: PCR helps in early diagnosis because it
qa.a: amplifies very low concentrations of pathogen nucleic acid
qa.e: Even a few copies of viral DNA or RNA can be multiplied and detected.

qa.q: ELISA is based on the principle of
qa.e: ELISA detects antigens or antibodies through specific binding.

qa.q: A radioactive probe fails to appear on the photographic film for a clone because
qa.a: the clone has a mutated gene that is not complementary to the probe
qa.e: Non-complementary (mutated) DNA does not hybridise, so no signal appears.

qa.q: PCR is routinely used to detect
qa.e: NCERT mentions PCR detection of HIV.

qa.q: A probe used in molecular diagnosis is
qa.a: a single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule
qa.e: The probe hybridises with complementary DNA.

qa.q: ELISA can detect infection by detecting
qa.a: either pathogen antigens or antibodies made against the pathogen
qa.e: Antigen or antibody presence indicates infection.

qa.q: Conventional methods of diagnosis such as serum and urine analysis
qa.e: Molecular methods are needed for early detection.

qa.q: Detection of a hybridised radioactive probe is done by
qa.e: Autoradiography records radioactive signals on film.

qa.q: Over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are
qa.e: Mice are by far the most common transgenic animals.

qa.q: The human protein α-1-antitrypsin produced by transgenic animals is used to treat
qa.e: α-1-antitrypsin is used to treat emphysema.

qa.q: Rosie, the first transgenic cow, produced milk containing
qa.e: Its milk had 2.4 g/L human alpha-lactalbumin.

qa.q: The concentration of human protein in Rosie's milk was (in grams per litre)
qa.e: NCERT states 2.4 grams per litre.

qa.q: Transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of
qa.e: If reliable, they could replace monkeys in vaccine batch testing.

qa.q: Transgenic animals used for toxicity testing carry genes that make them
qa.e: Higher sensitivity gives results in less time.

qa.q: Transgenic animals are those that
qa.a: possess and express an extra (foreign) gene
qa.e: Their DNA has been manipulated to carry a foreign gene.

qa.q: Rosie was produced in the year
qa.e: The first transgenic cow, Rosie, was produced in 1997.

qa.q: GEAC stands for
qa.e: NCERT expands GEAC as Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (renamed Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee in 2010); it decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of GM organisms in India.

qa.q: Biopiracy is
qa.a: the use of bio-resources without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment
qa.e: Biopiracy exploits bio-resources and traditional knowledge unfairly.

qa.q: In 1997, an American company got patent rights on
qa.e: The Basmati patent was obtained through the US Patent and Trademark Office.

qa.q: Attempts were made to patent uses of which Indian traditional herbal products?
qa.e: NCERT names turmeric and neem.

qa.q: How many documented varieties of Basmati are grown in India, according to NCERT?
qa.e: NCERT states 27 documented varieties.

qa.q: Why is GEAC needed?
qa.a: Genetic modification may have unpredictable results when GM organisms are introduced into ecosystems
qa.e: A regulatory body checks the validity and safety of GM research.

qa.q: The 'new' Basmati variety patented in the US was actually derived from
qa.a: Indian farmers' varieties crossed with semi-dwarf varieties
qa.e: It was based on Indian Basmati, claimed as an invention.

qa.q: The Indian Parliament's response to biopiracy concerns includes
qa.a: clearing the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill
qa.e: The amendment addresses patent terms and related issues.

qa.q: Ecology is the study of interactions
qa.a: among organisms and between organisms and their physical environment
qa.e: Ecology covers both biotic and abiotic interactions.

qa.q: Which is the correct sequence of levels of organisation studied in ecology?
qa.e: Organisms form populations, populations form communities, and communities make up biomes.

qa.q: A population is best defined as
qa.a: a group of individuals of a species in a defined area, sharing or competing for resources and potentially interbreeding
qa.e: A population is single-species and area-specific.

qa.q: Which is an example of a population?
qa.a: All teakwood trees in a forest tract
qa.e: One species in a defined area forms a population.

qa.q: Why is population ecology an important area of ecology?
qa.a: It links ecology to population genetics and evolution
qa.e: Natural selection acts on populations, linking ecology and evolution.

qa.q: For asexually reproducing organisms, a population is defined without the condition of
qa.e: Asexual organisms do not interbreed, so that criterion is dropped.

qa.q: Natural selection operates at the level of the
qa.e: Evolution of traits happens in populations.

qa.q: How many levels of biological organisation are dealt with in ecology, according to NCERT?
qa.e: Organisms, populations, communities and biomes.

qa.q: In a pond, there were 20 lotus plants last year; 8 new plants were added by reproduction. What is the birth rate?
qa.e: Birth rate = 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year.

qa.q: In a laboratory population of 40 fruit flies, 4 died in a week. What is the death rate?
qa.e: Death rate = 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week.

qa.q: A population of 250 birds produced 75 young in a breeding season. What is the per capita birth rate?
Which of these is an attribute of a population but not of an individual?
qa.e: An individual is male or female; a population has a sex ratio.

qa.q: A population of 1200 ants had 60 deaths in a day. What is the death rate per ant per day?
Birth and death rates of a population are expressed as
qa.e: Per capita rates allow comparison of populations of different sizes.

qa.q: The sex ratio example given by NCERT is
qa.a: 60 per cent females and 40 per cent males
qa.e: NCERT uses 60% females and 40% males as an example.

qa.q: A pond had 50 frogs; 20 tadpoles matured into frogs in a season and 10 frogs died. What is the per capita birth rate?
qa.e: Birth rate = 20/50 = 0.4; deaths do not enter the birth rate.

qa.q: An urn-shaped age pyramid indicates a
qa.e: Fewer pre-reproductive individuals than reproductive ones means decline.

qa.q: A bell-shaped age pyramid represents a
qa.e: Pre-reproductive and reproductive groups are about equal.

qa.q: The tiger census in Indian national parks is often based on
qa.e: Indirect estimates using pug marks and faecal pellets are used.

qa.q: Why is total number not a meaningful measure when comparing 200 Parthenium plants with one large banyan tree?
qa.a: It underestimates the enormous role of the banyan; per cent cover or biomass is better
qa.e: Size differences make biomass or cover more meaningful.

qa.q: The number of fish caught per trap is an example of
qa.e: Relative densities are good enough for many ecological studies.

qa.q: The three age groups shown in an age pyramid are
qa.e: Age pyramids divide the population by reproductive stage.

qa.q: A triangular age pyramid shows a population that is
qa.e: A broad base of young individuals means growth.

qa.q: Population size is technically called
qa.e: N represents population density.

qa.q: A population has 2000 individuals. In a year there are 200 births, 50 immigrants, 150 deaths and 100 emigrants. What will the population be after one year?
qa.e: (B + I) − (D + E) = 250 − 250 = 0, so the population stays at 2000.

qa.q: In the exponential growth equation dN/dt = rN, 'r' represents
qa.a: the intrinsic rate of natural increase
qa.e: r = b − d, the intrinsic rate of natural increase.

qa.q: A bacterial population of 5000 has r = 0.2 per hour under unlimited resources. What is dN/dt at this moment?
qa.e: dN/dt = rN = 0.2 × 5000 = 1000 per hour.

qa.q: Exponential growth plotted against time gives a
qa.e: Unlimited resources give accelerating, J-shaped growth.

qa.q: According to NCERT, the r value for the Indian human population in 1981 was
qa.e: Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12, India (1981) 0.0205.

qa.q: Which processes increase population density?
qa.e: Births and arrivals add individuals; deaths and departures remove them.

qa.q: If per capita birth rate is 0.25 and death rate is 0.1, what is r?
The integral form of the exponential growth equation is
qa.e: Integrating dN/dt = rN gives Nₜ = N₀ eʳᵗ.

qa.q: For r = 0.1, K = 800 and N = 400, what is dN/dt in the logistic model?
When N equals K in the logistic model, the population growth rate dN/dt is
qa.e: (K − N)/K = 0 when N = K, so growth stops.

qa.q: The logistic growth curve is
qa.e: Logistic growth levels off at carrying capacity.

qa.q: The maximum number of individuals that a habitat's resources can support is called the
qa.e: K is the carrying capacity.

qa.q: Which model of population growth is considered more realistic?
qa.e: Resources for most populations are finite, so logistic growth is more realistic.

qa.q: The correct sequence of phases in logistic growth is
qa.e: The curve starts slow, speeds up, slows down and levels off at K.

qa.q: The Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth equation is
qa.e: The extra factor (K − N)/K slows growth as N approaches K.

qa.q: A population with K = 1000 has N = 100 and r = 0.5. What is dN/dt?
Pacific salmon fish and bamboo are examples of organisms that
qa.a: breed only once in their lifetime
qa.e: They reproduce once and then die.

qa.q: Oysters and pelagic fishes produce
qa.a: a large number of small-sized offspring
qa.e: They follow the many-small-offspring strategy.

qa.q: Reproductive fitness is also called
qa.e: Populations evolve to maximise Darwinian fitness (high r).

qa.q: Birds and mammals generally produce
qa.a: a small number of large-sized offspring
qa.e: They invest more in fewer, larger offspring.

qa.q: Life history traits have evolved in relation to
qa.a: constraints imposed by abiotic and biotic components of the habitat
qa.e: Ecologists link life history traits to habitat constraints.

qa.q: Which organism breeds many times during its lifetime?
qa.e: Most birds and mammals breed many times.

qa.q: Darwinian fitness is associated with a high value of
qa.a: r, the intrinsic rate of natural increase
qa.e: High r means high reproductive success.

qa.q: Organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy under
qa.a: a particular set of selection pressures
qa.e: Selection pressures shape life history traits.

qa.q: Which interaction is represented as (+, 0)?
qa.e: One species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited.

qa.q: The prickly pear cactus in Australia was brought under control by introducing
qa.a: a cactus-feeding moth from its natural habitat
qa.e: A natural predator (moth) controlled the invasive cactus.

qa.q: The monarch butterfly is distasteful to birds because

qa.e: Cardiac glycosides are a chemical defence.

qa.q: Why do host and parasite tend to co-evolve?
qa.a: Many parasites are host-specific, so if the host evolves resistance, the parasite must evolve a counter-mechanism

qa.q: Ticks on dogs are

qa.q: The eggs of brood parasites resemble the host's eggs in size and colour to

qa.q: Endoparasites generally have

qa.q: The relationship between a cattle egret and grazing cattle is an example of

qa.q: The clown fish living among sea anemone tentacles is an example of

qa.q: An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch shows
qa.e: The orchid benefits from support; the mango is not harmed.

qa.q: In mycorrhiza, the plant provides the fungus with
qa.e: The fungus helps nutrient absorption and receives carbohydrates.

qa.q: If the female bee's colour pattern changes during evolution, the Ophrys orchid must
qa.a: co-evolve to maintain its resemblance and pollination success
qa.e: Pollination by deceit depends on close mimicry.

qa.q: Vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels in an ecosystem is called
qa.e: Stratification describes vertical layers like trees, shrubs and herbs.

qa.q: Which of these is a man-made ecosystem?
qa.e: Crop fields and aquaria are man-made ecosystems.

qa.q: The four functions of an ecosystem are
qa.a: productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling
qa.e: These are the basic functional aspects of ecosystems.

qa.q: In a forest, the bottom layer is generally occupied by
qa.e: Trees form the top layer, shrubs the middle and herbs and grasses the bottom.

qa.q: Identification and enumeration of plant and animal species of an ecosystem gives its
qa.e: Listing and counting species gives species composition.

qa.q: Which is an aquatic ecosystem?
qa.e: Ponds, lakes, wetlands, rivers and estuaries are aquatic ecosystems.

qa.q: An ecosystem is best described as
qa.a: a functional unit of nature where organisms interact with each other and with the physical environment
qa.e: Ecosystems include biotic and abiotic components interacting.

qa.q: Many ecologists regard the entire biosphere as
qa.e: The biosphere can be seen as one large ecosystem.

qa.q: In a pond ecosystem, zooplankton are
qa.e: Zooplankton feed on phytoplankton and other matter.

qa.q: Decomposers in a pond such as fungi, bacteria and flagellates are especially abundant
qa.a: at the bottom of the pond
qa.e: Dead matter settles at the bottom where decomposers act.

qa.q: Movement of energy in an ecosystem is
qa.a: unidirectional, towards higher trophic levels, with loss as heat
qa.e: Energy is not recycled; it flows one way and dissipates as heat.

qa.q: Which is an abiotic component of a pond ecosystem?
qa.a: Water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances
qa.e: Abiotic components are non-living.

qa.q: The rate of function of the whole pond is regulated by
qa.a: solar input, temperature cycle, day length and other climatic conditions
qa.e: Climatic factors control pond processes.

qa.q: Floating, submerged and marginal plants in a pond are
qa.e: They photosynthesise, like phytoplankton.

qa.q: Release of nutrients from dead organic matter for reuse by autotrophs in a pond happens through
qa.e: Decomposers return nutrients to the water for producers.

qa.q: A pond is described as a self-sustainable unit because it
qa.a: performs all functions of an ecosystem: production, consumption, decomposition and nutrient return
qa.e: The pond repeatedly converts, consumes and recycles materials, powered by the sun.

qa.q: The relationship between gross and net primary productivity is
qa.e: Net productivity is what remains after plants' respiration.

qa.q: If NPP is 3000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ and respiration losses are 1500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹, what is GPP?
Annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere is approximately (in billion tons, dry weight)
qa.e: About 170 billion tons, of which oceans produce about 55 billion tons.

qa.q: Despite covering about 70 per cent of Earth's surface, oceans produce about how many billion tons of the annual NPP?
qa.e: Oceans produce only about 55 of the 170 billion tons.

qa.q: NPP is the biomass available for
qa.e: Herbivores and decomposers use NPP.

qa.q: Secondary productivity is defined as
qa.a: the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers
qa.e: It measures production at consumer levels.

qa.q: Productivity is expressed in units of
qa.a: g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or (kcal m⁻²) yr⁻¹
qa.e: It is a rate per unit area per unit time.

qa.q: Which factor does NOT affect primary productivity?
qa.a: The number of letters in the plant's scientific name
qa.e: Productivity depends on species, environment, nutrients and photosynthetic capacity.

qa.q: Breaking down of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores like earthworms is called
qa.e: Detritivores physically fragment the detritus.

qa.q: In leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients
qa.a: go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts
qa.e: Leaching moves soluble nutrients downward in the soil.

qa.q: The degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances by bacterial and fungal enzymes is
qa.e: Enzymatic breakdown by microbes is catabolism.

qa.q: Detritus consists of
qa.a: dead plant remains and dead animal remains including faecal matter
qa.e: Detritus is the dead organic matter that decomposers use.

qa.q: Earthworms are called the farmer's friend because they
qa.a: break down organic matter and loosen the soil
qa.e: Their activity improves soil structure and nutrient recycling.

qa.q: The end products of decomposition are
qa.a: inorganic substances like CO₂, water and nutrients
qa.e: Decomposers convert complex organic matter into simple inorganic substances.

qa.q: The steps of decomposition such as fragmentation, leaching and catabolism
qa.e: NCERT notes that these steps operate simultaneously.

qa.q: Which organism is a detritivore?
qa.e: Earthworms feed on detritus and fragment it.

qa.q: Humification leads to the formation of
qa.a: humus, a dark amorphous substance resistant to microbial action
qa.e: Humus forms during humification and decomposes very slowly.

qa.q: Release of inorganic nutrients by microbial degradation of humus is called
qa.e: Mineralisation makes nutrients available again.

qa.q: Decomposition is slower when detritus is rich in
qa.e: Lignin and chitin are tough to break down.

qa.q: Which conditions favour decomposition?
qa.e: Microbes are most active in warm, moist conditions.

qa.q: Humus serves as a reservoir of nutrients because it is
qa.e: Its colloidal nature holds nutrients.

qa.q: The two most important climatic factors that regulate decomposition are
qa.e: They affect the activity of soil microbes.

qa.q: Low temperature and anaerobiosis lead to
qa.a: inhibition of decomposition and build-up of organic material
qa.e: Slower microbial activity allows organic matter to accumulate.

qa.q: Decomposition is largely
qa.e: Most decomposers respire aerobically.

qa.q: Plants capture what percentage of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)?
qa.e: This small fraction sustains the entire living world.

qa.q: The only ecosystems on Earth that do not depend on the sun for energy are
qa.e: All others depend on solar energy.

qa.q: Less than what percentage of incident solar radiation is photosynthetically active?
qa.e: Less than 50 per cent of incident solar radiation is PAR.

qa.q: Ecosystems need a constant supply of energy because of the
qa.a: second law of thermodynamics, i.e. the tendency towards increasing disorderliness
qa.e: Energy is needed to counteract disorder.

qa.q: Animals that feed on herbivores are called
qa.e: They are at the third trophic level.

qa.q: In aquatic ecosystems, primary producers include
qa.e: These photosynthesise in water.

qa.q: Energy flow in an ecosystem is
qa.a: unidirectional, from the sun to producers to consumers
qa.e: Energy does not return to the sun.

qa.q: If plants capture 2 per cent of 600 units of PAR, how many units are captured?

qa.e: Most terrestrial energy passes through dead organic matter and decomposers.

qa.q: The detritus food chain begins with
qa.e: Decomposers feed on detritus.

qa.q: Decomposers are also known as
qa.e: Sapro means to decompose; they absorb nutrients from dead matter.

qa.q: The mass of living material at a trophic level at a particular time is called
qa.e: Standing crop is measured as biomass or number per unit area.

qa.q: Measurement of biomass in terms of which weight is more accurate?
qa.e: Dry weight removes variable water content.

qa.q: Which animals act as omnivores linking detritus and grazing food chains, according to NCERT?
qa.e: Omnivores feed at multiple levels, linking chains into a web.

qa.q: In the food chain grass → goat → man, man is the

qa.q: The interconnection of food chains in nature forms a
qa.e: Interlinked food chains make a food web.

qa.q: If producers fix 10,000 J of energy, how much energy (in J) reaches the secondary carnivores (fourth trophic level) by the 10 per cent law?
qa.e: 10,000 → 1000 (herbivores) → 100 (primary carnivores) → 10 J (secondary carnivores).

qa.q: The 10 per cent law states that
qa.a: only about 10 per cent of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next
qa.e: About 90 per cent is used or lost as heat; 10 per cent passes on.

qa.q: A herbivore population receives 4000 J. How much energy (in J) is available to the carnivores that eat it?
qa.e: 10 per cent of 4000 = 400 J.

qa.q: The number of trophic levels in a grazing food chain is limited because
qa.a: energy decreases sharply at each level, following the 10 per cent law
qa.e: Too little energy remains after a few transfers to support more levels.

qa.q: Secondary consumers receive 60 J. How much energy (in J) did the producers fix in this chain (10 per cent law)?
qa.e: Producers → herbivores → secondary consumers: two transfers, so 60 × 10 × 10 = 6000 J.

qa.q: Most of the energy not transferred to the next trophic level is
qa.a: used in respiration and lost as heat
qa.e: Energy is dissipated mainly as heat.

qa.q: Producers fix 80,000 kJ. How much energy (in kJ) reaches the primary consumers?
qa.e: 10 per cent of 80,000 = 8000 kJ.

qa.q: Which trophic level has the least energy in a food chain grass → deer → tiger?
qa.e: Energy decreases at each level, so the top carnivore has least.

qa.q: The pyramid of biomass in the sea is generally
qa.a: inverted, because the biomass of fishes exceeds that of phytoplankton
qa.e: At a given time, standing fish biomass exceeds phytoplankton biomass.

qa.q: The pyramid of numbers in a tree ecosystem with insects feeding on it is
qa.e: One tree (producer) supports many insects.

qa.q: The base of an ecological pyramid represents the
qa.e: Producers form the base; top consumers form the apex.

qa.q: A sparrow eating seeds and also insects shows that
qa.a: a species can occupy more than one trophic level
qa.e: A trophic level is functional; species may belong to several.

qa.q: In a grassland, the pyramid of numbers is generally
qa.e: Grass plants outnumber herbivores, which outnumber carnivores.

qa.q: Which are the three types of ecological pyramids?
qa.e: These are the three ecological pyramids.

qa.q: In terrestrial ecosystems, the pyramid of biomass is generally
qa.e: Biomass decreases sharply at higher levels on land.

qa.q: Calculations for an ecological pyramid must include
qa.a: all organisms at that trophic level
qa.e: Generalisations fail if only a few individuals are counted.

qa.q: The pyramid of energy is always upright because
qa.a: some energy is always lost as heat at each transfer to the next trophic level
qa.e: Energy decreases at every level, so the pyramid cannot be inverted.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of ecological pyramids?
qa.a: They do not accommodate food webs
qa.e: Pyramids assume simple food chains and ignore saprophytes.

qa.q: Saprophytes in ecological pyramids are
qa.a: not given any place, even though they play a vital role
qa.e: This is one of the limitations.

qa.q: Which pyramid can never be inverted?
qa.e: Energy always decreases upward.

qa.q: In most ecosystems,

qa.e: Producers usually exceed consumers in number, biomass and energy.

qa.q: Ecological pyramids assume
qa.a: a simple food chain, which almost never exists in nature
qa.e: This assumption is a key limitation.

qa.q: Each bar in a pyramid of energy indicates

qa.e: Energy pyramids show energy per trophic level.

qa.q: The Western Ghats having greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats illustrates

qa.q: The three most important levels of biodiversity are
qa.e: These are the levels emphasised in NCERT.

qa.q: The number of mango varieties in India mentioned by NCERT is about

qa.q: According to Robert May, the global species diversity is about

qa.e: Nearly 45,000 plant species and twice as many animal species.

qa.q: According to IUCN (2004), the number of described plant and animal species is slightly more than
qa.e: IUCN (2004) reports slightly more than 1.5 million described species.

qa.q: Species diversity generally
qa.a: decreases from the equator towards the poles

qa.q: According to NCERT, Greenland at 71° N has how many bird species?
qa.e: Colombia ~1,400, New York 105, Greenland 56.

qa.q: Which is NOT a hypothesis for greater biodiversity in the tropics?
qa.e: Frequent glaciations affected temperate regions, not the tropics.

qa.q: The tropics lie in the latitudinal range of
qa.e: The tropics span 23.5° N to 23.5° S.

qa.q: Constant and predictable tropical environments promote
qa.a: niche specialisation, leading to greater species diversity
qa.e: Stable conditions let species specialise.

qa.q: New York at 41° N has how many bird species, according to NCERT?
qa.e: New York has 105 bird species.

qa.e: NCERT gives Z = 1.15 for this continental comparison.

qa.q: Current species extinction rates are estimated to be

qa.q: Which is NOT an effect of biodiversity loss listed by NCERT?

qa.q: The 'sixth extinction' differs from the previous five because

qa.e: Bioprospecting is a legitimate search for useful products.

qa.q: Pollination by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats is an example of a

qa.e: NCERT states more than 25 per cent.

qa.q: Aesthetic pleasures like walking through thick woods are considered

qa.e: Although hotspots cover less than 2 per cent of land, protecting them could cut extinctions by almost 30 per cent.

qa.q: According to NCERT, India has how many national parks?

qa.q: Sacred groves of Meghalaya are found in the

qa.e: It is a key tool to identify threatened species.

qa.q: The Convention on Biological Diversity emerged from the
qa.a: Earth Summit at Rio de Janeiro, 1992
